Ethylene (C2H4)is a typical light hydrocarbon and essential building block. It has been reported that in 2021 the global requirement for C2H4was 220–230 million tons. There are also reports of the oxidative coupling of methane for C2H4production.[5] However, in addition to C2H4formation, the byproducts of acetylene (C2H2)and carbon dioxide (CO2)are also generated.[6] Therefore, the selective removal of the two impurities C2H2and CO2is crucial for the recovery of polymer-grade C2H4from a ternary mixture of C2H2/CO2/C2H4because C2H2can poison the catalyst during C2H4polymerization while CO2reduces the

quality of the polyethylene (PE).[7] Current industrial separation technology mainly adopts multistep purification processes, including chemical adsorption of CO2(with associated huge solvent waste) and catalytic hydrogenation of C2H2(involving the use of noble-metal catalysts at high pressure/temperature),[8] wherein the energy consumption is huge.

Physical adsorption offers a potential solution for energyefficient separation.[9] It is noteworthy that although good separation of binary mixtures, including C2H2/C2H4[10]and C2H2/CO2[11]mixtures, is achieved by using adsorbents under ambient conditions, C2H4purification from CO2and C2H2contained in ternary mixtures presents a great challenge, as there is a lack of physisorbents that can selectively capture CO2/C2H2over C2H4. [12] A possible solution is the application of synergistic sorbent separation technology (SSST), by packing two or more physisorbents together.[13] Nevertheless, exploring the use of a single adsorbent that can exclude C2H4from a ternary mixture is considered most desirable. In addition, addressing the practical problem of determining the arrangement order and weight ratio of the corresponding adsorbents of the SSST also warrants attention.

Porous coordination polymers (PCPs), assembled from an organic linker and inorganic node, are a new type of crystalline material that exhibits significant ability to be tuned in nanopore chemistry for gas separation applications.[9b,14] Generally, in a sieving mechanism, the focus is on the use of differences

[Figure: Scheme 1. Schematic of the trap-and-flow channel crystal that allows shape- and size-dependent kinetic sieving and molecular trapping for highly efficient C2H4purification from a ternary mixture.]

in gas sizes, found in rigid PCPs with narrow apertures—only the molecule with the smaller size is adsorbed, while the molecule with the larger size is excluded.[9c,15] But the competitive host–guest interactions of two or more impurities in such a fitted porous system confound the adsorption equilibrium, especially in a tandem 1D channel. PCPs with framework dynamics are regarded as another platform for multicomponent separation because the corresponding response can enable the material to distinguish small differences within the multicomponent,[16] but the external conditions need to be accurately controlled (e.g., specific temperature, pressure, and gas ratio), and further coadsorption may occur once the pore is opened. Kinetic-dependent molecular diffusion has also been proposed for gas separation by creating sites of local motion in the crystal.[17] However, when the number of components in the gas mixture increases to three or more, special recognition devices are required in the channels.

In this work, we installed a three-bladed trap-and-flow channel in a crystal and were then subsequently able to achieve highly efficient C2H4purification from a ternary mixture that contained CO2and C2H2, even in the presence of moisture, and at a high temperature and wide gas ratio (Scheme 1). The flow channel featuring an optimized window aperture can kinetically distinguish between linear molecules of CO2or C2H2and a butterflylike molecule of C2H4while the trap in another channel allows the efficient capture of adsorbed molecules, as was determined computationally and observed experimentally at molecular level. In addition, the crystal synthesis in boiling alkaline solution offered excellent robustness under hot acid/base conditions.

2. Results and Discussion

2.1. Synthesis and Structural Characterization

The crystal transformation of NTU-65 in alkaline aqueous solution at 100°Cafforded a polyhedral-shaped crystal (NTU-67) (Figure S1, Supporting Information). This is mainly based on the consideration that crystal conversion in an aqueous solution may tailor nanopore in light of the size of the water template and inherit functional sites to a greater extent. Crystal transformation in alkaline aqueous may also reduce the energy state of the generated framework, realizing the assembly of chemically robust structure.[18] Direct synthesis of NTU-67 has also been attempted by tuning conditions and other solvent-triggered crystal conversions, but these attempts were unsuccessful.

Crystal analysis revealed that NTU-67 crystallizes in the space group of R32, where the asymmetric unit includes onehalf Cu2+cation, one-half SiF62-anion, and one L1 ligand, thus giving the same formula (MATH)·xSolvent) with that of NTU-65 (Table S1 and Figure S4, Supporting Information). In NTU-67, each ligand and SiF62-anion was connected by two Cu atoms, respectively, and each Cu2+cation was bridged by two F atoms from two SiF62-ions and four imidazoles (IM) N atoms from four ligands. The two F atoms in the para position of the SiF62-ion join the octahedral coordination of the two adjacent Cu2+cations to establish an inorganic helical chain along the axis. Therefore, the self-catenated square grid sheets formed between Cu2+cations and organic linkers are further connected by this chain to establish a three-dimensional (3D) framework (Figure S5, Supporting Information). Further topology analysis revealed that NTU-67 features a mmo net after subsuming the doubly connected ligands and SiF62-ions into the sixfold-connected Cu nodes, forming a new group of porous isomers with NTU-65 (pcu) (Figure 1a,b; Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Interestingly, two face-shared triangular channels (A and B) were observed in this new framework. Channel B with the narrowest hole of 3.4 Acan be considered a nanochannel for diffusion-promoted kinetic selectivities of CO2/C2H4and C2H2/C2H4. The limited space (MATH)that is regulated by three SiF62-anions and six IMs in Channel A can be regarded as a molecular trap for preferred adsorption. In addition, the arrangement of the molecular trap and nanochannel is trifoliate and interconnected (Figure  1c–j; Figures  S8 and  S9, Supporting Information). Calculated by Platon, the ideal porosity of NTU-67 is 28.4%. The structures and phase purities of the as-synthesized and activated NTU-67 were confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis and Le-Bail analysis (Figures  S10 and S11, Supporting Information). The thermogravimetric analysis collected from 25°Cto 300°Cshowed that the structure of NTU-67 was thermally stable up to 250°C, confirmed by variable temperature PXRD (Figures S12 and S13, Supporting Information).

While the numbers of CO2(13.3) and C2H4(9.5) in one unit cell are slightly higher than calculated numbers (11.5 and 7.4) from adsorption isotherms due to the slightly higher occupancy of CO2and C2H4. Despite these, the current crystallographic analysis remains rational for unveiling the host–guest interactions.

2.5. Crystallographic Study under Mixture

To explore the competitive binding of the gases, we analyzed the crystal structure of NTU-67 exposed to CO2/C2H4(2/8, v/v, 1 bar, 298 K). Of note here is that a mixture of C2H2/C2H4cannot be distinguished by X-ray diffraction measurement. Interestingly, one CO2molecule that interacts with F atoms was found in the molecular trap of channel A, while a unique onedimensional (1D) array of CO2and C2H4was found in channels B (Figure 4). This observation offers support that CO2is more preferentially adsorbed by the molecular trap, even under relative low partial pressure. In addition, 1D molecular array confirms that channel B provides an effective flow channel. This is a rare observation of competitive binding of the gases by a molecule-level crystallographic study.

2.6. Ab Initio Calculation of Functional Aperture of Channels A and B

To determine the origin of the effective molecular sieving for a gas mixture through NTU-67, we performed ab initio

calculations for the size function (where the vdW radius is defined by the electronic density: isovalue 0.002). The molecular sizes of CO2, C2H2, and C2H4are given in Figure 5a–c. The largest pore size (indicated by the red ball in channel A (Figure  5d,e) is only 0.92 Å, which is much smaller than the molecular sizes of CO2, C2H2, and C2H4. Thus, all of these three gases can hardly pass through channel A. This result agrees well with the existence of a separated and isolated space in channel A (Figure 1d). The effective pore size of channel B was estimated on the three different cross sections, namely the center cross-section, the entrance cross-section, and the lower cross-section (Figure 5f–i). The red balls in Figure 5g–i express the vdW radius of a C atom (≈ 1.7 Å )for comparison. A comparison of Figure 5g,h indicates that there is a bottleneck going through channel B; there is a hole at the entrance cross-section of ≈ 3 . 4 Åin size. CO2and C2H2, with molecular sizes 3.40 and 3.68 Å, respectively, can pass through channel B, taking into account fluctuation and deformation of the channel structure. The hole size can be even larger than the molecular size of C2H2, depending on a time-dependent instantaneous channel structure. This means that structural modulation and deformation of the channel structure can play a critical role in molecular flow in NTU-67. In contrast, due to the restricted space, C2H4(molecular size 4.30 Å) passes through channel B with much more difficulty than CO2and C2H2.

Of even greater importance is the following. To pass through channel B, linear molecules such as C2H2and CO2should be aligned in wavy lines, as indicated in Figure  5j. In channel B, linear molecules can pass through only the channel indicated with a red arrow, along which the passable holes of ≈ 3.4 Åexist. Such wavy nanochannels coincide with the 1D molecular array observed in Figure  4b. Because the energetically most stable adsorbed structure of C2H2does not form the wavy line, but rather leads to the zigzag adsorbed structure in channel B (Figures S38 and S39, Supporting Information), the actual adsorption structure of C2H2is determined not only energetically but also dynamically; duplicating upside down the most stable adsorbed structure achieved in the unit cell leads to the zigzag adsorbed structure in channel B. 2.7. Ab Initio Calculation of Functional Molecular Trap

To support the molecular trap scenario discussed above, we performed ab initio calculations for the adsorption energy of C2H2and C2H4. The numbers of bonds formed in channel A–C2H4and channel B·C2H4are higher than the numbers of bonds formed in channel A–C2H2and channel B·C2H2, respectively (Figures S36–S38, Supporting Information). We note that the computationally obtained bond distance is shorter than the experimentally observed bond distance, as the former corresponds to the minimum energy structure calculated at 0Kwhile the latter includes thermal fluctuation and structural disorder at 298 K. We then selected three SiF62-ions and a gas molecule to calculate the adsorption energy because SiF62-ions are the most important and essential adsorption sites (Figures  S40 and S41, Supporting Information). The resulting adsorption energy of C2H2is higher than that of C2H4(in channel A 1.5 times and in channel B 1.25 times). The C2H2-involved bond distance is shorter than the C2H4-involved bond distance, in both channels A and B. The shorter distance

overcomes the order of the numbers of bonds and makes the adsorption energy of C2H2higher than the adsorption energy of C2H4. The faster flow and the higher adsorption energy enable C2H2to locate molecular traps existing in channel A more effectively than C2H4, leading to the sieving separation of C2H4from a C2H2/C2H4mixture. These computational insights are in good agreement with the experimental observations of the isosteric enthalpy and the gas-loaded crystal analysis, as well as with the higher adsorption rates of C2H2compared with C2H4as seen in Figures 2–4.

2.8. Improved Kinetic Selectivity Achieved with a Three-Bladed Array

To validate the collaborative roles of the nanospace, the adsorption kinetics of each gas were evaluated on NTU-67 at 298 K (Figure 6; Figures S42 and S43, Supporting Information). The pressure change indicates that the adsorption rate of CO2is much higher than that of C2H4. The kinetic selectivity of CO2/C2H4is 5.26, while that of C2H2/C2H4is 3.86. For comparison, adsorption kinetics of the gases were also collected in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i, the framework with the same SiF62-ion and a square window aperture. The kinetic selectivities of both CO2/C2H4(3.50) and C2H2/C2H4(2.49) in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i are lower than on NTU-67. The advantages of NTU-67 can be rationalized by the enhanced CO2and C2H2diffusion and molecular trapping by the three-bladed array. As computationally indicated above, the nanochannel allows CO2and C2H2to smoothly flow along channel B, while the molecular trap provides effective trapping sites for them, resulting in the current dynamic sieving in NTU-67. In contrast, because adsorption sites and flow paths exist in the same 1D channel in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i, the adsorbed molecules occupy the limited space in the 1D channel, making it difficult for subsequent molecules to pass through.

2.9. Molecular Trapping Effect

Based on the different trap–guest interactions and size effect, as well as the computational insights supporting them, the effect of molecular trapping was explored under dynamic conditions. Sequential controlled blowing tests on NTU-67 were carried out. At 298 K, adsorption-saturated NTU-67 with C2H2/CO2mixtures (NTU-67@C2H2·CO2)was swept by He flow to remove the loosely adsorbed components. Effluents of

C2H2and CO2were detected after heating the system to 393K(Figure 7a). Negligible amounts of C2H2and CO2were eluted from the bed after changing the sweeping gas of He to C2H4(Figure 7b). Further He sweeping was performed until no more gas was detected. C2H2and CO2, but no C2H4, were detected in the final heating stage, thus confirming the preferred selection of C2H2and CO2compared with C2H4by the molecular trap in NTU-67. In fact, only a small amount of adsorbed C2H4was adsorbed in NTU-67@C2H4that can also be replaced by the C2H2/CO2mixture (Figure 7c,d).

2.10. Breakthrough Separations

Encouraged by the functions of the trap-and-flow channel, the separation ability of NTU-67 to gas mixture was evaluated by breakthrough experiments. With the feed gas of C2H2/C2H4mixtures (MATH), 1/99, v/v), polymer-grade C2 H4 (> 99.95%)elutes out at 8.1 min, while C2H2was captured before the breakpoint at 41.4  min (Figure 8a). When the gas feed changed to CO2/C2H4(5 mL min−1 , 50/50, v/v) (Figure 8b), pure C2H4was also detected at first, while, CO2was absorbed. The retention time for CO2was 37.4 min, confirming the outstanding ability for selective CO2capture from CO2/C2H4mixtures.

In light of these outstanding performances, we next conducted separation experiments with ternary feed gas of C2H2/CO2/C2H4/5 m L m i n-1, 1/9/90, v/v/v, 1 bar), a general industrial mixture from oxidative coupling of methane.[6a] Likewise, NTU-67 selectively captured C2H2and CO2simultaneously, and yielded C2H4(> 99.95%)within 27.0 minin the column outlet at 298 K (Figure 8c). we can rationally infer that the separation ability is based on thermodynamics in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i and SIFSIX-17-Ni, making them be good purifier for C2H4from C2H2contained binary mixture, but not from the ternary mixture of C2H2/CO2/C2H4.

2.11. Stability Evaluation

The adsorbent should own good water stability, which is necessary for practical application.[22] Due to the alkaline solutioninduced crystal conversion, the stability of NTU-67 is strongly expected. After treating the crystals in an acid-based solution (MATH), 7, and 12) at 373 K for 4 days or at 298 K for 120 days, respectively, the crystallinity, morphology, pore volume, and pore size distribution of NTU-67 were analyzed (Figure 9a, Figure S71–S73 and Table S4, Supporting Information). From the PXRD, nearly all peak positions are same with the as-synthesized phase. Meanwhile, we also note the intensity change of some peaks, such as the peak at 13.3°and 24.7°for the samples of NTU-67 (MATH), 373 K, 4 days and pH = 12, 373 K, 4 days). This may be due to the partial change of the exposed crystal plane during high-temperature treatment. In addition, CO2uptakes and pore size distribution of the treated samples are slightly higher or larger than that of the as-synthesized phase, as the generated tiny cracks of the treated crystals, validated by SEM images. In contrast, SIFSIX-2-Cu-i and SIFSIX-17-Ni totally lost their crystallinity after chemical treatment, while UTSA-300 dissolved in all solution immediately at room temperature (Figure S74, Supporting Information). Moreover, after all breakthrough experiments, the NTU-67 also keeps the same diffraction with original peaks. In light of these, a breakthrough experiment of CO2/C2H2/C2H4(1/9/90, v/v/v)with water vapor (relative humidity: 22%) was also conducted. The breakpoints of C2H4and C2H2were same as for the curves with dry feed gas, however, the breakpoint of CO2becomes a little earlier when compared with that of the measurement under dry gas. Further cycle measurements under moisture reveal that same curves were observed, despite it has vapor uptake (Figure  9b and Figure S76, Supporting Information). Keeping the structures and preparation method in mind, this excellent stability should be assigned as a reduction in the framework energy

3. Conclusion

Adsorption-based gas purification from multicomponent mixtures offers a very good opportunity to replace the conventional energy-consuming separation process, the requirements being a porous material having integrated properties of simultaneous adsorption selectivity toward one component, high capacity, and excellent stability. Using the post-synthetic method of crystal transformation in boiling alkaline solution, we achieved these required factors in NTU-67, a new trapand-flow crystal. Crystallographic studies under pure gas and mixed gases validate the positive effect of the molecular trap for C2H2and CO2capture. Further Ab calculations and blowing tests reveal that linear molecules of C2H2and CO2diffuse much faster than the butterfly-like C2H4in flow channel B. In addition, the interchannel window between channels A and B allows the gas to flow into the molecular trap existing in channel A. More interestingly, the three-bladed array of the trap and flow channels promotes the crystal to afford increased kinetic selectivity. This unique and promising architecture allows highly efficient polymer-grade C2H4purification from C2H2/CO2/C2H4mixtures under dynamic condition, even in the presence of moisture, at high temperature and with a wide gas ratio. Meanwhile, it is worthy to note that the robustness of the NTU-67 framework reflects that crystal conversion in hot water or chemical solution is a good choice to establish stable PCPs. Therefore, our findings, specifically, the record C2H4productivity achieved here, coupled with molecular-level insight gained into the trap-and-flow channels, offer an innovative route for the design of advanced physisorbents for further challenging separations.

Shape- and Size-Dependent Kinetic Ethylene Sieving from a Ternary Mixture by a Trap-and-Flow Channel Crystal

Qiubing Dong, Yuhang Huang, Kim Hyeon-Deuk, I-Ya Chang, Jingmeng Wan, Changlin Chen, Jingui Duan,* Wanqin Jin, and Susumu Kitagawa*

Ethylene (C2H4)purification from multicomponent mixtures by physical adsorption presents a great challenge in the chemical industry. This work successfully uses the postsynthetic method of crystal transformation in boiling alkaline solution to synthesize a trap-and-flow channel crystal (namely NTU-67), the flow channel of which provides an effective shape- and sizedependent sieving path for linear molecules such as acetylene (C2H2)and carbon dioxide (CO2), while the adjacent channel possesses customized space for efficient molecular trapping. The three-bladed array of the nanospace enables the crystal to afford a record productivity of C2H4(121.5 mL g−1 , (MATH)from 22/2/24(7/9/90, v/v/v)mixtures in a single adsorption–desorption cycle under humid and dynamic conditions, even at a high temperature of 343 K and wide gas ratio. The molecular-level insight and mechanism of the cooperative role of the trap-and-flow channel, found computationally and observed experimentally, demonstrates a new design philosophy toward extending the application boundaries of porous coordination polymers to further challenging tasks.

1. Introduction

Separations by porous materials is a crucial process in our daily lives as well as in industry.[1] For example, zeolite adsorbents in respirators can increase the oxygen concentration to meet medical standards,[2] while activated carbons are used as typical adsorbents for water purification.[3] However, a most challenging process in industry is the separation of light

Ethylene (C2H4)is a typical light hydrocarbon and essential building block. It has been reported that in 2021 the global requirement for C2H4was 220–230 million tons. There are also reports of the oxidative coupling of methane for C2H4production.[5] However, in addition to C2H4formation, the byproducts of acetylene (C2H2)and carbon dioxide (CO2)are also generated.[6] Therefore, the selective removal of the two impurities C2H2and CO2is crucial for the recovery of polymer-grade C2H4from a ternary mixture of C2H2/CO2/C2H4because C2H2can poison the catalyst during C2H4polymerization while CO2reduces the

quality of the polyethylene (PE).[7] Current industrial separation technology mainly adopts multistep purification processes, including chemical adsorption of CO2(with associated huge solvent waste) and catalytic hydrogenation of C2H2(involving the use of noble-metal catalysts at high pressure/temperature),[8] wherein the energy consumption is huge.

Physical adsorption offers a potential solution for energyefficient separation.[9] It is noteworthy that although good separation of binary mixtures, including C2H2/C2H4[10]and C2H2/CO2[11]mixtures, is achieved by using adsorbents under ambient conditions, C2H4purification from CO2and C2H2contained in ternary mixtures presents a great challenge, as there is a lack of physisorbents that can selectively capture CO2/C2H2over C2H4. [12] A possible solution is the application of synergistic sorbent separation technology (SSST), by packing two or more physisorbents together.[13] Nevertheless, exploring the use of a single adsorbent that can exclude C2H4from a ternary mixture is considered most desirable. In addition, addressing the practical problem of determining the arrangement order and weight ratio of the corresponding adsorbents of the SSST also warrants attention.

Porous coordination polymers (PCPs), assembled from an organic linker and inorganic node, are a new type of crystalline material that exhibits significant ability to be tuned in nanopore chemistry for gas separation applications.[9b,14] Generally, in a sieving mechanism, the focus is on the use of differences

[Figure: Scheme 1. Schematic of the trap-and-flow channel crystal that allows shape- and size-dependent kinetic sieving and molecular trapping for highly efficient C2H4purification from a ternary mixture.]

in gas sizes, found in rigid PCPs with narrow apertures—only the molecule with the smaller size is adsorbed, while the molecule with the larger size is excluded.[9c,15] But the competitive host–guest interactions of two or more impurities in such a fitted porous system confound the adsorption equilibrium, especially in a tandem 1D channel. PCPs with framework dynamics are regarded as another platform for multicomponent separation because the corresponding response can enable the material to distinguish small differences within the multicomponent,[16] but the external conditions need to be accurately controlled (e.g., specific temperature, pressure, and gas ratio), and further coadsorption may occur once the pore is opened. Kinetic-dependent molecular diffusion has also been proposed for gas separation by creating sites of local motion in the crystal.[17] However, when the number of components in the gas mixture increases to three or more, special recognition devices are required in the channels.

In this work, we installed a three-bladed trap-and-flow channel in a crystal and were then subsequently able to achieve highly efficient C2H4purification from a ternary mixture that contained CO2and C2H2, even in the presence of moisture, and at a high temperature and wide gas ratio (Scheme 1). The flow channel featuring an optimized window aperture can kinetically distinguish between linear molecules of CO2or C2H2and a butterflylike molecule of C2H4while the trap in another channel allows the efficient capture of adsorbed molecules, as was determined computationally and observed experimentally at molecular level. In addition, the crystal synthesis in boiling alkaline solution offered excellent robustness under hot acid/base conditions.

2. Results and Discussion

2.1. Synthesis and Structural Characterization

The crystal transformation of NTU-65 in alkaline aqueous solution at 100°Cafforded a polyhedral-shaped crystal (NTU-67) (Figure S1, Supporting Information). This is mainly based on the consideration that crystal conversion in an aqueous solution may tailor nanopore in light of the size of the water template and inherit functional sites to a greater extent. Crystal transformation in alkaline aqueous may also reduce the energy state of the generated framework, realizing the assembly of chemically robust structure.[18] Direct synthesis of NTU-67 has also been attempted by tuning conditions and other solvent-triggered crystal conversions, but these attempts were unsuccessful.

Crystal analysis revealed that NTU-67 crystallizes in the space group of R32, where the asymmetric unit includes onehalf Cu2+cation, one-half SiF62-anion, and one L1 ligand, thus giving the same formula (MATH)·xSolvent) with that of NTU-65 (Table S1 and Figure S4, Supporting Information). In NTU-67, each ligand and SiF62-anion was connected by two Cu atoms, respectively, and each Cu2+cation was bridged by two F atoms from two SiF62-ions and four imidazoles (IM) N atoms from four ligands. The two F atoms in the para position of the SiF62-ion join the octahedral coordination of the two adjacent Cu2+cations to establish an inorganic helical chain along the axis. Therefore, the self-catenated square grid sheets formed between Cu2+cations and organic linkers are further connected by this chain to establish a three-dimensional (3D) framework (Figure S5, Supporting Information). Further topology analysis revealed that NTU-67 features a mmo net after subsuming the doubly connected ligands and SiF62-ions into the sixfold-connected Cu nodes, forming a new group of porous isomers with NTU-65 (pcu) (Figure 1a,b; Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Interestingly, two face-shared triangular channels (A and B) were observed in this new framework. Channel B with the narrowest hole of 3.4 Acan be considered a nanochannel for diffusion-promoted kinetic selectivities of CO2/C2H4and C2H2/C2H4. The limited space (MATH)that is regulated by three SiF62-anions and six IMs in Channel A can be regarded as a molecular trap for preferred adsorption. In addition, the arrangement of the molecular trap and nanochannel is trifoliate and interconnected (Figure  1c–j; Figures  S8 and  S9, Supporting Information). Calculated by Platon, the ideal porosity of NTU-67 is 28.4%. The structures and phase purities of the as-synthesized and activated NTU-67 were confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis and Le-Bail analysis (Figures  S10 and S11, Supporting Information). The thermogravimetric analysis collected from 25°Cto 300°Cshowed that the structure of NTU-67 was thermally stable up to 250°C, confirmed by variable temperature PXRD (Figures S12 and S13, Supporting Information).

2.5. Crystallographic Study under Mixture

To explore the competitive binding of the gases, we analyzed the crystal structure of NTU-67 exposed to CO2/C2H4(2/8, v/v, 1 bar, 298 K). Of note here is that a mixture of C2H2/C2H4cannot be distinguished by X-ray diffraction measurement. Interestingly, one CO2molecule that interacts with F atoms was found in the molecular trap of channel A, while a unique onedimensional (1D) array of CO2and C2H4was found in channels B (Figure 4). This observation offers support that CO2is more preferentially adsorbed by the molecular trap, even under relative low partial pressure. In addition, 1D molecular array confirms that channel B provides an effective flow channel. This is a rare observation of competitive binding of the gases by a molecule-level crystallographic study.

2.6. Ab Initio Calculation of Functional Aperture of Channels A and B

To determine the origin of the effective molecular sieving for a gas mixture through NTU-67, we performed ab initio

calculations for the size function (where the vdW radius is defined by the electronic density: isovalue 0.002). The molecular sizes of CO2, C2H2, and C2H4are given in Figure 5a–c. The largest pore size (indicated by the red ball in channel A (Figure  5d,e) is only 0.92 Å, which is much smaller than the molecular sizes of CO2, C2H2, and C2H4. Thus, all of these three gases can hardly pass through channel A. This result agrees well with the existence of a separated and isolated space in channel A (Figure 1d). The effective pore size of channel B was estimated on the three different cross sections, namely the center cross-section, the entrance cross-section, and the lower cross-section (Figure 5f–i). The red balls in Figure 5g–i express the vdW radius of a C atom (≈ 1.7 Å )for comparison. A comparison of Figure 5g,h indicates that there is a bottleneck going through channel B; there is a hole at the entrance cross-section of ≈ 3 . 4 Åin size. CO2and C2H2, with molecular sizes 3.40 and 3.68 Å, respectively, can pass through channel B, taking into account fluctuation and deformation of the channel structure. The hole size can be even larger than the molecular size of C2H2, depending on a time-dependent instantaneous channel structure. This means that structural modulation and deformation of the channel structure can play a critical role in molecular flow in NTU-67. In contrast, due to the restricted space, C2H4(molecular size 4.30 Å) passes through channel B with much more difficulty than CO2and C2H2.

Of even greater importance is the following. To pass through channel B, linear molecules such as C2H2and CO2should be aligned in wavy lines, as indicated in Figure  5j. In channel B, linear molecules can pass through only the channel indicated with a red arrow, along which the passable holes of ≈ 3.4 Åexist. Such wavy nanochannels coincide with the 1D molecular array observed in Figure  4b. Because the energetically most stable adsorbed structure of C2H2does not form the wavy line, but rather leads to the zigzag adsorbed structure in channel B (Figures S38 and S39, Supporting Information), the actual adsorption structure of C2H2is determined not only energetically but also dynamically; duplicating upside down the most stable adsorbed structure achieved in the unit cell leads to the zigzag adsorbed structure in channel B. 2.7. Ab Initio Calculation of Functional Molecular Trap

To support the molecular trap scenario discussed above, we performed ab initio calculations for the adsorption energy of C2H2and C2H4. The numbers of bonds formed in channel A–C2H4and channel B·C2H4are higher than the numbers of bonds formed in channel A–C2H2and channel B·C2H2, respectively (Figures S36–S38, Supporting Information). We note that the computationally obtained bond distance is shorter than the experimentally observed bond distance, as the former corresponds to the minimum energy structure calculated at 0Kwhile the latter includes thermal fluctuation and structural disorder at 298 K. We then selected three SiF62-ions and a gas molecule to calculate the adsorption energy because SiF62-ions are the most important and essential adsorption sites (Figures  S40 and S41, Supporting Information). The resulting adsorption energy of C2H2is higher than that of C2H4(in channel A 1.5 times and in channel B 1.25 times). The C2H2-involved bond distance is shorter than the C2H4-involved bond distance, in both channels A and B. The shorter distance

overcomes the order of the numbers of bonds and makes the adsorption energy of C2H2higher than the adsorption energy of C2H4. The faster flow and the higher adsorption energy enable C2H2to locate molecular traps existing in channel A more effectively than C2H4, leading to the sieving separation of C2H4from a C2H2/C2H4mixture. These computational insights are in good agreement with the experimental observations of the isosteric enthalpy and the gas-loaded crystal analysis, as well as with the higher adsorption rates of C2H2compared with C2H4as seen in Figures 2–4.

2.8. Improved Kinetic Selectivity Achieved with a Three-Bladed Array

To validate the collaborative roles of the nanospace, the adsorption kinetics of each gas were evaluated on NTU-67 at 298 K (Figure 6; Figures S42 and S43, Supporting Information). The pressure change indicates that the adsorption rate of CO2is much higher than that of C2H4. The kinetic selectivity of CO2/C2H4is 5.26, while that of C2H2/C2H4is 3.86. For comparison, adsorption kinetics of the gases were also collected in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i, the framework with the same SiF62-ion and a square window aperture. The kinetic selectivities of both CO2/C2H4(3.50) and C2H2/C2H4(2.49) in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i are lower than on NTU-67. The advantages of NTU-67 can be rationalized by the enhanced CO2and C2H2diffusion and molecular trapping by the three-bladed array. As computationally indicated above, the nanochannel allows CO2and C2H2to smoothly flow along channel B, while the molecular trap provides effective trapping sites for them, resulting in the current dynamic sieving in NTU-67. In contrast, because adsorption sites and flow paths exist in the same 1D channel in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i, the adsorbed molecules occupy the limited space in the 1D channel, making it difficult for subsequent molecules to pass through.

2.9. Molecular Trapping Effect

Based on the different trap–guest interactions and size effect, as well as the computational insights supporting them, the effect of molecular trapping was explored under dynamic conditions. Sequential controlled blowing tests on NTU-67 were carried out. At 298 K, adsorption-saturated NTU-67 with C2H2/CO2mixtures (NTU-67@C2H2·CO2)was swept by He flow to remove the loosely adsorbed components. Effluents of

C2H2and CO2were detected after heating the system to 393K(Figure 7a). Negligible amounts of C2H2and CO2were eluted from the bed after changing the sweeping gas of He to C2H4(Figure 7b). Further He sweeping was performed until no more gas was detected. C2H2and CO2, but no C2H4, were detected in the final heating stage, thus confirming the preferred selection of C2H2and CO2compared with C2H4by the molecular trap in NTU-67. In fact, only a small amount of adsorbed C2H4was adsorbed in NTU-67@C2H4that can also be replaced by the C2H2/CO2mixture (Figure 7c,d).

2.10. Breakthrough Separations

Encouraged by the functions of the trap-and-flow channel, the separation ability of NTU-67 to gas mixture was evaluated by breakthrough experiments. With the feed gas of C2H2/C2H4mixtures (MATH), 1/99, v/v), polymer-grade C2 H4 (> 99.95%)elutes out at 8.1 min, while C2H2was captured before the breakpoint at 41.4  min (Figure 8a). When the gas feed changed to CO2/C2H4(5 mL min−1 , 50/50, v/v) (Figure 8b), pure C2H4was also detected at first, while, CO2was absorbed. we can rationally infer that the separation ability is based on thermodynamics in SIFSIX-2-Cu-i and SIFSIX-17-Ni, making them be good purifier for C2H4from C2H2contained binary mixture, but not from the ternary mixture of C2H2/CO2/C2H4.

2.11. Stability Evaluation

The adsorbent should own good water stability, which is necessary for practical application.[22] Due to the alkaline solutioninduced crystal conversion, the stability of NTU-67 is strongly expected. After treating the crystals in an acid-based solution (MATH), 7, and 12) at 373 K for 4 days or at 298 K for 120 days, respectively, the crystallinity, morphology, pore volume, and pore size distribution of NTU-67 were analyzed (Figure 9a, Figure S71–S73 and Table S4, Supporting Information). From the PXRD, nearly all peak positions are same with the as-synthesized phase. Meanwhile, we also note the intensity change of some peaks, such as the peak at 13.3°and 24.7°for the samples of NTU-67 (MATH), 373 K, 4 days and pH = 12, 373 K, 4 days). This may be due to the partial change of the exposed crystal plane during high-temperature treatment. In addition, CO2uptakes and pore size distribution of the treated samples are slightly higher or larger than that of the as-synthesized phase, as the generated tiny cracks of the treated crystals, validated by SEM images. In contrast, SIFSIX-2-Cu-i and SIFSIX-17-Ni totally lost their crystallinity after chemical treatment, while UTSA-300 dissolved in all solution immediately at room temperature (Figure S74, Supporting Information). Moreover, after all breakthrough experiments, the NTU-67 also keeps the same diffraction with original peaks. In light of these, a breakthrough experiment of CO2/C2H2/C2H4(1/9/90, v/v/v)with water vapor (relative humidity: 22%) was also conducted. The breakpoints of C2H4and C2H2were same as for the curves with dry feed gas, however, the breakpoint of CO2becomes a little earlier when compared with that of the measurement under dry gas. Further cycle measurements under moisture reveal that same curves were observed, despite it has vapor uptake (Figure  9b and Figure S76, Supporting Information). Keeping the structures and preparation method in mind, this excellent stability should be assigned as a reduction in the framework energy

3. Conclusion

Adsorption-based gas purification from multicomponent mixtures offers a very good opportunity to replace the conventional energy-consuming separation process, the requirements being a porous material having integrated properties of simultaneous adsorption selectivity toward one component, high capacity, and excellent stability. Using the post-synthetic method of crystal transformation in boiling alkaline solution, we achieved these required factors in NTU-67, a new trapand-flow crystal. Crystallographic studies under pure gas and mixed gases validate the positive effect of the molecular trap for C2H2and CO2capture. Further Ab calculations and blowing tests reveal that linear molecules of C2H2and CO2diffuse much faster than the butterfly-like C2H4in flow channel B. In addition, the interchannel window between channels A and B allows the gas to flow into the molecular trap existing in channel A. More interestingly, the three-bladed array of the trap and flow channels promotes the crystal to afford increased kinetic selectivity. This unique and promising architecture allows highly efficient polymer-grade C2H4purification from C2H2/CO2/C2H4mixtures under dynamic condition, even in the presence of moisture, at high temperature and with a wide gas ratio. Meanwhile, it is worthy to note that the robustness of the NTU-67 framework reflects that crystal conversion in hot water or chemical solution is a good choice to establish stable PCPs. Therefore, our findings, specifically, the record C2H4productivity achieved here, coupled with molecular-level insight gained into the trap-and-flow channels, offer an innovative route for the design of advanced physisorbents for further challenging separations.

We propose that the V[TCNE]xmagnet has a disordered, percolating, network of [TCNE]- and that its magnetic couplings are also 3D. Hence, these results provide insight into spin-coupling interactions, suggest a topology for the amorphous room temperature magnets, and the behavior of other organic-based magnets.

By Kevin H. Stone, Peter W. Stephens,* Amber C. McConnell, Endrit Shurdha, Konstantin I. Pokhodnya, and Joel S. Miller*

Organic-based magnets utilize unpaired electrons residing on organic species to form magnetically ordered materials. Unlike traditional atom/ion-based magnets, they enable the controllable modulation and combination of magnetic properties with other technologically important properties (e.g., electrical and optical) via synthetic methodologies pervasive to organic chemistry.[1] Most intriguing are several room temperature magnets, but their understanding and exploitation has been thwarted by their amorphous nature.[2–5] The best studied is V[TCNE]x[tetracyanoethylene (TCNE); (MATH)—a ferrimagnetic semiconductor that magnetically orders above room temperature (Tc~400K).[2,6,7] Its valence and conduction bands are spinpolarized[8] suggestive of multifunctional and ‘‘spintronic’’ applications.[9] However, the paucity of structural information has thwarted elucidation of the spin coupling mechanism, and rational development of enhanced materials. Related magnets known to date are, at most, 2D magnetically coupled with significantly lower Tcs~100K.[10,11] Herein, we describe a new ferrimagnet, Mn(II), which orders with a significant remnant magnetization at a substantially higher temperature (MATH)at ambient pressure and 273 K (0°C)at 14.2 kbar] than any previously structurally characterized TCNE-based magnet.

The M[TCNE]x(MATH), Fe, Co, Fe; ) family of magnets has been extensively studied.[12] While not representative for V[TCNE]x, due to it being amorphous, the structure of Fe[TCNE]2•zCH2Cl2(Tc~100K)possesses corrugated layers of µ4·[TCNE]•-bonded to four Fe(II)ions, and these layers are connected by diamagnetic µ4-[C4(CN)8]2-that is also bonded to four Fe(II)ions, and the compound is, therefore, best described as Fe[TCNE][C4(CN)8]1/2•zCH2Cl2. [10]

TCNE (50 mg; 0.390 mmol)) dissolved in CH2Cl2was added drop wise to a slurry of Mnl2(THF)3[13] (198 mg; 0.377 mmol) in CH2Cl2to form Mn[TCNE]3/2(I3)1/2•zTHFin a Vacuum Atmospheres DriLab. The slurry turned from pink to red to black. After stirring for 2 days, the black precipitate was filtered and washed with dichloromethane. The solid was dried in vacuo for 30 min at room temperature. IR absorptions (KBr): νCN2231 and 2789 cm-1; Raman: ν13- 770 cm-1. This preparation can form 3 additional phases, and details leading to reproducible synthesis have not been established. Insufficient material was available for combustion analysis to determine elemental percentage.

IR spectra were recorded from 400 to 4000 cm-1on a Bruker Tensor 37 spectrometer (± 1 cm-1)as KBr pellets. TGAs were performed at a scan rate of 5°Cmin-1using a TGA 2050 TA instrument located in a DriLab under nitrogen to protect air- and moisture-sensitive samples. Samples were placed in an aluminum pan and heated at 5°C-1under a continuous l 0 m L m i n-1nitrogen flow.

Magnetic susceptibilities were measured in 1000 Oe applied field between 5 and 350Kon a Quantum Design MPMS superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) equipped with a reciprocating sample measurement system, low field option, and continuous low temperature control with enhanced thermometry features, as previously described [24]. Powder samples for magnetic measurements were loaded in gelatin capsules. The DC magnetization temperature dependence was obtained by cooling in zero-field and then data was collected on warming in a 5 Oe field. The remnant magnetization was taken in zero applied field upon warming after cooling in a 5 Oe field.

AC susceptibilities were measured at 10, 100, and 1000 Hz. In addition to correcting for the diamagnetic contribution from the sample holder, the core diamagnetic corrections of - 168 × 10-6emu mol1 were used.

The crystal structures were determined from high-resolution powder diffraction patterns collected at beamline X16C at the National Synchrotron Light Source at Brookhaven National Laboratory at ambient temperature. Samples were sealed in thin-walled glass capillaries of nominal diameter 1.0 mm, which were spun during data collection. A Si(111) double-crystal monochromator selected a highly collimated incident beam of λ ~0.7 AX-rays. Structures were solved and refined using TOPAS-Academic [25], and the structure was visualized with the program VESTA [26].

Prior to structure solution, the composition of Mn[TCNE]3/2(I3)1/2-zTHF was substantially unknown, therefore the structure was attacked via simulated annealing, hypothesizing different ratios of Mn and TCNE. Roughly half of an equivalent of THF was known to be present by thermogravimetric-mass spectrometry, which is consistent with the density of highly disordered solvent in the network channels according to the crystallographic analysis.

These results clarify the behavior of other organic-based magnets. For example, [Fe(TCNE)(NCMe)2][FeCl4]shares a similar (MATH)network with Mn[TCNE] (MATH),

and a comparable TC(100K).[11] Structurally, the difference is that there are no chemical bonds connecting the layers for [Fe(TCNE)(NCMe)2][FeCl4], and the metal ions on adjacent layers are offset such that they are eclipsed in every other layer. However, unlike M[TCNE][C4(CN)8]1/2(MATH), Fe), it exhibits significant FC magnetization and (MATH); thus, its magnetic behavior is comparable to the 3D coupled Mn[TCNE]3/2(I3)1/2. This is attributed to the interlayer exchange of [Fe(TCNE)(NCMe)2]- [FeCl4]being essentially zero, but there is a strong Ising-like anisotropy that allows for the development of 2D long range order within each plane.[21] When cooled in a weak field, the planes will magnetize in a common direction; if cooled in zero field, each plane will be magnetized, but there will be no correlation between adjacent planes. Subsequent application of a field in the ZFC state will not be able to overcome the 2D exchange interaction, explaining the bifurcation of M(T)FCand M(T)ZFC. Likewise, the magnetically ordered phase of [Fe(TCNE)(NCMe)2][FeCl4]exhibits significant hysteresis.

The magnetic properties of Mn[TCNE][C4(CN)8]1/2are very similar to that of [Ru2(O2CMe)4]3[Cr(CN)6]where they were attributed to antiferromagnetic coupling between two interpenetrating ferromagnetic lattices.[22] Both have little differences between the M(T)FCand M(T)ZFCand no (MATH), and their magnetic behaviors can be attributed to a primarily ferro- or ferrimagnetic interaction within sublattices, and the introduction of a weak antiferromagnetic interaction, either exchange or magnetic dipole, between the sublattices, either layered or interpenetrating.[23] The signature of antiferromagnetic ordering is a broad peak in the M(T)ZFCdata that is observed at ~68K(Fig. 4b). In moderate fields (few kOe), the sublattice magnetizations will align leading to a significant magnetization. However, upon removal of the field, the system relaxes to the antiferromagnetic state, suppressing magnetic domain formation, and therefore hysteresis.

Magnetic hysteresis is the basis of magnetic information storage, whereas other technologies, such as ferrite electrical elements, seek to avoid hysteresis. The dramatically different reversibility behavior of the two materials described here suggests targeted synthesis of hybrid structures to achieve a specific functionality.

A new 3D structured organic-based magnet of Mn[TCNE]3/2I3/2-zTHF composition is reported. Mn[TCNE]3/2I3/2has a substantially increased Tccompared to the related 2D magnet, Mn(II), which is also structurally and magnetically characterized here. The structure of Mn(II)leads to strong spin coupling, not only within, but between the layers via direct antiferromagnetic exchange between the S = 5/2 MnIIand the S = 1/2m4-[TCNE]- ions (Fig. 1). These antiferromagnetic couplings lead to magnetic ordering as a ferrimagnet at 171K, more than twice that of the related 2D Mn-based material that increases substantially to 273 K under the application of moderate pressure. In contrast, the related 2D Mn(II)material orders at a substantially lower temperature of 68K.

The structural features present for Mn(II)have been proposed, though not observed, for the amorphous room temperature V[TCNE]xmagnet, whereby it is described by V(II)(1 ≤ γ ≤ 2).[14] In this limiting model, one-third of the TCNEs are S = 0[TCNE]2, as there is no other

counter anion, whereas Mn(II)is charge compensated with all of the TCNEs being S = 1/2 [T C N E]•-. We propose that the V[TCNE]xmagnet has a disordered, percolating, network of [TCNE]- and that its magnetic couplings are also 3D. Hence, these results provide insight into spin-coupling interactions, suggest a topology for the amorphous room temperature magnets, and the behavior of other organic-based magnets.

Mesoporous Metal-Organic Frameworks with Size-tunable Cages: Selective CO2Uptake, Encapsulation of (MATH)Cations for Luminescence, and Column-Chromatographic Dye Separation

Ya-Qian Lan , Hai-Long Jiang , Shun-Li Li , and Qiang Xu *

Emerging as a new class of porous materials in the last two decades, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have been met with great interest owing to their tunable structures and porosities and a wide range of potential applications as functional materials. [1,2] A key feature in MOFs is the porosity, which plays a crucial role in the functional properties, typically in gas/liquid sorption and separation and transport of catalytic substrates/ products. [1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. To the best of our knowledge, only Schröder, Zhou, and Lin’s groups have constructed a series of mesoporous Cu-/Zn-MOFs with fi xed framework topology but varied pore sizes by systematically varying the length of the bridged ligands, where they have concerned the high gas uptake capabilities or catalytic enantioselectivities, while no selective gas sorption behavior was found for these pore size-tailored MOFs. [7]

Global warming caused by rapid accumulation of CO2, the predominant greenhouse gas, is emerging as a challenging environmental issue. Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. [8] It is imperative to develop an alternative strategy to effectively remove CO2with low cost and low energy consumption. Currently, MOFs are promising and being intensively investigated to address this

challenge because their pore characteristics can be rationally adjusted for specifi c CO2selective adsorption [9] and the alkyl ether fragment involved in the MOF framework was demonstrated to be benefi cial to selective CO2uptake. [9f ]

In this work, we present a series of mesoporous MOFs with retained framework topology but tailored pore sizes, all of which exhibit high and selective CO2/N2adsorption as expected, by elaborate ligand design with fl exible C–O–C bonds and successful controlling of interpenetration. Moreover, the MOF can serve as a host for encapsulating extra-framework lanthanide cations to exhibit mono- or bi-modal luminescence. In addition, by making use of the merits of the mesoporous pores, the MOFs are demonstrated to be useful for column-chromatographic separation for large dye molecules.

Currently, a number of MOF nets are found to be analogous to those of inorganic materials, for example, the MOFs with classical topologies of diamond, NbO, fl uorite, PtS and corundum, etc. [10,11] Among them, the (4,6)-connected MOFs, whose structural interpenetration is diffi cult because of the intrinsical structural features of corundum, are rarely reported. [11] Therefore, it is likely to obtain corundum analogues having large pore sizes without interpenetration. Bearing this in mind, we have designed a series of tetratopic ligands with alterable lengths (namely, H4L1, H4L2and H4L3, Figure 1 ) for the fi rst time. We combined them with a typical six-connected secondary building unit (SBU), Zn4O(CO2)6, which is readily available under solvothermal conditions based on previous results. [1a] The reaction with these ligands and Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oin DMF or DEF/NMP under similar solvothermal conditions afforded three mesoporous MOFs, Zn4O(L)1.5(MATH)), with the same (4,6)-connected corundum-type frameworks and hierachical pore sizes, based on single crystal X-ray structural and elemental analyses. [12]

All three MOFs are isostructural and crystallize in the trigonal space group R -3c. The asymmetric unit contains unique Zn1 and Zn2 atoms having 1/3 and 1 occupancy factors, respectively, a central oxygen with 1/3 occupancy factor and a half L ligand. The Zn2 is coordinated to three same oxygens from carboxylates and one central oxygen, whereas Zn1 atom coordinates to three oxygens from three carboxylates and one central oxygen. The central oxygen atom connects with one Zn1 and three Zn2 atoms to form a Zn4Ocluster, which is coordinated by six ligands to be a 6-connected node. Each tetratopic ligand connects with four Zn4Oclusters, where each carboxylic group binds to one cluster. Such connectivity leads to an extended 3D highly porous framework with ideal (4,6)-connected corundum topology ( Figure 2 a). The resultant non-interpenetrated MOFs

Motivated by the existing large cages, crystals of 3 have been employed as column-chromatographic fi ller for separation of large dye molecules based on the size-exclusion effect, further favoring the structural integrity of the mesoporous framework in solution. Dye molecules with different sizes have been selected for experiments and results clearly showed that a dye with a size smaller than that of a MOF pore can be incorporated whereas larger dyes were excluded ( Figure 5 , top left). In conclusion, a series of mesoporous MOFs with rare corundum topology and tunable cage sizes has been rationally constructed by classical Zn4Oclusters and pre-designed sizeextendable tetratopic ligands. They all exhibit high and selective CO2/N2uptake under ambient conditions and the CO2uptake capability increases with larger cage sizes. Preliminary studies for lanthanide(III) cation encapsulation have indicated that the MOFs could potentially serve as barcoded luminescent materials. [1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. [7]

Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. [1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. [7]

[1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. [7]

Global warming caused by rapid accumulation of CO2, the predominant greenhouse gas, is emerging as a challenging environmental issue. Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. [1,2] A key feature in MOFs is the porosity, which plays a crucial role in the functional properties, typically in gas/liquid sorption and separation and transport of catalytic substrates/ products. [1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. To the best of our knowledge, only Schröder, Zhou, and Lin’s groups have constructed a series of mesoporous Cu-/Zn-MOFs with fi xed framework topology but varied pore sizes by systematically varying the length of the bridged ligands, where they have concerned the high gas uptake capabilities or catalytic enantioselectivities, while no selective gas sorption behavior was found for these pore size-tailored MOFs. [7]

Global warming caused by rapid accumulation of CO2, the predominant greenhouse gas, is emerging as a challenging environmental issue. Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. [8] It is imperative to develop an alternative strategy to effectively remove CO2with low cost and low energy consumption. Currently, MOFs are promising and being intensively investigated to address this

In addition, by making use of the merits of the mesoporous pores, the MOFs are demonstrated to be useful for column-chromatographic separation for large dye molecules.

Bearing this in mind, we have designed a series of tetratopic ligands with alterable lengths (namely, H4L1, H4L2and H4L3, Figure 1 ) for the fi rst time. We combined them with a typical six-connected secondary building unit (SBU), Zn4O(CO2)6, which is readily available under solvothermal conditions based on previous results. [1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. To the best of our knowledge, only Schröder, Zhou, and Lin’s groups have constructed a series of mesoporous Cu-/Zn-MOFs with fi xed framework topology but varied pore sizes by systematically varying the length of the bridged ligands, where they have concerned the high gas uptake capabilities or catalytic enantioselectivities, while no selective gas sorption behavior was found for these pore size-tailored MOFs. [7]

Global warming caused by rapid accumulation of CO2, the predominant greenhouse gas, is emerging as a challenging environmental issue. Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. [8] It is imperative to develop an alternative strategy to effectively remove CO2with low cost and low energy consumption. Currently, MOFs are promising and being intensively investigated to address this

In addition, by making use of the merits of the mesoporous pores, the MOFs are demonstrated to be useful for column-chromatographic separation for large dye molecules.

[1,3] The MOFs with tunable pore sizes ranging from non-pores to mesopores are regarded to bridge the gap between zeolites and mesoporous silica. [4] In recent years much effort has been dedicated to develop MOFs with large and tunable pores, and there are a few mesoporous MOFs reported with various synthetic strategies. [1e,5] Increasing the length of bridging ligands has been adopted as a main strategy, but reduced porosity imposed by interpenetration is nevertheless almost unavoidable. [6] Because of these diffi culties it has been rarely reported to obtain a series of mesoporous MOFs that retain both structure and tunable mesopores upon suppressed interpenetration. [7]

Conventional technology for CO2removal usually requires high energy with environmental issues and physical adsorption of CO2on activated carbon or zeolites is feasible while their regeneration is very costly. Magnetodielectric (MD) materials, defined as materials for which the dielectric properties can be controlled by an applied magnetic field,[1] have attracted much attention because of their potential applications in a new generation of devices.[2] From the viewpoint of practical application, ideal magnetodielectric materials should simultaneously possess a giant magnetodielectric response, a low operating magnetic field, and a roomtemperature (or higher) operating temperature. However, such materials are extremely rare because a giant magnetodielectric response upon the application of an external field often requires strong coupling between spins and electric dipoles.[2]

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are regarded as promising candidates for multiferroics owing to their structural diversity and amenability to design. By selecting proper bridge ligands to connect the neighboring spin carriers and polarizable guest molecules to fill in the pore of the MOFs, chemists have successfully prepared some MOF-based multiferroic materials.[3–7] However, the magnetodielectric response in these

tric materials will be obtained based on the electron hopping between the transition metal ions in the MOFs. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are regarded as promising candidates for multiferroics owing to their structural diversity and amenability to design. tric materials will be obtained based on the electron hopping between the transition metal ions in the MOFs. Magnetodielectric (MD) materials, defined as materials for which the dielectric properties can be controlled by an applied magnetic field,[1] have attracted much attention because of their potential applications in a new generation of devices.[2] From the viewpoint of practical application, ideal magnetodielectric materials should simultaneously possess a giant magnetodielectric response, a low operating magnetic field, and a roomtemperature (or higher) operating temperature. However, such materials are extremely rare because a giant magnetodielectric response upon the application of an external field often requires strong coupling between spins and electric dipoles.[2]

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are regarded as promising candidates for multiferroics owing to their structural diversity and amenability to design. By selecting proper bridge ligands to connect the neighboring spin carriers and polarizable guest molecules to fill in the pore of the MOFs, chemists have successfully prepared some MOF-based multiferroic materials.[3–7] However, the magnetodielectric response in these

tric materials will be obtained based on the electron hopping between the transition metal ions in the MOFs. In summary, we have reported the first example of a MOF that displays a giant room-temperature magnetodielectric response under a small applied field. Design of Frameworks with Mixed Triangular and Octahedral Building Blocks Exemplified by the Structure of [Zn4O(TCA)2]Having the Pyrite Topology **

Hee K. Chae, Jaheon Kim, Olaf Delgado Friedrichs, Michael OKeeffe, and Omar M. Yaghi*

A prerequisite to the design of crystalline materials is the knowledge of the possible structures that potentially may form by linking together specific molecular shapes. In this context, we recently argued that, from the large number of possible structures that could in principle be assembled from various molecular shapes, those with the highest symmetry are most likely to form in practice. Thus it is particularly important to identify these special structures since they represent the default structures for the assembly of shapes.[1]

This approach has been useful in the chemistry of extended metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) in which 3D structures assembled entirely from triangles,[2] squares,[3] tetrahedra,[4] or octahedra[5] usually form structures based on the SrSi2, NbO, diamond and primitive cubic nets, respectively. Indeed, these have the highest possible symmetry for their respective building block shapes and have become as important to crystal designers as the Platonic solids are to molecular chemists. Herein we point out that the FeS2(pyrite) net found in [Zn4O(TCA)2]·(DMF)3(H2O)3(hereafter MOF-150; (MATH)-Tricarboxytriphenylamine, (MATH)-dimethylforamide), is the most regular net (and the most likely to form) for linking together triangles and octahedra and that it has some additional net properties that lead to its classification as a default net.

We use TCA and [Zn4O(CO2)6]as secondary building units (SBUs) (Figure 1 a) to provide three- and six-coordinated vertices, respectively. The SBUs are produced by employing previously determined reaction parameters to

The structure consists of two identical interpenetrating nets, one of which is shown in Figure 1 b. In this structure, the basic zinc acetate octahedral SBUs, each composed of four ZnO4tetrahedra sharing a common corner, are linked by the tritopic TCA to form a 6,3-coordinated net shown in stylized form in Figure 1 c. The two interpenetrating frameworks are depicted in Figure 1 d. The underlying 6,3-coordinated framework has symmetry , and the two interpenetrating frameworks have symmetry Ia3¯ (as found in the crystal, Figure 1 d). The topology of each framework is related to the structure of the pyrite form of FeS2; it has the same topology if the SS bonding in pyrite is ignored, so we call it the pyrite net.[7] It has been observed, not interpenetrating, in a [Hg (T P T)3]3+(MATH)i(4-pyridyl)-1,3,5-triazine) framework.[8] A cyanide with the pyrite topology (but now with the SS link included) was also reported, again not interpenetrating.[9] We believe MOF-150 is the first example of a fully catenated structure (one in which all rings of one net are mechanically linked to rings of the other and vice versa) with mixed

coordination. Interpenetration of nets of mixed coordination is well known,[3g, 10] but they are never fully catenated.

Three DMF and three water molecules per formula unit fill the space remaining after interpenetration in the crystal. This space is calculated to be 52%of the crystal volume and it is in the form of small capsules of 7 - 8 Ådiameter that are interconnected by 4 Åopenings. The solvent guests can be removed from the pores in air: A sample (18.526 mg)heated at 10°Cmin-1in air from 30 to 700°Cshowed a weight loss (20.9%)step at 240°Ccorresponding to the loss of all guests (MATH)calcd for three DMF and three H2Omolecules per unit formula).

MOF-150 is important both in its intrinsic net properties and in the fact that it led to the identification of the pyrite net as the default structure for the assembly of triangles and octahedra. It is instructive to discuss the topology of the net in terms of tilings of space.[11] Figure 1 e shows space-filling tiles (cages) that underlie the pyrite net. The tiling is composed of trihedral tiles (green) and hexahedral tiles (red) in the ratio 2:1 and the vertices and edges of the tiling are the vertices and edges of the pyrite net. The tiling is an example of a natural tiling in that all the rings of the net are faces of the tiles and vice versa.[12] Tilings are characterized by a transitivity pqrs which signifies that there are kinds of vertex, kinds of edge, kinds of face (ring), and kinds of tile.[13] The simple cubic network, which is derived from a tiling of space with congruent cubes, is an example of a net with transitivity 1111 (all vertices, edges, faces and tiles related by symmetry). The most regular net with two kinds of vertex is that of the fluorite (CaF2)structure which has transitivity 2111; we believe that it is the only net in this class.[12]

The next most regular tilings with two kinds of vertex have transitivity 2112 and pyrite is a member of this very small class. The dual structure is obtained by placing new vertices inside the original tiles and allowing new edges to connect these new vertices in the interior of adjacent tiles. It should be clear that a net and its dual are fully catenated, and that for a net with transitivity pqrs, the dual has transitivity srqp. For a net to be self-dual the transitivity must be palindromic; and indeed the pyrite net is self-dual.

The pyrite net has other interesting properties that it shares only with the diamond net. All the rings are 6-rings and all are related by symmetry. There are two 6-rings per vertex and the average coordination number is four.

It is our thesis that unless specific information in the form of low-symmetry features of the SBU is provided, the default net will form for a given connectivity and indeed this is overwhelmingly the case.[1] Thus it might be expected that for 6,3-coordination the pyrite net would be the default net. However most framework materials with this connectivity reported to date have the rutile topology and in fact this was identified as the default structure,[1] but rutile is significantly less symmetric than pyrite having two kinds of edge and three kinds of ring (transitivity 2232). Most of the rutile-structured materials reported have been cyanides with interpenetrating, partly catenated, frameworks such as [C(CN)3]2\;[10, 14] in some instances the three-coordinated vertex has more than one kind of link as in compounds with a [N(CN)2]2\framework, so the appearance of a less-symmetrical network

is less surprising in this instance.[15] The occurrence of the rutile net in bis(isonicotinate) Fe(II)is understandable on the same grounds.[16] We also note that in the case of MOF-150, the “octahedral” SBU actually has tetrahedral symmetry with the planes of opposite carboxylate groups at 90°. However, as can be seen from Figure 1 c, opposite triangular groups have to be coplanar. TCA is flexible enough to provide the twist angle of 45°needed between the carboxylates and triangles. With less-flexible linkers we might expect to find other, less-symmetrical nets; we are exploring this possibility.

The next most regular tilings with two kinds of vertex have transitivity 2112 and pyrite is a member of this very small class. The dual structure is obtained by placing new vertices inside the original tiles and allowing new edges to connect these new vertices in the interior of adjacent tiles. It should be clear that a net and its dual are fully catenated, and that for a net with transitivity pqrs, the dual has transitivity srqp. For a net to be self-dual the transitivity must be palindromic; and indeed the pyrite net is self-dual.

The pyrite net has other interesting properties that it shares only with the diamond net. All the rings are 6-rings and all are related by symmetry. There are two 6-rings per vertex and the average coordination number is four.

It is our thesis that unless specific information in the form of low-symmetry features of the SBU is provided, the default net will form for a given connectivity and indeed this is overwhelmingly the case.[1] Thus it might be expected that for 6,3-coordination the pyrite net would be the default net. However most framework materials with this connectivity reported to date have the rutile topology and in fact this was identified as the default structure,[1] but rutile is significantly less symmetric than pyrite having two kinds of edge and three kinds of ring (transitivity 2232). Most of the rutile-structured materials reported have been cyanides with interpenetrating, partly catenated, frameworks such as [C(CN)3]2\;[10, 14] in some instances the three-coordinated vertex has more than one kind of link as in compounds with a [N(CN)2]2\framework, so the appearance of a less-symmetrical network

is less surprising in this instance.[15] The occurrence of the rutile net in bis(isonicotinate) Fe(II)is understandable on the same grounds.[16] We also note that in the case of MOF-150, the “octahedral” SBU actually has tetrahedral symmetry with the planes of opposite carboxylate groups at 90°. However, as can be seen from Figure 1 c, opposite triangular groups have to be coplanar. TCA is flexible enough to provide the twist angle of 45°needed between the carboxylates and triangles. With less-flexible linkers we might expect to find other, less-symmetrical nets; we are exploring this possibility.

The next most regular tilings with two kinds of vertex have transitivity 2112 and pyrite is a member of this very small class. The dual structure is obtained by placing new vertices inside the original tiles and allowing new edges to connect these new vertices in the interior of adjacent tiles. It should be clear that a net and its dual are fully catenated, and that for a net with transitivity pqrs, the dual has transitivity srqp. For a net to be self-dual the transitivity must be palindromic; and indeed the pyrite net is self-dual.

The pyrite net has other interesting properties that it shares only with the diamond net. All the rings are 6-rings and all are related by symmetry. There are two 6-rings per vertex and the average coordination number is four.

It is our thesis that unless specific information in the form of low-symmetry features of the SBU is provided, the default net will form for a given connectivity and indeed this is overwhelmingly the case.[1] Thus it might be expected that for 6,3-coordination the pyrite net would be the default net. However most framework materials with this connectivity reported to date have the rutile topology and in fact this was identified as the default structure,[1] but rutile is significantly less symmetric than pyrite having two kinds of edge and three kinds of ring (transitivity 2232). Most of the rutile-structured materials reported have been cyanides with interpenetrating, partly catenated, frameworks such as [C(CN)3]2\;[10, 14] in some instances the three-coordinated vertex has more than one kind of link as in compounds with a [N(CN)2]2\framework, so the appearance of a less-symmetrical network

is less surprising in this instance.[15] The occurrence of the rutile net in bis(isonicotinate) Fe(II)is understandable on the same grounds.[16] We also note that in the case of MOF-150, the “octahedral” SBU actually has tetrahedral symmetry with the planes of opposite carboxylate groups at 90°. However, as can be seen from Figure 1 c, opposite triangular groups have to be coplanar. TCA is flexible enough to provide the twist angle of 45°needed between the carboxylates and triangles. With less-flexible linkers we might expect to find other, less-symmetrical nets; we are exploring this possibility.

Design of Frameworks with Mixed Triangular and Octahedral Building Blocks Exemplified by the Structure of [Zn4O(TCA)2]Having the Pyrite Topology **

Hee K. Chae, Jaheon Kim, Olaf Delgado Friedrichs, Michael OKeeffe, and Omar M. Yaghi*

A prerequisite to the design of crystalline materials is the knowledge of the possible structures that potentially may form by linking together specific molecular shapes. In this context, we recently argued that, from the large number of possible structures that could in principle be assembled from various molecular shapes, those with the highest symmetry are most likely to form in practice. Thus it is particularly important to identify these special structures since they represent the default structures for the assembly of shapes.[1]

This approach has been useful in the chemistry of extended metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) in which 3D structures assembled entirely from triangles,[2] squares,[3] tetrahedra,[4] or octahedra[5] usually form structures based on the SrSi2, NbO, diamond and primitive cubic nets, respectively. Indeed, these have the highest possible symmetry for their respective building block shapes and have become as important to crystal designers as the Platonic solids are to molecular chemists. Herein we point out that the FeS2(pyrite) net found in [Zn4O(TCA)2]·(DMF)3(H2O)3(hereafter MOF-150; (MATH)-Tricarboxytriphenylamine, (MATH)-dimethylforamide), is the most regular net (and the most likely to form) for linking together triangles and octahedra and that it has some additional net properties that lead to its classification as a default net.

We use TCA and [Zn4O(CO2)6]as secondary building units (SBUs) (Figure 1 a) to provide three- and six-coordinated vertices, respectively. The SBUs are produced by employing previously determined reaction parameters to
