The solvated 2 is not stable under UV irradiation similar to 1.

The X-ray powder diffraction pattern of desolvated 1 matched reasonably well with that of desolvated 2 (see Supporting Information), which implies that the crystal structure and the orientations of the coordination polymers in the desolvated lattice of 1 are similar to those present in desolvated 2. This XRD result helps visualizing the anisotropic molecular movements in 1.

The transformation of a linear 1D coordination polymer to a ladder-type polymeric structure is depicted in Scheme 1. Immediately after removal of the coordinated water molecule and the lattice CH3CNthe crystal structure starts to collapse,

which is transmitted throughout the stacked layers. To balance the stress, simultaneous cooperative lateral movements of the coordination polymers and (MATH)ions occur within the crystal (B). During this phase-rebuilding process, the thermodynamically favored Ag·sAginteraction becomes activated between the adjacent strands along the axis, rather than with the parallel strands in the ac plane that are nearly 10 Åaway. The average Ag···O distance between the silver atom and the oxygen atom of the (MATH)ions is about 4.45 Åin A.

It is proposed that the trifluoroacetate ions migrate to bridge the adjacent silver atoms in the direction. Such movements of the carboxylate groups that form bonds to the metal are well documented.[3c,d, 5a] For example, in the topochemical conversion of a hydrogen-bonded to a covalently bonded supramolecular network, a carboxylate oxygen atom of the reduced Schiff base ligand from the neighboring molecule forms a bond to Zn(II)guided by N-H·sOhydrogen bonds on thermal dehydration.[3c,d] In this transformation, the distance between Zn(II)and the oxygen atoms of the carboxylate group changed from 3.736(2) to 2.010(2) ,. On the other hand, molecular rotation of the trifluoroacetate group competes for coordination and forms a bridge between two Ag atoms.[5a] Completion of phase transformation leads to the formation of a ladder structure (C), but the bond breaking and bond making probably create high strain and the crystal disintegrates. This reveals that the influence of strain generated by desolvation of the crystal and the Ag·sAgand interactions in the resultant lattice leads to the transformation and hence the molecular reactions within the crystalline solid.

Anisotropic Movements of Coordination Polymers upon Desolvation: Solid-State Transformation of a Linear 1D Coordination Polymer to a Ladderlike Structure**

Mangayarkarasi Nagarathinam and Jagadese J. Vittal*

Despite the inherent strong barriers of simultaneous bond breaking and formation in more than one direction, many interesting transformations of one coordination polymer to another in the solid state have been studied widely in recent years.[1–4] A notable success has already been achieved in positioning the ligands with olefinic double bonds in a coordination polymer, and in the isolation of their photodimerized products through single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation.[5] Generally, these photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions of the olefinic double bonds are expected to occur with the minimal atomic and molecular movements when they are aligned parallel and within the range of 3.0–4.1 ,.[5–8] There are also a few interesting reports on rare phenomena, such as the anisotropic long-range molecular-movement-induced/assisted [2+2] photodimerizations of organic molecules that have been visualized in single crystals only through grazing incidence diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and near-field optical microscopy.[9] Indeed, long-range molecular movements have been demonstrated in a few coordination complexes by SCSC transformation.[10] However, the studies have not been extended to crystals that have lost their crystallinity or undergone a mild change in the crystal structure as a result of the desolvation process. To the best of our knowledge, cooperative anisotropic molecular movements resulting from desolvation in a coordination polymer have not been observed to date.

While we were investigating the photochemical activity of coordination polymers, we found that the double bonds in the desolvated crystals of the single-stranded coordination polymers [Ag (µ2 - b p e)]nn+( (MATH)-bipyridylethylene) undergo [2+2] cycloaddition under UV irradiation. This polymer has neither Ag···Ag interaction nor satisfies Schmidt7s topochemical criteria in the solvated structure. However, when a desolvated crystalline powder of 1 was irradiated by UV light for 8h, complete conversion of the olefins to cyclobutane derivatives was observed. The 1HNMR spectrum in [D6]DMSOshows the complete disappearance of the olefinic proton signal at δ = 7.56 ppm, a new signal attributable to cyclobutane protons at δ = 4.68 : ppm, and a shift in the bipyridyl proton signals from δ = 8.61and 7.65 ppmto δ = 8.35and (MATH), which confirms the formation of the expected photodimerized product (see Supporting Information).

Quantitative photodimerization on irradiation of desolvated 1 confirms that molecular movement occurs on removal of the solvents. The packing diagram of the crystal structure also shows clearly that there must be enough freedom for the reactive molecules to undergo the necessary lateral movements to reorganize once the solvents are removed.

The free movement of the coordination polymers, their reorganization from a linear 1D to a ladderlike structure, and the reorientation of the adjacent olefinic double bonds suitable for photodimerization in 1 on desolvation are evident from the isolation and characterization of colorless, platelike crystals of (MATH)(2). Compound 2 was obtained on reaction of equimolar amounts of bpe and Ag(O2CCF3)under different reaction conditions with the same solvents. The crystals obtained were of poor X-ray diffraction quality and readily lost lattice water to become opaque in air. Although the bpe ligands were severely disordered, which was further complicated by a crystallographic inversion center, the connectivity in the ladderlike 1D coordination polymeric structure has been proved beyond any doubt.

In 2 two linear polymers (MATH)are bridged by two trifluoroacetate ligands to form a double-stranded, molecularladder-like coordination polymer (Figure 2). The distances of Ag·sAgand two olefinic double bonds aligned in parallel are 3.15 and 3.62 - 4.06 A, respectively. The and Ag·sAginteractions provide thermodynamic stability to this laddertype arrangement. The crystal structure of 2 signifies that we have successfully isolated a molecular-ladder-like coordina-

The desolvated crystalline powder of 2 was irradiated for 8hand the 1HNMR spectrum of the colorless product revealed that the product was completely photodimerized. This result supports the finding that the carboxylate-bridged silver dimer is a reliable supramolecular synthon for the alignment of bpe ligands as a silver coordination polymer. Furthermore, it confirms that the ladder structure is preserved in the desolvated 2. But SCSC transformation was not observed because the single crystals disintegrated upon desolvation. The solvated 2 is not stable under UV irradiation similar to 1.

The X-ray powder diffraction pattern of desolvated 1 matched reasonably well with that of desolvated 2 (see Supporting Information), which implies that the crystal structure and the orientations of the coordination polymers in the desolvated lattice of 1 are similar to those present in desolvated 2. This XRD result helps visualizing the anisotropic molecular movements in 1.

The transformation of a linear 1D coordination polymer to a ladder-type polymeric structure is depicted in Scheme 1. Immediately after removal of the coordinated water molecule and the lattice CH3CNthe crystal structure starts to collapse,

which is transmitted throughout the stacked layers. To balance the stress, simultaneous cooperative lateral movements of the coordination polymers and (MATH)ions occur within the crystal (B). During this phase-rebuilding process, the thermodynamically favored Ag·sAginteraction becomes activated between the adjacent strands along the axis, rather than with the parallel strands in the ac plane that are nearly 10 Åaway. The average Ag···O distance between the silver atom and the oxygen atom of the (MATH)ions is about 4.45 Åin A.

It is proposed that the trifluoroacetate ions migrate to bridge the adjacent silver atoms in the direction. Such movements of the carboxylate groups that form bonds to the metal are well documented.[3c,d, 5a] For example, in the topochemical conversion of a hydrogen-bonded to a covalently bonded supramolecular network, a carboxylate oxygen atom of the reduced Schiff base ligand from the neighboring molecule forms a bond to Zn(II)guided by N-H·sOhydrogen bonds on thermal dehydration.[3c,d] In this transformation, the distance between Zn(II)and the oxygen atoms of the carboxylate group changed from 3.736(2) to 2.010(2) ,. On the other hand, molecular rotation of the trifluoroacetate group competes for coordination and forms a bridge between two Ag atoms.[5a] Completion of phase transformation leads to the formation of a ladder structure (C), but the bond breaking and bond making probably create high strain and the crystal disintegrates. This reveals that the influence of strain generated by desolvation of the crystal and the Ag·sAgand interactions in the resultant lattice leads to the transformation and hence the molecular reactions within the crystalline solid.

Anisotropic Movements of Coordination Polymers upon Desolvation: Solid-State Transformation of a Linear 1D Coordination Polymer to a Ladderlike Structure**

Mangayarkarasi Nagarathinam and Jagadese J. Vittal*

Despite the inherent strong barriers of simultaneous bond breaking and formation in more than one direction, many interesting transformations of one coordination polymer to another in the solid state have been studied widely in recent years.[1–4] A notable success has already been achieved in positioning the ligands with olefinic double bonds in a coordination polymer, and in the isolation of their photodimerized products through single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation.[5] Generally, these photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions of the olefinic double bonds are expected to occur with the minimal atomic and molecular movements when they are aligned parallel and within the range of 3.0–4.1 ,.[5–8] There are also a few interesting reports on rare phenomena, such as the anisotropic long-range molecular-movement-induced/assisted [2+2] photodimerizations of organic molecules that have been visualized in single crystals only through grazing incidence diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and near-field optical microscopy.[9] Indeed, long-range molecular movements have been demonstrated in a few coordination complexes by SCSC transformation.[10] However, the studies have not been extended to crystals that have lost their crystallinity or undergone a mild change in the crystal structure as a result of the desolvation process. To the best of our knowledge, cooperative anisotropic molecular movements resulting from desolvation in a coordination polymer have not been observed to date.

While we were investigating the photochemical activity of coordination polymers, we found that the double bonds in the desolvated crystals of the single-stranded coordination polymers [Ag (µ2 - b p e)]nn+( (MATH)-bipyridylethylene) undergo [2+2] cycloaddition under UV irradiation. This polymer has neither Ag···Ag interaction nor satisfies Schmidt7s topochemical criteria in the solvated structure. Such a reaction can occur only when the bpe ligands are preorganized during desolvation.[5–9] The transformation from a single-stranded to

As the crystal was desolvated and lost its crystallinity readily upon irradiation, the photoreactivity of the solvated crystal could not be studied. However, when a desolvated crystalline powder of 1 was irradiated by UV light for 8h, complete conversion of the olefins to cyclobutane derivatives was observed. The 1HNMR spectrum in [D6]DMSOshows the complete disappearance of the olefinic proton signal at δ = 7.56 ppm, a new signal attributable to cyclobutane protons at δ = 4.68 : ppm, and a shift in the bipyridyl proton signals from δ = 8.61and 7.65 ppmto δ = 8.35and (MATH), which confirms the formation of the expected photodimerized product (see Supporting Information).

Quantitative photodimerization on irradiation of desolvated 1 confirms that molecular movement occurs on removal of the solvents. The packing diagram of the crystal structure also shows clearly that there must be enough freedom for the reactive molecules to undergo the necessary lateral movements to reorganize once the solvents are removed.

The free movement of the coordination polymers, their reorganization from a linear 1D to a ladderlike structure, and the reorientation of the adjacent olefinic double bonds suitable for photodimerization in 1 on desolvation are evident from the isolation and characterization of colorless, platelike crystals of (MATH)(2). Compound 2 was obtained on reaction of equimolar amounts of bpe and Ag(O2CCF3)under different reaction conditions with the same solvents. The crystals obtained were of poor X-ray diffraction quality and readily lost lattice water to become opaque in air. Although the bpe ligands were severely disordered, which was further complicated by a crystallographic inversion center, the connectivity in the ladderlike 1D coordination polymeric structure has been proved beyond any doubt.

In 2 two linear polymers (MATH)are bridged by two trifluoroacetate ligands to form a double-stranded, molecularladder-like coordination polymer (Figure 2). The distances of Ag·sAgand two olefinic double bonds aligned in parallel are 3.15 and 3.62 - 4.06 A, respectively. The and Ag·sAginteractions provide thermodynamic stability to this laddertype arrangement. The crystal structure of 2 signifies that we have successfully isolated a molecular-ladder-like coordina-

The desolvated crystalline powder of 2 was irradiated for 8hand the 1HNMR spectrum of the colorless product revealed that the product was completely photodimerized. This result supports the finding that the carboxylate-bridged silver dimer is a reliable supramolecular synthon for the alignment of bpe ligands as a silver coordination polymer. Furthermore, it confirms that the ladder structure is preserved in the desolvated 2. But SCSC transformation was not observed because the single crystals disintegrated upon desolvation. The solvated 2 is not stable under UV irradiation similar to 1.

The X-ray powder diffraction pattern of desolvated 1 matched reasonably well with that of desolvated 2 (see Supporting Information), which implies that the crystal structure and the orientations of the coordination polymers in the desolvated lattice of 1 are similar to those present in desolvated 2. This XRD result helps visualizing the anisotropic molecular movements in 1.

The transformation of a linear 1D coordination polymer to a ladder-type polymeric structure is depicted in Scheme 1. Immediately after removal of the coordinated water molecule and the lattice CH3CNthe crystal structure starts to collapse,

which is transmitted throughout the stacked layers. To balance the stress, simultaneous cooperative lateral movements of the coordination polymers and (MATH)ions occur within the crystal (B). During this phase-rebuilding process, the thermodynamically favored Ag·sAginteraction becomes activated between the adjacent strands along the axis, rather than with the parallel strands in the ac plane that are nearly 10 Åaway. The average Ag···O distance between the silver atom and the oxygen atom of the (MATH)ions is about 4.45 Åin A.

It is proposed that the trifluoroacetate ions migrate to bridge the adjacent silver atoms in the direction. Such movements of the carboxylate groups that form bonds to the metal are well documented.[3c,d, 5a] For example, in the topochemical conversion of a hydrogen-bonded to a covalently bonded supramolecular network, a carboxylate oxygen atom of the reduced Schiff base ligand from the neighboring molecule forms a bond to Zn(II)guided by N-H·sOhydrogen bonds on thermal dehydration.[3c,d] In this transformation, the distance between Zn(II)and the oxygen atoms of the carboxylate group changed from 3.736(2) to 2.010(2) ,. On the other hand, molecular rotation of the trifluoroacetate group competes for coordination and forms a bridge between two Ag atoms.[5a] Completion of phase transformation leads to the formation of a ladder structure (C), but the bond breaking and bond making probably create high strain and the crystal disintegrates. This reveals that the influence of strain generated by desolvation of the crystal and the Ag·sAgand interactions in the resultant lattice leads to the transformation and hence the molecular reactions within the crystalline solid.

Anisotropic Movements of Coordination Polymers upon Desolvation: Solid-State Transformation of a Linear 1D Coordination Polymer to a Ladderlike Structure**

Mangayarkarasi Nagarathinam and Jagadese J. Vittal*

Despite the inherent strong barriers of simultaneous bond breaking and formation in more than one direction, many interesting transformations of one coordination polymer to another in the solid state have been studied widely in recent years.[1–4] A notable success has already been achieved in positioning the ligands with olefinic double bonds in a coordination polymer, and in the isolation of their photodimerized products through single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation.[5] Generally, these photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions of the olefinic double bonds are expected to occur with the minimal atomic and molecular movements when they are aligned parallel and within the range of 3.0–4.1 ,.[5–8] There are also a few interesting reports on rare phenomena, such as the anisotropic long-range molecular-movement-induced/assisted [2+2] photodimerizations of organic molecules that have been visualized in single crystals only through grazing incidence diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and near-field optical microscopy.[9] Indeed, long-range molecular movements have been demonstrated in a few coordination complexes by SCSC transformation.[10] However, the studies have not been extended to crystals that have lost their crystallinity or undergone a mild change in the crystal structure as a result of the desolvation process. To the best of our knowledge, cooperative anisotropic molecular movements resulting from desolvation in a coordination polymer have not been observed to date.

While we were investigating the photochemical activity of coordination polymers, we found that the double bonds in the desolvated crystals of the single-stranded coordination polymers [Ag (µ2 - b p e)]nn+( (MATH)-bipyridylethylene) undergo [2+2] cycloaddition under UV irradiation. This polymer has neither Ag···Ag interaction nor satisfies Schmidt7s topochemical criteria in the solvated structure. Such a reaction can occur only when the bpe ligands are preorganized during desolvation.[5–9] The transformation from a single-stranded to

Mangayarkarasi Nagarathinam and Jagadese J. Vittal*

Despite the inherent strong barriers of simultaneous bond breaking and formation in more than one direction, many interesting transformations of one coordination polymer to another in the solid state have been studied widely in recent years.[1–4] A notable success has already been achieved in positioning the ligands with olefinic double bonds in a coordination polymer, and in the isolation of their photodimerized products through single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation.[5] Generally, these photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions of the olefinic double bonds are expected to occur with the minimal atomic and molecular movements when they are aligned parallel and within the range of 3.0–4.1 ,.[5–8] There are also a few interesting reports on rare phenomena, such as the anisotropic long-range molecular-movement-induced/assisted [2+2] photodimerizations of organic molecules that have been visualized in single crystals only through grazing incidence diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and near-field optical microscopy.[9] Indeed, long-range molecular movements have been demonstrated in a few coordination complexes by SCSC transformation.[10] However, the studies have not been extended to crystals that have lost their crystallinity or undergone a mild change in the crystal structure as a result of the desolvation process. To the best of our knowledge, cooperative anisotropic molecular movements resulting from desolvation in a coordination polymer have not been observed to date.

While we were investigating the photochemical activity of coordination polymers, we found that the double bonds in the desolvated crystals of the single-stranded coordination polymers [Ag (µ2 - b p e)]nn+( (MATH)-bipyridylethylene) undergo [2+2] cycloaddition under UV irradiation. This polymer has neither Ag···Ag interaction nor satisfies Schmidt7s topochemical criteria in the solvated structure. Such a reaction can occur only when the bpe ligands are preorganized during desolvation.[5–9] The transformation from a single-stranded to

Anisotropic Movements of Coordination Polymers upon Desolvation: Solid-State Transformation of a Linear 1D Coordination Polymer to a Ladderlike Structure**

Mangayarkarasi Nagarathinam and Jagadese J. Vittal*

Despite the inherent strong barriers of simultaneous bond breaking and formation in more than one direction, many interesting transformations of one coordination polymer to another in the solid state have been studied widely in recent years.[1–4] A notable success has already been achieved in positioning the ligands with olefinic double bonds in a coordination polymer, and in the isolation of their photodimerized products through single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation.[5] Generally, these photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions of the olefinic double bonds are expected to occur with the minimal atomic and molecular movements when they are aligned parallel and within the range of 3.0–4.1 ,.[5–8] There are also a few interesting reports on rare phenomena, such as the anisotropic long-range molecular-movement-induced/assisted [2+2] photodimerizations of organic molecules that have been visualized in single crystals only through grazing incidence diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and near-field optical microscopy.[9] Indeed, long-range molecular movements have been demonstrated in a few coordination complexes by SCSC transformation.[10] However, the studies have not been extended to crystals that have lost their crystallinity or undergone a mild change in the crystal structure as a result of the desolvation process. To the best of our knowledge, cooperative anisotropic molecular movements resulting from desolvation in a coordination polymer have not been observed to date.

While we were investigating the photochemical activity of coordination polymers, we found that the double bonds in the desolvated crystals of the single-stranded coordination polymers [Ag (µ2 - b p e)]nn+( (MATH)-bipyridylethylene) undergo [2+2] cycloaddition under UV irradiation. This polymer has neither Ag···Ag interaction nor satisfies Schmidt7s topochemical criteria in the solvated structure. Dedicated to Professor Werner Uhl on the occasion of his 60th birthday

Abstract: Phosphorus-containing heterocycles have evolved from laboratory curiosities to functional components, such as ligands in catalytically active metal complexes or molecular constituents in electronic devices. The straightforward synthesis of functionalized heterocycles on a larger scale remains a challenge. Herein, we report the use of the phosphaethynolate (MATH)anion as a building block for various sterically unprotected and functionalized hydroxy substituted phosphorus heterocycles. Because the resulting heterocycles are themselves anions, they are building blocks in their own right and allow further facile functionalization. This property may be of interest in coordination chemistry and material science.

Abstract: Phosphorus-containing heterocycles have evolved from laboratory curiosities to functional components, such as ligands in catalytically active metal complexes or molecular constituents in electronic devices. The straightforward synthesis of functionalized heterocycles on a larger scale remains a challenge. Herein, we report the use of the phosphaethynolate (MATH)anion as a building block for various sterically unprotected and functionalized hydroxy substituted phosphorus heterocycles. Because the resulting heterocycles are themselves anions, they are building blocks in their own right and allow further facile functionalization. Unlike its nitrogen analogue, the cyanate salt Na-(OCN), which behaves as an ambivalent pseudohalogenide, the -triple bond in the (MATH)anion undergoes [2+2], [3+2], and [4+2] cycloadditions. Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. They are electrically neutral systems without external doping but feature degenerate semiconductor character.

Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

To further probe the electronic structure of CuxC6S6, the Ultraviolet Photoelectron Spectroscopy (UPS) measurements were used first to reveal their Density of States (DOS) near the Fermi level. Clear Fermi edges can be observed in the UPS spectra for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6at 300K, suggesting that both of them have electronic bands crossing the Fermi level (Figure S10). The observation of Fermi edges leads to the conclusion that Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6would be either metallic conductors or degenerated semiconductors, which explains why they have high electrical conductivity.

Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). The electron contribution can be calculated from the measured electrical conductivities according to Wiedemann-Franz law,[25] while the lattice contribution is obtained by subtracting from The value of shows almost temperature-independent behavior with a constant value of 0.5 and 0.4Wm-1K-1for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6in the whole measured temperature range (Figures 4 e,f), and these values

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

To further probe the electronic structure of CuxC6S6, the Ultraviolet Photoelectron Spectroscopy (UPS) measurements were used first to reveal their Density of States (DOS) near the Fermi level. Clear Fermi edges can be observed in the UPS spectra for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6at 300K, suggesting that both of them have electronic bands crossing the Fermi level (Figure S10). The observation of Fermi edges leads to the conclusion that Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6would be either metallic conductors or degenerated semiconductors, which explains why they have high electrical conductivity.

Firstly, the electronic structures of CuxC6S6sshow some similarities: all of them have dispersed valence band and conduction band with a band gap of 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8 eVfor Cu3C6S6, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, respectively. As a result, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is larger than Cu3C6S6. More significantly, the Fermi level of Cu5.5C6S6moves up further and approaches the top of the valence band. Therefore, there is a sharp change in the DOS near the Fermi level, which brings a higher Seebeck coefficient. Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The electron contribution can be calculated from the measured electrical conductivities according to Wiedemann-Franz law,[25] while the lattice contribution is obtained by subtracting from The value of shows almost temperature-independent behavior with a constant value of 0.5 and 0.4Wm-1K-1for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6in the whole measured temperature range (Figures 4 e,f), and these values

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

To further probe the electronic structure of CuxC6S6, the Ultraviolet Photoelectron Spectroscopy (UPS) measurements were used first to reveal their Density of States (DOS) near the Fermi level. Clear Fermi edges can be observed in the UPS spectra for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6at 300K, suggesting that both of them have electronic bands crossing the Fermi level (Figure S10). The observation of Fermi edges leads to the conclusion that Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6would be either metallic conductors or degenerated semiconductors, which explains why they have high electrical conductivity.

Seebeck coefficients of CuxC6S6were also measured. The room-temperature Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are (MATH)and (MATH), respectively, suggesting that holes are the dominant charge carriers in CuxC6S6s(Figure 4 d). The absolute value of the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is significantly larger than that of Cu3C6S6(-5mathrm--10µVK-1)[10b]and slightly increases as the temperature rises. Although the electrical conductivity of Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are similar, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6is nearly two-fold larger than that of Cu4C6S6at room temperature. Furthermore, there is an apparent increasing trend in the temperature function of the Seebeck

coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6. The different absolute values and temperature functions of the Seebeck coefficient of CuxC6S6sstrongly suggest that they have different electronic structures.

To gain a more in-depth insight into the difference between the electronic structures among CuxC6S6sthe band structures of these three phases have been calculated based on their crystal structure using first principle DFT methods and plotted along the representative k path (Figure 5). Firstly, the electronic structures of CuxC6S6sshow some similarities: all of them have dispersed valence band and conduction band with a band gap of 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8 eVfor Cu3C6S6, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, respectively. Their Fermi levels cut the dispersed valence band, which agrees with the Fermi edge found in UPS spectra (Figure S11). However, the position of the Fermi level differs among them. Cu3C6S6has a metallic nature and small Seebeck coefficient, attributed to a Fermi level that lies deep into the valence band.[10b] The energy difference between the Fermi level and the top of the valence band in Cu4C6S6becomes smaller compared to that in Cu3C6S6, making it more like a degenerate semiconductor with heavy -doping. As a result, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is larger than Cu3C6S6. More significantly, the Fermi level of Cu5.5C6S6moves up further and approaches the top of the valence band. Therefore, there is a sharp change in the DOS near the Fermi level, which brings a higher Seebeck coefficient. Based on the energy band structure, both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can be classified as degenerated semiconductors. In addition, according to the absorption spectrum, their optical band gaps are 2.3 eVand 2.7 eV, respectively (Figure S12). Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. Based on their electrically neutral formulas, two electrons per ligand have been removed in Cu4C6S6, and one electron per two ligands is removed for Cu5.5C6S6. It means that the oxidation level of BHT in Cu4C6S6is higher than Cu5.5C6S6, which indicates a higher doping level in Cu4C6S6and results in the different positions of the Fermi level.

The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). These are among the highest power factor values ever reported for p-type conductive CPs. To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). The electron contribution can be calculated from the measured electrical conductivities according to Wiedemann-Franz law,[25] while the lattice contribution is obtained by subtracting from The value of shows almost temperature-independent behavior with a constant value of 0.5 and 0.4Wm-1K-1for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6in the whole measured temperature range (Figures 4 e,f), and these values

are smaller compared to bulk metal sulfide materials but larger than that of previously reported p-type CP: Cu-ett.[26] It can be concluded that the changes in the thermal conductivity of these materials originate mainly from electronic contributions. The ZT value of Cu5.5C6S6varies from 0.08@π300Kto 0.12 @ 390K. This value represents the best performance for p-type conducting CPs and is comparable with the performance of copper sulfides at the same temperature range.[27] Since all the thermoelectric measurements were performed on polycrystalline pellet samples, the improvement in the crystallinity of CuxC6S6swould further enhance their thermoelectric properties.

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. They are electrically neutral systems without external doping but feature degenerate semiconductor character.

Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared.
