Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

Electronic structures of Cu×C6S6s

To further probe the electronic structure of CuxC6S6, the Ultraviolet Photoelectron Spectroscopy (UPS) measurements were used first to reveal their Density of States (DOS) near the Fermi level. Clear Fermi edges can be observed in the UPS spectra for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6at 300K, suggesting that both of them have electronic bands crossing the Fermi level (Figure S10). The observation of Fermi edges leads to the conclusion that Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6would be either metallic conductors or degenerated semiconductors, which explains why they have high electrical conductivity.

Seebeck coefficients of CuxC6S6were also measured. The room-temperature Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are (MATH)and (MATH), respectively, suggesting that holes are the dominant charge carriers in CuxC6S6s(Figure 4 d). The absolute value of the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is significantly larger than that of Cu3C6S6(-5mathrm--10µVK-1)[10b]and slightly increases as the temperature rises. Although the electrical conductivity of Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are similar, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6is nearly two-fold larger than that of Cu4C6S6at room temperature. Furthermore, there is an apparent increasing trend in the temperature function of the Seebeck

coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6. The different absolute values and temperature functions of the Seebeck coefficient of CuxC6S6sstrongly suggest that they have different electronic structures.

To gain a more in-depth insight into the difference between the electronic structures among CuxC6S6sthe band structures of these three phases have been calculated based on their crystal structure using first principle DFT methods and plotted along the representative k path (Figure 5). Firstly, the electronic structures of CuxC6S6sshow some similarities: all of them have dispersed valence band and conduction band with a band gap of 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8 eVfor Cu3C6S6, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, respectively. Their Fermi levels cut the dispersed valence band, which agrees with the Fermi edge found in UPS spectra (Figure S11). However, the position of the Fermi level differs among them. Cu3C6S6has a metallic nature and small Seebeck coefficient, attributed to a Fermi level that lies deep into the valence band.[10b] The energy difference between the Fermi level and the top of the valence band in Cu4C6S6becomes smaller compared to that in Cu3C6S6, making it more like a degenerate semiconductor with heavy -doping. As a result, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is larger than Cu3C6S6. More significantly, the Fermi level of Cu5.5C6S6moves up further and approaches the top of the valence band. Therefore, there is a sharp change in the DOS near the Fermi level, which brings a higher Seebeck coefficient. Based on the energy band structure, both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can be classified as degenerated semiconductors. In addition, according to the absorption spectrum, their optical band gaps are 2.3 eVand 2.7 eV, respectively (Figure S12). Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. Based on their electrically neutral formulas, two electrons per ligand have been removed in Cu4C6S6, and one electron per two ligands is removed for Cu5.5C6S6. It means that the oxidation level of BHT in Cu4C6S6is higher than Cu5.5C6S6, which indicates a higher doping level in Cu4C6S6and results in the different positions of the Fermi level.

The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). These are among the highest power factor values ever reported for p-type conductive CPs. To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). The electron contribution can be calculated from the measured electrical conductivities according to Wiedemann-Franz law,[25] while the lattice contribution is obtained by subtracting from The value of shows almost temperature-independent behavior with a constant value of 0.5 and 0.4Wm-1K-1for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6in the whole measured temperature range (Figures 4 e,f), and these values

are smaller compared to bulk metal sulfide materials but larger than that of previously reported p-type CP: Cu-ett.[26] It can be concluded that the changes in the thermal conductivity of these materials originate mainly from electronic contributions. The ZT values of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are calculated based on the formula: Z T = S2 0T/κ(Figure 4 h). For Cu4C6S6, the ZT value is 0.02 and remains unchanged as temperature increases. The ZT value of Cu5.5C6S6varies from 0.08@π300Kto 0.12 @ 390K. This value represents the best performance for p-type conducting CPs and is comparable with the performance of copper sulfides at the same temperature range.[27] Since all the thermoelectric measurements were performed on polycrystalline pellet samples, the improvement in the crystallinity of CuxC6S6swould further enhance their thermoelectric properties.

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. They are electrically neutral systems without external doping but feature degenerate semiconductor character.

Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

Electronic structures of Cu×C6S6s

To further probe the electronic structure of CuxC6S6, the Ultraviolet Photoelectron Spectroscopy (UPS) measurements were used first to reveal their Density of States (DOS) near the Fermi level. Clear Fermi edges can be observed in the UPS spectra for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6at 300K, suggesting that both of them have electronic bands crossing the Fermi level (Figure S10). The observation of Fermi edges leads to the conclusion that Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6would be either metallic conductors or degenerated semiconductors, which explains why they have high electrical conductivity.

Seebeck coefficients of CuxC6S6were also measured. Although the electrical conductivity of Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are similar, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6is nearly two-fold larger than that of Cu4C6S6at room temperature. Furthermore, there is an apparent increasing trend in the temperature function of the Seebeck

coefficient of Cu5.5C6S6. The different absolute values and temperature functions of the Seebeck coefficient of CuxC6S6sstrongly suggest that they have different electronic structures.

To gain a more in-depth insight into the difference between the electronic structures among CuxC6S6sthe band structures of these three phases have been calculated based on their crystal structure using first principle DFT methods and plotted along the representative k path (Figure 5). Firstly, the electronic structures of CuxC6S6sshow some similarities: all of them have dispersed valence band and conduction band with a band gap of 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8 eVfor Cu3C6S6, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, respectively. Their Fermi levels cut the dispersed valence band, which agrees with the Fermi edge found in UPS spectra (Figure S11). However, the position of the Fermi level differs among them. Cu3C6S6has a metallic nature and small Seebeck coefficient, attributed to a Fermi level that lies deep into the valence band.[10b] The energy difference between the Fermi level and the top of the valence band in Cu4C6S6becomes smaller compared to that in Cu3C6S6, making it more like a degenerate semiconductor with heavy -doping. As a result, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is larger than Cu3C6S6. More significantly, the Fermi level of Cu5.5C6S6moves up further and approaches the top of the valence band. Therefore, there is a sharp change in the DOS near the Fermi level, which brings a higher Seebeck coefficient. Based on the energy band structure, both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can be classified as degenerated semiconductors. In addition, according to the absorption spectrum, their optical band gaps are 2.3 eVand 2.7 eV, respectively (Figure S12). Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. Based on their electrically neutral formulas, two electrons per ligand have been removed in Cu4C6S6, and one electron per two ligands is removed for Cu5.5C6S6. It means that the oxidation level of BHT in Cu4C6S6is higher than Cu5.5C6S6, which indicates a higher doping level in Cu4C6S6and results in the different positions of the Fermi level.

The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). These are among the highest power factor values ever reported for p-type conductive CPs. To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). are smaller compared to bulk metal sulfide materials but larger than that of previously reported p-type CP: Cu-ett.[26] It can be concluded that the changes in the thermal conductivity of these materials originate mainly from electronic contributions. The ZT values of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are calculated based on the formula: Z T = S2 0T/κ(Figure 4 h). For Cu4C6S6, the ZT value is 0.02 and remains unchanged as temperature increases. The ZT value of Cu5.5C6S6varies from 0.08@π300Kto 0.12 @ 390K. This value represents the best performance for p-type conducting CPs and is comparable with the performance of copper sulfides at the same temperature range.[27] Since all the thermoelectric measurements were performed on polycrystalline pellet samples, the improvement in the crystallinity of CuxC6S6swould further enhance their thermoelectric properties.

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. They are electrically neutral systems without external doping but feature degenerate semiconductor character.

Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

As a result, the Seebeck coefficient of Cu4C6S6is larger than Cu3C6S6. More significantly, the Fermi level of Cu5.5C6S6moves up further and approaches the top of the valence band. Since both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act like degenerated semiconductors, which means they are highly doped, it is crucial to clarify how they are doped. First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. It means that the oxidation level of BHT in Cu4C6S6is higher than Cu5.5C6S6, which indicates a higher doping level in Cu4C6S6and results in the different positions of the Fermi level.

The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). These are among the highest power factor values ever reported for p-type conductive CPs. To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). are smaller compared to bulk metal sulfide materials but larger than that of previously reported p-type CP: Cu-ett.[26] It can be concluded that the changes in the thermal conductivity of these materials originate mainly from electronic contributions. The ZT values of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are calculated based on the formula: Z T = S2 0T/κ(Figure 4 h). For Cu4C6S6, the ZT value is 0.02 and remains unchanged as temperature increases. The ZT value of Cu5.5C6S6varies from 0.08@π300Kto 0.12 @ 390K. This value represents the best performance for p-type conducting CPs and is comparable with the performance of copper sulfides at the same temperature range.[27] Since all the thermoelectric measurements were performed on polycrystalline pellet samples, the improvement in the crystallinity of CuxC6S6swould further enhance their thermoelectric properties.

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Highly Conducting Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Copper Sulfides CuxC6S6or 5.5): Ligand-Based Oxidation-Induced Chemical and Electronic Structure Modulation

Xing Huang+, Yi Qiu+, Yishan Wang, Liyao Liu, Xiaoyu Wu, Yingying Liang, Yutao Cui, Yimeng Sun, Ye Zou, Jia Zhu,* Weihai Fang, Junliang Sun,* Wei Xu,* and Daoben Zhu*

Abstract: Conductive coordination polymers (CPs) have potential in a wide range of applications because of their inherent structural and functional diversity. Three electrically conductive CPs ( CuxC6S6, 4 or 5.5) derived from the same organic linker (benzenehexathiol) and metal node (copper(I)) were synthesized and studied. CuxC6S6materials are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides comprising a p-p stacking structure and cooper sulfur networks. Charge-transport pathways within the network facilitate conductivity and offer control of the Fermi level through modulation of the oxidation level of the non-innocent redox-active ligand. Two CuxC6S6( or 5.5) CPs display high electrical conductivity and they feature a tunable structural topology and electronic structure. Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors. Moreover, Cu5.5C6S6is a -type thermoelectric material with a ZT value of 0.12 at 390 K, which is a record-breaking performance for -type CPs.

Introduction

Electrically conductive coordination polymer (CP)[1] is a burgeoning form of hybrid materials that have efficient electrical transport properties, rendering them excellent candidates for applications in energy conversion[2] and storage,[3] electrocatalysts,[3b, 4] chemiresistive sensors,[3a, 5] etc. Besides these practical applications, conductive CPs display fascinating features in more fundamental areas, such as spintronics,[6] superconductors,[7] quantum materials, and topological insulators.[8] There are several well-established approaches for CPs to realize electrical transport, such as the construction of a mix-valance system, efficient p-p overlapping between conjugated ligands, or the extension of the

p-conjugation system mediated by the d-orbitals of metal nodes.[9] Among these conductive CPs, the two-dimensional d-p conjugation systems constructed by the tetra-coordinate late transition metal centers and highly symmetric multisubstitutional aromatic ligands with strong donor groups, such as benzenehexathiol (BHT),[10] hexaiminotriphenylene,[11] or hexahydroxybenzene,[12] display the most promising performance.[3c,7, 10–11, 12–13] As one of the representative members of this type of ligands, BHT has been used to construct 2D CP Cu-BHT (MATH)with a record high conductivity on the order of 3Scand superconductivity at 0.25K.[7] Furthermore, substitution of the metal center ,[10b,11b, 13b] Ni,[10a, 11a,b] Co,[13c] Fe,[10c, 14] Pt[15]) and BHT-like ligands (functionalized with -SH,[10, 14, 15] -OH,[12] - ·NH3,[11, 13a,b] - -SeH[13h]groups), a family of conductive CPs with graphene-like 2D systems have been created. The majority of them share two structure patterns, either a honeycomb structure with a ligand to the metal molar ratio of 3:1 or a more condensed Kagom8 lattice with a ratio of 3:2. Compared to inorganic semiconductors or conductors, such as metal oxides or metal chalcogenides, in which the metal contents can be easily modulated in a multitude of ways to fine-tune their chargetransport properties,[16] however, manipulating the structure and composition of conductive CPs is much more difficult. Furthermore, except for a few intrinsic metallic systems, postsynthetic oxidation or doping processes is a requisite for conductive CPs to achieve high electrical conductivity,[10a, 17] similar to that of conventional semiconducting polymers.[18] The introduction of the doping process will introduce new concerns such as de-doping, suggesting that conductive CPs with intrinsic high electrical conductivity are more desirable.

Herein, we discover that by taking advantage of the noninnocent nature of BHT, both the chemical and electronic structures of BHT-base CPs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation level of the ligand. Based on the same combination of the organic linker and metal node, two intrinsic highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6, and Cu5.5C6S6, with unusual nonstoichiometric compositions, have been prepared. They have diverse crystal structures, originating from the different assembly modes of similar hexagram subunits composed of BHT and six surrounding copper ions. Results and Discussion

Synthesis of 4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

In the previously reported Cu-BHT (Cu3C6S6),[10b] Cu(II)ions with electron configuration adopt a tetra-coordinated planar geometry, commonly found in conductive CPs based on BHT-like ligand,[19] which results in a conventional 2D structure. Contrary to Cu(II)ions, the coordination chemistry of Cu(I)ions is more complicated, partly because of the increase in the number of coordination bonds as well as the possibility of forming Cu-Cu bonds to add further diversity to potential structures.[20] Taking the difference of the coordination chemistry between Cu(I)and Cu(II)into consideration, two neutral copper(I) benzenehexathiol(BHT) CPs: Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6(Figure 1) have been synthesized by substituting the Cu(II)with Cu(I)as metal nodes.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were, respectively synthesized through the simple homogeneous reactions between Cu(I)and BHT in different solvents. Specifically, the reaction in methanol will afford a dark blue polycrystalline sample of Cu4C6S6, and the reaction in ethylene glycol can provide a dark green polycrystalline sample of Cu5.5C6S6. Both products cannot be dissolved in any common solvents, which indicates the formation of polymers. Additionally, the strong signal of thiol units at 2500 cm-1

disappears entirely in their Raman spectra (Supporting Information, Figure S1), indicating that all the thiol groups in BHT have participated in the reaction with Cu(I).

The components of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6were investigated by X-ray Photo-electron Spectroscopy (XPS), Elemental Analysis (EA), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), and Electron Probe Micro-analyzer (EPMA). First, the XPS results (Figure S2) reveal that only Cu, C, and S exist within the samples, suggesting the lack of solvent molecules or charge balancing ions in the final products. The thermogravimetric analysis results also suggest that no solvents molecules are contained in the final formed materials (Figure S3). According to the ICP-OES results, the copper contents in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are 56.37%, and 48.54%, respectively, and the EPMA results show that the Cu/Sratios in Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6are close to 5.5:6 and 4:6 (Figure S4), respectively. Accordingly, we can obtain their chemical formulas: [Cu5.5(C6S6)]nand [Cu4(C6S6)]n. Their chemical composition is quite different from the previously reported Cu3C6S6,[13c] indicating the synthesis of two new phases.

Since both Cu5.5C6S6and Cu4C6S6do not contain counter balancing ions, they should be neutral networks. Additionally, the XPS results (Figure S5) show that only Cu(I)exists in the structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6with the lack of the shakeup peak of Cu(II). Since the original C6S66-linker has six negative charges, it should have been partly oxidized during their formation process of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6to fulfill the requirement of charge balance. Looking back at the entire synthesis procedure of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, a trace amount of oxygen in the reaction container is the possible oxidant.

First, they have an organic–inorganic hybrid structure that contains two parts, a p-p stacking structure of organic ligand, just like in organic conductors, and cooper-sulfur networks being inorganic counterparts. According to the projected DOS contribution in Figure 5, the DOS near the Fermi level contains d orbital of Cu and p orbital of C and S, which means there is a strong electronic coupling between the metal ions and ligands. Since the BHT ligand is non-innocent, there is an in situ oxidation process that happened during the formation of both Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6. The oxidation levels of the ligand will further affect their electronic structure, which makes this oxidation process like a doping process, and the organic part plays a dopant-like role. Based on their electrically neutral formulas, two electrons per ligand have been removed in Cu4C6S6, and one electron per two ligands is removed for Cu5.5C6S6. It means that the oxidation level of BHT in Cu4C6S6is higher than Cu5.5C6S6, which indicates a higher doping level in Cu4C6S6and results in the different positions of the Fermi level.

The thermoelectric properties of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6

The high electrical conductivities and moderate Seebeck coefficients of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6lead to notable power factors for these two materials of 40µWm-1K-2(Cu4C6S6)and 140µWm-1K-2(Cu5.5C6S6)under room temperature (Figure 4 g). These are among the highest power factor values ever reported for p-type conductive CPs. To get a full evaluation of the thermoelectric performance, thermal conductivities of them are measured in the temperature range from 300 to 390 K. The room temperature of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are 0.72 and 0.59Wm-1K-1, respectively, which increase linearly with temperature (Figures 4 e,f). The electron contribution can be calculated from the measured electrical conductivities according to Wiedemann-Franz law,[25] while the lattice contribution is obtained by subtracting from The value of shows almost temperature-independent behavior with a constant value of 0.5 and 0.4Wm-1K-1for Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6in the whole measured temperature range (Figures 4 e,f), and these values

are smaller compared to bulk metal sulfide materials but larger than that of previously reported p-type CP: Cu-ett.[26] It can be concluded that the changes in the thermal conductivity of these materials originate mainly from electronic contributions. The ZT values of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6are calculated based on the formula: Z T = S2 0T/κ(Figure 4 h). For Cu4C6S6, the ZT value is 0.02 and remains unchanged as temperature increases. The ZT value of Cu5.5C6S6varies from 0.08@π300Kto 0.12 @ 390K. This value represents the best performance for p-type conducting CPs and is comparable with the performance of copper sulfides at the same temperature range.[27] Since all the thermoelectric measurements were performed on polycrystalline pellet samples, the improvement in the crystallinity of CuxC6S6swould further enhance their thermoelectric properties.

Conclusion

In conclusion, through the reactions of non-innocent ligand BHT and a Cu(I)complex, two highly conductive CPs, Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6, were developed thus enlarging the family of CuxC6S6, 4, or 5.5). The crystal structures of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6have been well characterized by PXRD and RED, revealing that they are organic–inorganic hybrid copper sulfides composed of 3D Cu-S networks filled with p-p stacking six-member carbon rings. This unique structure endows them with high electrical conductivity, that is, the conductivities of Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6can reach up to 270 and 220Scm-1, respectively.

Cu4C6S6and Cu5.5C6S6act as degenerate semiconductors, and an oxidation doping-like process occurs spontaneously during their formation. Different from the normal doping process for organic semiconductors, this doping-like process occurs in situ, and the organic moiety within the structure plays the role of dopant. Since the framework itself is neutral with good thermostability, the de-doping issue that commonly occurs in doped systems has been circumvented, thus making these two materials promising organic–inorganic hybrid semiconductors.

Among CuxC6S6sthe favorable electronic structure of Cu5.5C6S6makes it a promising thermoelectric material with Z T = 0.12 @ 390K, the highest value ever reported for CPbased p-type thermoelectric materials. Our results demonstrate the great prospect of using BHT to construct highly conducting CPs in which the crystal structure and charge-

transport properties can be tailored to meet different application requirements through the oxidation modulation of BHT. Although, it is still a challenging task to fully understand the intrinsic doping mechanism within CuxC6S6swe believe that numerous new members of hybrid materials based on BHT-like ligands, which have diverse components, crystal structures, and charge-transport properties, will be discovered soon and will further expand the applications of these interesting materials.

Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. In recent years, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have attracted immense attention as promising adsorbents for various gases such as CO2, H2, and CH4, owing to their programmable structures with tunable pore sizes and high surface areas.[5] Particularly, the appearance of highly water stable MOFs, e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs,[6] opened up the use of MOFs in water harvesting processes. Fortunately, quite lately highly connected MOFs with high porosity for enhancing adsorption properties were fabricated by utilizing rigid, highly connected carboxylate linkers.[15] In particular, corresponding MOFs like Cr-soc-MOF and MIII-acs-MOFs derived from the carboxylate linkers with 4 and 6 coordinating functions have been demonstrated to exhibit large water uptake capacities as well as increased water stability associated with the limited accessibility of water vapor to the metal nodes.[15] However, highly water stable Al/Cr/Zr- based MOFs based on rigid 8-connected (8-c) quadrangular organic ligands have not yet been achieved, to the best of our knowledge, possibly owing to the lack of synthesis feasibility of the rigid quadrangular ligands.

Herein we describe the design and synthesis of two 8,8-c bcu -based MOFs (named ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2) built from 8-c cubic Zr6O4(OH)4(H2O)8(Zr6)clusters and 8-c peripherally extended pentiptycene ligands (MATH)and (MATH).[16] Single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD)

Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. Particularly, ZrMOF-1 exhibits microporous structure with large Bruno-Emmett-Teller surface area and high water stability, endowing it a promising water harvesting material with a high water uptake capacity of 0.83:gH2OgMOF-1at P/P0 = 0.90and 25°C, a steep uptake at a low P/P0of 0.30, and excellent durability over 500 water adsorption-desorption cycles. Moreover, self-consistent charge density functional tight-binding calculations were carried out, rationalizing the water adsorbing process and amount in ZrMOF-1.

After the totally covering of both the Zr6O4(OH)4(H2O)8unit and carboxyl groups by extrinsic H2Omolecules, the third water wave with 55–60 H2Omolecues as a “water bridge” then has to fill the space between the water aggregates depicted as Region 3 in Figure 4b with diminished average binding energy of (MATH)(MATH)(MATH)molecule). This is followed by the subsequent ~20H2Omolecules adsorption into the rest spaces denoted as Region 4 in Figure 4b with further reduced binding energy of - 26 ± 6 k J m o l-1(MATH)0.06 eV '/molecule). In conclusion, we have constructed two highly connected MOFs with unprecedented 8,8-c bcu topology from Zr6clusters and rigid 8-c carboxylate ligands with quadrangular prism shape. In particular, ZrMOF-1 exhibits microporous structure with large BET surface area and high water stability, enabling it to be a promising water harvesting material with high water uptake capacity, steep uptake at low RH, and excellent durability. The water adsorbing process in ZrMOF-1 was explored and rationalized on the basis of SCC-DFTB theoretical investigation results. The present result should be helpful for the design and fabrication of highly stable MOFs with targeted topology and pore size for advanced water vapor sorbents.

Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. Herein, we describe the construction of two bcu Zr-based MOFs (named ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2) from peripherally extended pentiptycene ligands H8PEP-1and H8PEP-2) with rigid quadrangular prism shape possessing 8 carboxylic groups at the prism vertices. Despite the significant progress achieved thus far, MOF-based water harvesting from air however is still in its infancy stage.[13] The practical atmospheric water harvesting efficiency based on MOFs is still unsatisfactory, as disclosed by their low water productivity < 1L k gMOF-1 d a y-1in energy-efficient devices.[14] More robust MOFs with promising water sorption properties are therefore highly desired. pristine sample, Figure S6, indicating the collapsible pore structure of ZrMOF-2.

After the totally covering of both the Zr6O4(OH)4(H2O)8unit and carboxyl groups by extrinsic H2Omolecules, the third water wave with 55–60 H2Omolecues as a “water bridge” then has to fill the space between the water aggregates depicted as Region 3 in Figure 4b with diminished average binding energy of (MATH)(MATH)(MATH)molecule). This is followed by the subsequent ~20H2Omolecules adsorption into the rest spaces denoted as Region 4 in Figure 4b with further reduced binding energy of - 26 ± 6 k J m o l-1(MATH)0.06 eV '/molecule). Obviously, the totlaly simulated water injection amount following the four-steps injection process amounts to 95–100 H2Omolecules for one unit cell of ZrMOF-1, in good consistence with the experimentally disclosed result, 96-100H2Omolecules per one unit cell.

In conclusion, we have constructed two highly connected MOFs with unprecedented 8,8-c bcu topology from Zr6clusters and rigid 8-c carboxylate ligands with quadrangular prism shape. In particular, ZrMOF-1 exhibits microporous structure with large BET surface area and high water stability, enabling it to be a promising water harvesting material with high water uptake capacity, steep uptake at low RH, and excellent durability. The water adsorbing process in ZrMOF-1 was explored and rationalized on the basis of SCC-DFTB theoretical investigation results. The present result should be helpful for the design and fabrication of highly stable MOFs with targeted topology and pore size for advanced water vapor sorbents.

Reticular Synthesis of Metal-Organic Frameworks by 8-Connected Quadrangular Prism Ligands for Water Harvesting

Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

Abstract: Utilization of rigid, highly connected organic linkers is critical for the reticular synthesis of functional metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. Herein, we describe the construction of two bcu Zr-based MOFs (named ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2) from peripherally extended pentiptycene ligands H8PEP-1and H8PEP-2) with rigid quadrangular prism shape possessing 8 carboxylic groups at the prism vertices. Particularly, ZrMOF-1 exhibits microporous structure with large Bruno-Emmett-Teller surface area and high water stability, endowing it a promising water harvesting material with a high water uptake capacity of 0.83:gH2OgMOF-1at P/P0 = 0.90and 25°C, a steep uptake at a low P/P0of 0.30, and excellent durability over 500 water adsorption-desorption cycles. Moreover, self-consistent charge density functional tight-binding calculations were carried out, rationalizing the water adsorbing process and amount in ZrMOF-1.

Freshwater scarcity is one of the great challenges worldwide, particularly in desert and arid regions.[1] Water harvesting from air holds a great potential to help solve the global water challenge, which however is strongly dependent on the performance of the water adsorbents.[2] To data, inorganic porous materials, e.g. silica gels and zeolites, have been widely used in these aspects.[3] However, these conven-

In recent years, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have attracted immense attention as promising adsorbents for various gases such as CO2, H2, and CH4, owing to their programmable structures with tunable pore sizes and high surface areas.[5] Particularly, the appearance of highly water stable MOFs, e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs,[6] opened up the use of MOFs in water harvesting processes. Since the pioneer report of water harvesting by using MIL-100(Fe) and MIL-101(Cr) in (MATH)and a series of -based MOFs in 2014,[8] the water sorption properties of MOFs have been well studied. Investigations revealed a few MOF samples such as MIL-53(Al),[9] MOF-801(Zr),[10] MOF-303(Al),[11] and Ni2Cl2(BTDD)[12]exhibit ideal S-shaped water sorption isotherms with large uptake capacity, high uptake at low relative humidity (RH), and excellent recyclability, ranking MOFs at the forefront of the material-based alternatives for water harvesting. Despite the significant progress achieved thus far, MOF-based water harvesting from air however is still in its infancy stage.[13] The practical atmospheric water harvesting efficiency based on MOFs is still unsatisfactory, as disclosed by their low water productivity < 1L k gMOF-1 d a y-1in energy-efficient devices.[14] More robust MOFs with promising water sorption properties are therefore highly desired. Fortunately, quite lately highly connected MOFs with high porosity for enhancing adsorption properties were fabricated by utilizing rigid, highly connected carboxylate linkers.[15] In particular, corresponding MOFs like Cr-soc-MOF and MIII-acs-MOFs derived from the carboxylate linkers with 4 and 6 coordinating functions have been demonstrated to exhibit large water uptake capacities as well as increased water stability associated with the limited accessibility of water vapor to the metal nodes.[15] However, highly water stable Al/Cr/Zr- based MOFs based on rigid 8-connected (8-c) quadrangular organic ligands have not yet been achieved, to the best of our knowledge, possibly owing to the lack of synthesis feasibility of the rigid quadrangular ligands.

analysis of ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2 revealed the rigid quadrangular prism shape of PEP-1 and PEP-2 with 8 carboxylic groups located at the prism vertices, which guide the in situ formation of 8-c Zr6clusters for the construction of the bcu nets. Importantly, ZrMOF-1 maintained its crystallinity and microporous structure after long time soak in water, acid, and base solvents, indicating its ultrahigh stability. Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. Herein, we describe the construction of two bcu Zr-based MOFs (named ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2) from peripherally extended pentiptycene ligands H8PEP-1and H8PEP-2) with rigid quadrangular prism shape possessing 8 carboxylic groups at the prism vertices. Wenbo Liu, Enyu Wu, Baoqiu Yu, Zhixin Liu, Kang Wang,* Dongdong Qi,* Bin Li,* and Jianzhuang Jiang*

Abstract: Utilization of rigid, highly connected organic linkers is critical for the reticular synthesis of functional metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). However, highlystable MOFs (e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs) based on rigid ligands with more than 6 coordinating functions have been rarely achieved thus far. Herein, we describe the construction of two bcu Zr-based MOFs (named ZrMOF-1 and ZrMOF-2) from peripherally extended pentiptycene ligands H8PEP-1and H8PEP-2) with rigid quadrangular prism shape possessing 8 carboxylic groups at the prism vertices. Particularly, ZrMOF-1 exhibits microporous structure with large Bruno-Emmett-Teller surface area and high water stability, endowing it a promising water harvesting material with a high water uptake capacity of 0.83:gH2OgMOF-1at P/P0 = 0.90and 25°C, a steep uptake at a low P/P0of 0.30, and excellent durability over 500 water adsorption-desorption cycles. Moreover, self-consistent charge density functional tight-binding calculations were carried out, rationalizing the water adsorbing process and amount in ZrMOF-1.

Freshwater scarcity is one of the great challenges worldwide, particularly in desert and arid regions.[1] Water harvesting from air holds a great potential to help solve the global water challenge, which however is strongly dependent on the performance of the water adsorbents.[2] To data, inorganic porous materials, e.g. silica gels and zeolites, have been widely used in these aspects.[3] However, these conven-

In recent years, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have attracted immense attention as promising adsorbents for various gases such as CO2, H2, and CH4, owing to their programmable structures with tunable pore sizes and high surface areas.[5] Particularly, the appearance of highly water stable MOFs, e.g. Al/Cr/Zr-based MOFs,[6] opened up the use of MOFs in water harvesting processes. Since the pioneer report of water harvesting by using MIL-100(Fe) and MIL-101(Cr) in (MATH)and a series of -based MOFs in 2014,[8] the water sorption properties of MOFs have been well studied. Investigations revealed a few MOF samples such as MIL-53(Al),[9] MOF-801(Zr),[10] MOF-303(Al),[11] and Ni2Cl2(BTDD)[12]exhibit ideal S-shaped water sorption isotherms with large uptake capacity, high uptake at low relative humidity (RH), and excellent recyclability, ranking MOFs at the forefront of the material-based alternatives for water harvesting. Despite the significant progress achieved thus far, MOF-based water harvesting from air however is still in its infancy stage.[13] The practical atmospheric water harvesting efficiency based on MOFs is still unsatisfactory, as disclosed by their low water productivity < 1L k gMOF-1 d a y-1in energy-efficient devices.[14] More robust MOFs with promising water sorption properties are therefore highly desired. Fortunately, quite lately highly connected MOFs with high porosity for enhancing adsorption properties were fabricated by utilizing rigid, highly connected carboxylate linkers.[15] In particular, corresponding MOFs like Cr-soc-MOF and MIII-acs-MOFs derived from the carboxylate linkers with 4 and 6 coordinating functions have been demonstrated to exhibit large water uptake capacities as well as increased water stability associated with the limited accessibility of water vapor to the metal nodes.[15] However, highly water stable Al/Cr/Zr- based MOFs based on rigid 8-connected (8-c) quadrangular organic ligands have not yet been achieved, to the best of our knowledge, possibly owing to the lack of synthesis feasibility of the rigid quadrangular ligands.

Multi-stage Transformations of a Cluster-Based Metal-Organic Framework: Perturbing Crystals to Glass-Forming Liquids that Re-Crystallize at High Temperature

Ming-Zhu Chen, Jian Li, Sheng Liao, Yi-Hang Guo, Tao Liu, Rui-Fang Ma, Tian-Yi Xie, Wei-Dong Liu, Si-Xu Peng, Xiaojun Kuang, Zheng Yin,* Yingbo Zhao,* and Ming-Hua Zeng*

Abstract: Glassy and liquid state metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are emerging type of materials subjected to intense research for their rich physical and chemical properties. In this report, we obtained the first glassy MOF that involves metal-carboxylate cluster building units via multi-stage structural transformations. This MOF is composed of linear [Mn3(COO)6]node and flexible pyridyl-ethenylbenzoic linker. The crystalline MOF was first perturbed by vapor hydration and thermal dehydration to give an amorphous state, which can go through a glass transition at 505Kinto a super-cooled liquid. The super-cooled liquid state is stable through a wide temperature range of 40Kand has the largest fragility index of 105, giving a broad processing window. Abstract: Glassy and liquid state metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are emerging type of materials subjected to intense research for their rich physical and chemical properties. In this report, we obtained the first glassy MOF that involves metal-carboxylate cluster building units via multi-stage structural transformations. This MOF is composed of linear [Mn3(COO)6]node and flexible pyridyl-ethenylbenzoic linker. The crystalline MOF was first perturbed by vapor hydration and thermal dehydration to give an amorphous state, which can go through a glass transition at 505Kinto a super-cooled liquid. The super-cooled liquid state is stable through a wide temperature range of 40Kand has the largest fragility index of 105, giving a broad processing window. Remarkably, the super-cooled liquid can not only be quenched into glass, but also recrystallize into the initial MOF when heated to a higher temperature above 558K. The mechanism of the multi-stage structural transformations was studied by systematic characterizations of in situ X-ray diffraction, calorimetry, rheological, spectroscopic and pair-distribution function analysis. These multi-stage transformations not only represent a rare example of high temperature coordinative recognition and self-assembly, but also provide new MOF processing strategy through crystal-amorphous-liquid-crystal transformations.

Glassy materials have been on the frontier of chemical, physical and material science research for their rich physical and chemical properties, complex structural transformations and broad scope of applications.[1] Glasses of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are emerging types of glassy materials that could combine the processibility of glasses and the designability and structural diversity of MOFs.[2,3] Conventional melt-quenching method has produced a series of MOF glasses, mainly including some special zeolitic imidazolate frameworks and coordination polymers.[4–8] Other methods have also been developed to prepare MOF glasses, such as crystallization supression[9] and solution synthesis.[10] However, considering MOF glasses derived from crystalline MOFs with 3D network structure, none of them incorpo-

rates metal-carboxylate cluster building units (Table S1), which accounts for a large part of the MOF database.[11] Though yet to be realized, MOF glasses and liquids composed of metal-carboxylate cluster building blocks could show much more complex chemical dynamics than those composed of single metal ions.[12, 13] Specifically, the metalcarboxylate cluster could have profound structural directing effect for coordinative assembly.[14] In this report, we aim to achieve glassy MOFs incorporating cluster building units and utilize their structural directing effect to achieve recrystallization from liquid state.

As construction of MOFs with cluster building units often requires chelating linkers that form strong bonds with metal ions (i.e. carboxylate), the melt-quenching method would not be applicable due to thermal decomposition prior

to melting (Scheme 1).[15, 16] To achieve glassy material from crystalline MOFs, partially breaking the metal-linker bond is required to give necessary configurational motion for the transformations.[1] In a previous study, we showed that water adsorption could perturb the metal coordination sphere and partially break the metal-linker bond, which can be coupled with thermal excitation to vitrify MOFs that cannot be melted.[17, 18] This synergistic stimulus of water adsorption, desorption and heating harnessed the dynamics of MOFs at different levels, from coordination sphere distortion at the metal nodes, conformation change of the organic linkers, to configuration distortion of the framework backbones.[19, 20]

Herein, we show that the sequential chemical and thermal perturbation can be applied to enable multi-stage structure transformations of [Mn3(peb)6]· 2DMF (c-Mn3, Hpeb bis{4-[2-(4-pyridyl)ethenyl]} benzoic acid), a MOF with metal-carboxylate cluster building unit. The crystalline MOF first become amorphous after water adsorption and desorption, which then undergoes glass transition at 505Kand enters super-cooled liquid state. The super-cooled liquid can be quenched into glassy state, giving the first MOF glass based on metal-carboxylate cluster building unit (Scheme 1). Remarkably, the super-cooled liquid of the [Mn3]� MOF recrystallize to give back the original structure when heated to higher temperature above 558K. Such multi-stage transformation involving crystal, amorphous, glassy and liquid state is the key feature of the present MOF, which is unprecedented and represent a rare example of coordinative recognition and assembly at high temperature. Considering the sophisticated and modularly designed MOFs almost all have metal-carboxylate cluster building blocks, enabling MOFs with these cluster building units to enter liquid and glassy state is a fundamentally significant step forward for MOF chemistry and application. The recrystallization phenomenon also opens up new routes of MOF processing through crystalline-amorphous-liquid-crystalline transformations. This multi-stage transformation represents a lop in the energy diagram and further the fundamental understanding

In summary, the rationally selected MOF, featuring [Mn3(COO)6]nodes, dynamic linkers and small pore volume, has been transformed into its super-cooled liquid state by a carefully designed synergistic perturbation process. The glass-forming liquid is stable across a wide temperature range of more than 40K, endowing the glassy MOF with high processibility. When heated to higher temperature, the super-cooled liquid undergoes a recrystallization process to give the original MOF structure. The multi-stage structural transformations have been characterized by a series of in situ and ex situ PXRD, calorimetry, and pair distribution function analysis along with spectroscopic techniques including infrared, Raman and XPS spectroscopy. Such recrystallization is a rare example of molecular recognition driven

coordinative assembly for high temperature liquid, which could also enable a MOFs processing route through crystalline-liquid-crystalline transformations. As the modularity and versatility of reticular chemistry is best represented by MOFs with metal-carboxylate cluster, we believe bringing these MOFs into liquid and glassy states would lead to great opportunities for developing MOF chemistry in highly dynamic, high temperature condensed matter states.
