A light-induced spin crossover actuated single-chain magnet

Tao Liu1 , Hui Zheng1 , Soonchul Kang2, Yoshihito Shiota3, Shinya Hayami4, Masaki Mito5, Osamu Sato2, Kazunari Yoshizawa3, Shinji Kanegawa2 & Chunying Duan1

Both spin-crossover complexes and molecular nanomagnets display bistable magnetic states, potentially behaving as elementary binary units for information storage. It is a challenge to introduce spin-crossover units into molecular nanomagnets to switch the bistable state of the nanomagnets through external stimuli-tuned spin crossover. Here we report an iron(II) spincrossover unit and paramagnetic iron(III) ions that are incorporated into a well-isolated double-zigzag chain. The chain exhibits thermally induced reversible spin-crossover and lightinduced excited spin-state trapping at the iron(II) sites. Single-chain magnet behaviour is actuated accompanying the synergy between light-induced excited spin-state trapping at the iron(II) sites and ferromagnetic interactions between the photoinduced high-spin iron(II) and low-spin iron(III) ions in the chain. The result provides a strategy to switch the bistable state of molecular nanomagnets using external stimuli such as light and heat, with the potential to erase and write information at a molecular level.

t is a challenge to reduce the size of electronic devices and increase information density in materials area. As a result, molecules possessing magnetic bistable states are attracting a great deal of attention1–18, because these bistable states can act as elementary binary units (bits) used for information storage, providing potential applications in high-density information storage3,5, quantum computing10 and spintronics13. In general, spin-crossover (SCO) complexes1–7 a nd molecular nanomagnets8–18 show such magnetic bistable states. SCO complexes show reversible transformation between a high-spin (HS) and a low-spin (LS) state1–7. In particular, the light-induced excited spin-state trapping (LIESST)19–34, which induces conversion of a LS state to a HS state by means of light irradiation, has attracted considerable interest. LIESST effects have been observed in various Fe(II)(or a few Fe(III)) mononuclear complexes19–24. Moreover, SCO units and other paramagnetic ions have been linked via a short bridge to control intramolecular magnetic interactions25–33 and generate magnetic ordering34 via LIESST. However, no one has so far succeeded in introducing light-responsive SCO units into molecular nanomagnets, such as single-chain magnets (SCMs) and singlemolecule magnets, to switch the bistable states of the nanomagnets.

SCMs possess bistable states capable of interchanging between two magnetic polarization directions14–18. Although various types of SCMs have been synthesized, it is a challenge to produce and eliminate their bistable states using external stimuli, such as light, heat and so (MATH). The requirements for obtaining an SCM are uniaxial (Ising) anisotropy, strong intrachain magnetic interactions and weak interchain magnetic interactions14–18. Hence, the most effective approach towards tuning the SCM behaviour is to control directly the anisotropy of ions and intrachain magnetic interactions using external stimuli. LIESST can involve concomitant changes of spin state and anisotropy at the metal centres and subsequent changes of magnetic interaction pathways in the framework19–34. If the light-responsive SCO units can be incorporated in a chain, both the anisotropy of metal ions and the intrachain magnetic interactions will be tuned accompanying the LIESST effect25–34, producing a potential lightresponsive SCM. Moreover, LIESST involves only one type of metal ion, providing the possibility to combine SCO units and various metal ions to produce photoswitchable SCMs. However, the LIESST effect has not yet been adopted successfully to switch the SCM behaviour.

To synthesize a photoswitchable SCM using LIESST effect, the requirements of both SCM behaviours and LIESST effect should be considered. Until now, LIESST effects have been reported for Fe(II)and Fe(III)complexes19–34. Moreover, SCM behaviours have also been reported for complexes containing Fe(II)and LS Fe(III)ions38. Therefore, it is possible to obtain a photoswitchable SCM based on the LIESST effect of Fe(II). Herein, we incorporate Fe(II)SCO units and paramagnetic LS Fe(III)ions into a cyanide-bridged Fe(III)chain using the following building block: [Bu4N][Fe(Tp*)(CN)3](MATH)hydrotris(3,5-dimethylpyrazolyl) borate). The cyanide bridges are supposed to link and FeIII ions into a chain and provide efficient superexchange pathways for strong magnetic interactions. The HS FeiIion is paramagnetic (S = 2)) and usually has a strong anisotropy, whereas the Fe(II)ion is diamagnetic (S = 0)and has no anisotropy, providing a switchable anisotropy. Moreover, the intrachain magnetic interactions between Fe(III)and Fe(II)ions can be switched accompanying the diamagnetic and paramagnetic transformations at the Fe(II)sites. The bulky ligand is introduced to avoid interchain magnetic interactions. Furthermore, a long ditopic, magnetically inert organic linker -bis-pyridin-4- ylmethylene hydrazine (bpmh) is adopted to tune the ligand field of Fe(II)sites, to provide the possible light-induced spin transition and to link the Ising chains into two-dimensional networks,

maintaining a sufficiently large ratio of intra- to interchain magnetic interactions without changing the SCM behaviour significantly. Herein, based on the above strategy, the complex Fe(III)(1), composed of cyanidebridged Fe(III)chains, is synthesized. Complex 1 exhibits thermally induced reversible SCO and photoinduced spin transition at the Fe(II)sites. The SCM behaviour is switched, accompanying the synergy between the LIESST effect at the Fe(II)sites, and the ferromagnetic interactions between the photoinduced HS Fe(II)and LS Fe(III)ions in the chain.

Discussion

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out to estimate changes in electronic structures (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table S4). A three-cluster model was used to calculate the spin densities and electronic states of 1 (Supplementary Tables S5 and S6). These results suggest that a ferromagnetic exchange coupling between Fe(III)and Fe(II)units causes the predominant magnetic interaction in the double-zigzag chain in compound 1. Furthermore, to support the occurrence of the LIESST effect, we measured the ultraviolet–visible–near infrared absorption spectra of the high-temperature phase, low-temperature phase and the low-temperature phase after photoirradiation (Supplementary Fig. S9). When the HS state thermally changed to the LS state, the absorption peaks near 550 and 1, 100 nmincreased. This change in absorption intensity is induced by a spin transition from HS to LS at the Fe(II)sites, which has been confirmed via Mo¨ssbauer measurements and single crystal analysis. On the basis of previously reported results for Fe(II)SCO complexes, the broad absorption band near 550 nmfor the low-temperature phase with FeLSIfcan be mainly attributed to the metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) transition (Supplementary Fig. S9). Furthermore, the absorption near 1, 100 nmis probably attributable to the intervalence charge transfer from FeLSIIto Fe(III). The photoinduced magnetization was observed when the compound was irradiated with 473 and 532 nmlight; these wavelengths correspond to the excitation of the MLCT transition.

When the LIESST effect is actually induced by light, the hightemperature phase should be generated. Indeed, when the complex with Fe(II)was irradiated at 8Kthe intensity of the peaks near 550 and 1, 100 nmdecreased. This result suggests that the low-temperature phase with Fe(II)transformed into the hightemperature phase with FeHSIIand is consistent with the occurrence of a spin transition because of light exposure. Notably, the photoinduced change is incomplete, because the interiors of the particles in the complex remain unchanged.

To further confirm that the absorption change induced by light and temperature is consistent with the induction of a spin transition, time-dependent DFT calculations were used to

calculate the excited-state energies, oscillator strengths and the electron density difference maps (Supplementary Fig. S10). The time-dependent-DFT calculations show that the strong absorption near 550 nmis primarily because of the MLCT band. Similarly, the absorption near 1, 100 nmfor the low-temperature phase is because of the intervalence charge transfer from ΔFeIIΔLSto Fe(III). Thus, this result supports the conclusion that the thermally and photo-induced absorption changes are because of the spin transition in Fe(II).

In summary, Fe(II)SCO units and paramagnetic Fe(III)ions were alternated successfully in a double-zigzag chain. The SCM behaviour was switched with LIESST because of the formation of a ferromagnetic chain after irradiation. The present results provide an approach to combine the SCO and the SCM behaviour together to control the bistable state of molecular nanomagnets via LIESST effect, with the potential to erase and write information at a molecular level.

Methods

Synthesis of compound 1. All reagents were available commercially and used without further purification. The compound [Bu4N][Fe(Tp*)(CN)3]was synthesized according to a modified literature method39. A 1.0-ml aqueous solution containing 0.05 mmolof Fe(ClO4)2·6H2Owas placed at the bottom of a test tube, and a 2.0-ml methanol solution containing 0.1 mmol of [Bu4N][Fe(Tp*)(CN)3]and 0.1 mmol of bpmh was layered on the solution. Crystallization required several weeks, and crystals were obtained in 65%yield, based on Fe(ClO4)2·6H2O. The elemental analysis calculations yielded the following values for C48H58B2Fe3N22O2: C, 49.52; H, 5.02; and N, 26.47; on the other hand, the corresponding observed values were as follows: C, 49.56; H, 4.94; and N, 26.61.

Mo¨ssbauer spectra measurements. Mo¨ssbauer spectra (isomer shift versus metallic iron at room temperature) were measured using a Wissel MVT-1000 Mo¨ssbauer spectrometer with a 57Cosource in the transmission mode. Measurements at low temperature were performed using a closed-cycle helium

refrigerator cryostat (Iwatani Co., Ltd). The sample was encapsulated in a sample holder to avoid loss of crystal water when pulling a vacuum on the cryostat.

Ultraviolet–visible–near infrared spectroscopy. Variable-temperature ultraviolet–visible–near infrared absorption spectra were measured using a UV-3100 (Shimadzu) with a helium-flow type refrigerator (Helitran LT-3-110). We measured the ultraviolet–visible–near infrared absorption spectra of the hightemperature phase, low-temperature phase and the low-temperature phase after photoirradiation.

Thermogravimetric analysis. Thermogravimetric analysis was performed at a rate of 10°C*min-1under an Ar atmosphere using a TG/DTA Q600 system (Supplementary Fig. S11).

Magnetic studies. Magnetic measurements of the samples were performed using a Quantum Design SQUID (MPMS-XL-7) magnetometer. On pumping at room temperature, the uncoordinated water molecules of compound 1 are removed easily, which may change the magnetic properties significantly. To prevent the loss of these uncoordinated water molecules, measurements were performed on finely ground microcrystalline powders of compound 1 restrained in a frozen eicosane matrix with polycarbonate capsules. Data were corrected for the diamagnetic contribution calculated from Pascal constants.

Magnetic studies of the dehydrated samples were performed under a (MATH)field in the temperature range from 2 to 400K(Supplementary Fig. S12). The sample was mounted into the SQUID machine and purged at 400Kto avoid the adsorption of water during the measurement.

Photomagnetic measurements. A powdered sample, which was spread on a commercial transparent adhesive tape, was used to study the photo-effects. The weight of the sample on the tape was determined by measuring the weight of the tape before and after spreading the sample and determining the difference. To prevent the loss of uncoordinated water molecules, the sample was introduced directly into the sample chamber at 100K(He atmosphere) without purging.

The photoirradiation of the samples was performed at 5 K with a laser diode pumped Nd:YAG laser λ = 532 nm, (MATH), 12 h) or Nd:YAG laser ( λ = 473 nm, (MATH), 12 h). The temperature-dependent magnetization was measured both before and after irradiation in the temperature range from 2 to 150K. The difference in the magnetization before and after irradiation was extracted by subtracting the magnetization value before irradiation from that after irradiation. Furthermore, from these magnetization values and the sample weight, the difference in the wT values before and after irradiation (MATH)were calculated.

Structure determinations and refinements. The X-ray diffraction experiment for compound 1 was performed on a Rigaku charge-coupled device diffractometer using Mo-Ka radiation at 296 and 13K. The structures were solved by a direct method and refined by full-matrix least-squares on F2using the SHELX programme with anisotropic thermal parameters for all non-hydrogen atoms. Hydrogen atoms were added geometrically and refined using the riding model.

Computational methods. A three-cluster model of compound 1 was optimized in the LS triplet state (LSFM) and the HS septet state (HSFM) using the DFT. After optimization, we carried out single-point calculations (for HS and LS) and obtained electronic structures of the LS antiferromagnetic, HS antiferromagnetic and HS ferro- and antiferromagnetic states. The B3LYP* function40 was used. The SDD basis set41 was used for Fe atom and the basis (MATH)for H, C, B and N atoms. The programme we used is Gaussian 09 (ref. 43).

Jingui Duan , Masakazu Higuchi , Satoshi Horike , Maw Lin Foo , Koya Prabhakara Rao , Yasutaka Inubushi , Tomohiro Fukushima , and Susumu Kitagawa *

Because of the theoretically limitless possibilities in assembling organic linkers and metal or cluster connectors, a large number of structures have been reported, but only a few of them show outstanding selectivity for CO2over CH4,[5]which is mainly attributed to the large quadruple moment of CO2whereas CH4has none. In this light, several strategies have been employed to design frameworks with good water stability and high separation capability as follows. 1) Frameworks with dense open metal sites, such as MOF-74, [6h,8] have good separation capacity, but frameworks with divalent metals are very sensitive to water and are even worse in acidic and basic environments. 2) Carboranebased frameworks with small pores and open metal sites show the predicted selectivity [12] , however, the stability of these frameworks has not yet been demonstrated. 3) Tetravalent metal-based frameworks, such as UiO-66, [13] show good water stability, however, the 12-coordinated nodes may impede effi - cient adsorption sites. [13] Therefore, even now, there is still no clear solution.

To overcome these issues, our strategy is to employ the trivalent La3+ion and H3BTBligand (MATH)tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene) to construct porous frameworks. Because of

2. Results and Discussion

2.1. Preparation, Characterization and Structure of [La(BTB) (MATH)• solvent(1⊃guest)

The new PCP, [La(BTB)H2O]· solvent ( 1⊃guest), was hydrothermally synthesized by a new method, different from previously reported, [14] from a mixture of H3BTBand La(NO3)3·6H2Oin -dimethylformamide/methanol H2O. The structure was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis, and the phase purity of the powder materials was confi rmed by the powder X-ray diffraction pattern (PXRD) and elemental analysis. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) shows that 1 is thermally stable up to 350°Cunder N2atmosphere. After exchanging the guest solvents with methanol, we obtained the completely activated framework, as indicated by the IR and TG profi les (see the Supporting Information).

X-ray crystallography shows that 1 (Figure 1 and Supporting Information Figure S4–7) crystallizes in the R 32 space group, a = 28.764 (4)Å, c = 12.563 (3) sÅ. We note that although powder diffraction patterns of LaBTB have been reported, no single crystal structure has been reported yet. [14] The overall structure of 1 possesses 1D hexagonal channels (the size of the aperture window is ca.10 Å) with an open La chain. Because of the faceto-face assembly of the BTB ligands, the distances between the adjacent benzene rings vary from 3.53 to 4.47 A. In other words, between the two adjacent benzene rings, there is not enough space for the guest molecules, including even H2with the smallest molecular dimension. Thus, the well-packed benzene

rings with a high concentration of protons acts like a wall that can provide a hydrophobic environment for water stability. [15] In addition, the accessible volume of the fully desolvated 1 is ca. 52.3%, calculated using the PLATON program [16] . The total specifi c pore volume calculated from the maximum amount of N2adsorbed is 0.416 cm3 g-1.

2.2. Water and Chemical Stability

Water and chemical stability are an important properties for any sorbent that has the potential to be used in so many important applications, [17] especially for industry. However, the stability of PCP materials varies depending on the structure and the strength of the coordination bonds between metal clusters and ligands. [18] The water and chemical stability of 1 were examined by soaking the as-synthesized samples in harsh conditions: hot ( 60°Cand (MATH)) aqueous HCl (pH = 2)), aqueous NaOH (MATH)14) and water solutions for three days. The PXRD patterns of a series of samples strongly indicate the integrity of the framework under these conditions ( Figure 2 ). Smart Metal–Organic Frameworks with Reversible Luminescence/Magnetic Switch Behavior for HCl Vapor Detection

Zhong-Hong Zhu, Zhiqiang Ni, Hua-Hong Zou, Guangxue Feng,* and Ben Zhong Tang*

Smart luminescent metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) demonstrate promising performance in the detection of toxic gases. The incorporation of twisted or rotary organic ligands with aggregation-induced emission (AIE) characteristics can provide further opportunities in designing such smart MOFs with new topologies and stimuli-responsive behaviors. Herein, novel AIE MOFs are reported with reversible luminescence or a magnetic switch for HCl vapor detection. The twisted conformation of tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)ethylene (TCPE) ligand leads to the unique (MATH)(MATH)(MATH)metal clusters, (MATH)ligand) configuration for ZnMOF and CoMOF. Different from conventional MOFs with [M- L]∞topology, ZnMOF and CoMOF exhibit a blue-to-yellow greenish fluorescence transition and a ferrimagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic switch behavior, respectively, upon recognition of HCl vapor. The adsorbed HCl molecules rather than coordinated ones are determined to be the main reason, and such luminescence and magnetic switch can be induced in a reversible manner via HCl vapor adsorption/desorption processes with high reliability. This work of AIE MOFs with twisted and rotary ligands shall pave new avenue in design of smart MOFs with new topologies and stimuli-responsive behavior for real-time sensing and detection applications.

1. Introduction

Detection of toxic chemical vapors (e.g., NH3, H2S, HCl, NOxetc.) is attracting increasing attention owing to the health, environment and humanitarian concerns.[1] One of the particular examples is HCl vapor which is largely generated in fertilizer production, electroplating, textile and rubber industry, and its acute exposure could cause hoarseness, ulceration of respiratory tract and pulmonary edema, etc.[2] In addition, as a highly toxic and corrosive species, the workplace exposure limit for HCl is 5 ppm. Individuals cannot stand being exposed to HCl vapor in the range of 50–100  ppm and exposure to 1300–2000 ppm of HCl is deadly.[3] Hence, smart materials capable of toxic gases especially HCl vapor detection under ambient conditions is vitally important in modern age. Currently, the fluorescence detection of HCl vapor is mainly based on organic fluorescent molecular films or complexes, and their detection limits are about 20–80  ppm. Therefore, it is urgent

to develop smart materials with lower detection limits towards HCl vapor.[4] These smart materials should possess large specific surface area, good gas accessibility, quick responsive time and high sensitivity. In this regard, luminescent metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with inherent porosity and great synthetic versatility represent one of such ideal smart materials.[5]

MOFs are well-defined crystalline solid constructed from metal ions or clusters and organic linkers.[6] The vast choices of metal second building units (SBUs), organic linkers and topologies provide infinite active sites for gas interaction and detection.[7] The skeletons, metal nodes and the porous space could all be utilized to tune luminescence during such detection process.[8] Moreover, the definite crystal structure information and exact connection sequence of MOFs also promote the in-depth mechanism study.[7c] Therefore, significant progress has been made in the use of luminescent MOFs for toxic gas detection in recent years, including NOxH2S, SOxvoltaic organic compounds, etc.[9] However, luminescent MOFs for HCl vapor detection especially in a repeatable manner are still very rare due to their inertness and instability to the corrosive HCl vapors.

The discovery of fluorogens with aggregation-induced emission (AIE) (AIEgens) provides great opportunities for design of luminescent materials.[10] AIEgens usually possess propeller structures, which show negligible fluorescence in solution but exhibit largely intensified emission upon restriction of intramolecular motions (RIMs) in aggregated state.[11] Constructing luminescent MOFs with AIE ligands could block intramolecular motions to certain degree to generate bright emission for optical applications.[12] Moreover, the porous space provides exceptional opportunities to further modulate the intramolecular motions of AIE ligands in solid phase for design of smart luminescent MOFs.[13] In recent years, AIE MOFs with different metal cations (MATH), Mg2+, Sr2+, Zr4+, etc.) have gradually appeared, we and others have shown the promising performance of AIE MOFs in different applications.[14] However, the development of AIE MOFs for corrosive gas especially HCl vapor detection are still rare. Moreover, the twisted geometry of AIE ligands shall afford great opportunities for design MOFs with new topologies and more stimuli-responsive behaviors that might achieve such goals but remains to be explored.

Herein, we report two 3D MOFs (ZnMOF and CoMOF) with new topologies of [metal clusters –ligand (MATH)configuration for HCl vapor detection via luminescence or magnetic switch. The distort tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)ethylene (TCPE) ligands were connected to multiple SBUs with different charge states (MATH)in a single MOF. The resultant ZnMOF and CoMOF exhibited the unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration, which affords these MOFs the specific luminescence or magnetic switch behavior upon adsorbing and disrobing HCl vapor. HCl adsorption leads to a fast blue-to-yellow greenish fluorescence transition for ZnMOF, and a ferrimagnetic-toantiferromagnetic switch behavior for CoMOF (Scheme 1). Further analysis reveals that the adsorbed HCl molecules rather than coordinated ones contribute to such switch due to the introduced dipole effects and interchain antiferromagnetic interactions by guest HCl molecules. Hence, ZnMOF

[Figure: Scheme 1. Schematic illustration of [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configured AIE MOFs for HCl vapor induced reversible luminescence or magnetic switch.]

and CoMOF exhibited reversible luminescence and magnetic switch behavior, respectively. In addition, such unique topology also exposed large number of unsaturated Co2+ions in CoMOF, which leads to a fast and sensitive fluorescence light-up detection of histidine (His) via Co2+/H i scoupling induced MOF collapse. Our work of smart AIE MOFs with [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration that show HCl vapor induced reversible luminescence or magnetic switch shall pave new avenues for the design of new luminescent MOF-based sensors.

2. Results and Discussion

2.1. Synthesis and Characterization of AIE MOFs

Previous work reported that the solvothermal reaction between TCPE and Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oresulted in ZnTCPE, which showed staggered 2D MOF sheets made from paddlewheel shaped Zn2(TCPE)4SBUs bridged by TCPE ligands (Figure 1a).[13a,b] In this work, 3D ZnMOF-Solv was obtained by solvothermal reaction between TCPE and Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oin diethylformamide (DEF)/water (v/v = 1/1)mixture at 85°C(see the synthesis part of the Supporting Information). Single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) analysis reveals that ZnMOF-Solv crystallizes in the C2/cspace group of the monoclinic system (Tables S1 and S2, Supporting Information), with a very large single crystal unit cell volume of 47 192 (5) Å3 . Different from ZnTCPE which possesses neutrally charged SBUs, there exists three different geometries for TCPE ligands in the independent unit of ZnMOF-Solv, which coordinated with Zn2+ions via different coordination modes and formed Zn SBUs with three different charge states (MATH)(Figure  1b). In detail, Zn2(TCPE)2(H2O)2(NO3)cluster with charge is composed of two four-coordinated Zn2+ions with a triangular pyramid coordination configuration. The neutrally charged Zn2(TCPE)3(H2O)(NO3)cluster contains one five-coordinated Zn2+ion (pyramid coordination configuration) and one four-coordinated Zn2+ion (triangular pyramid coordination configuration). Two four-coordinated Zn2+ions (triangular pyramid coordination configuration) and one six-coordinated Zn2+ion (double quadrangular pyramid coordination configuration) linked via five TPCE, three end-coordinated H2Omolecules, one µ3-bridged O2-, form charged Zn3(O)(L1)5(H2O)3cluster. The alternating connection between these Zn clusters and TCPE forms an effective (MATH)(MATH)configuration with a pore size of 8.90 Å (Figure 1b). In the pores of ZnMOF-Solv, unsaturated Zn2+ions and O atoms are exposed. Density functional theory calculation based on such conformation also revealed similar distinct electrostatic surface potential distributions for these Zn SBUs, in consistence with their different charge states (Figure S1, Supporting Information). To the best of our knowledge, the synthesized ZnMOF-Solv represents one of these rare MOFs with multiple SBUs possessing different charge states,[15] which also is the first time to realize AIE MOF with [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration. Polycrystalline powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) shows that a large number of ZnMOF-Solv crystal samples we obtained are pure phases (Figure S2, Supporting Information). In addition, the scanning electron microscope (SEM) also showed that the surface of the columnar ZnMOF-Solv crystal is very clean

[Figure: Figure 1. Structures of a) ZnTCPE and b) ZnMOF-Solv.]

(Figure S3, Supporting Information). The thermogravimetric (TG-DTG) results indicated that ZnMOF-Solv had two weight loss processes before 300°C, corresponding to the loss of free 21 H2Omolecules (9.55%)and 6 DEF molecules (15.24%)in its pores (Figure S4, Supporting Information). As the temperature further rises above 400°C, the ZnMOF-Solv framework rapidly decomposes. The weak X-ray diffraction for the activated ZnMOF (soaking in methanol for 12 hand followed by drying) prevents further structure confirmation for ZnMOF, while it showed similar PXRD spectrum as compared to ZnMOF-Solv, indicating that the main crystal structures of ZnMOF remain the same as ZnMOF-Solv. ZnMOF are colorless and transparent block crystals under observation of a 20X stereo microscope, and these crystals show blue luminescence under the irradiation of a 365 nmultraviolet (UV) lamp (Figure S5, Supporting Information). ZnMOF showed a very similar emission spectrum as compared to TCPE powder, indicating the luminescence of ZnMOF is originated from TCPE. While the much higher fluorescence intensity of ZnMOF over TCPE shall be due to the MOF coordination, which immobilizes TCPE ligand to increase the emission via RIM. It should be noted that ZnMOF showed a very high tolerance towards acidic and alkali environment, as indicated by the unchanged PXRD data after immersing in aqueous solutions with different pH values for 24 h. 2.2. Luminescence Response to HCl Vapor

Considering the unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration in ZnMOF, we hypothesize that it can effectively show fluorescence response to gases with strong dipole effects, such as HCl vapor. To test this hypothesis, ZnMOF was fumigated with the HCl vapor from a HCl solution (12%)in a closed glass bottle 20°C, CHClvapor = 223.7ppm).[16] Within a very short fumigation time (<15 s), ZnMOF showed a fast white-to-yellow color change under daylight, and a blue-to-yellow greenish emission transition under a 365  nm UV lamp (Figure 2a). Solid-state fluorescence spectra revealed the linearly bathochromic-shifted emission maxima from 445 to 510 nmas well as linearly descended fluorescence intensity along with increased fumigation time (Figure  2b and Figure S8, Supporting Information). We further fumigated ZnMOF with HCl vapor from different HCl solutions at a fixed fumigation time (5 s). As expected, the bathochromic-shifted emission peaks and weakened emission intensities along with increased HCl solution concentration were observed (Figure 2c). By converting the HCl solution to HCl vapor concentration, ZnMOF showed a very excellent HCl vapor detection capability by monitoring the emission wavelength or intensity changes. The limit of detection (LOD)

Such an extremely low LOD permits the rapid and sensitive detection of HCl vapor exposure, and the high sensitivity shall be attributed to the porous nature of ZnMOF, which provided huge surface area for HCl vapor adsorption. In addition, ZnMOF showed negligible fluorescence and PXRD spectrum changes upon fumigation with other acidic or alkali volatile vapors (such as HBr, HNO3, NH3) (Figure 2e,f, and Figure S12, Supporting Information), indicating its good selectivity towards HCl vapor. With temperature rising above 400°C, ZnMOF-HCl framework rapidly decomposes with two DTG peaks (MATH)and (MATH)). This further prompted us to think whether adsorbed or coordinated ones are responsible for the fluorescence changes. The fluorescence spectrum of ZnMOF-HCl- 350°Cis basically recovered to ZnMOF (Figure  3b), indicating that the responsiveness of ZnMOF towards HCl vapor is caused by free adsorbed HCl molecules in the pores. 2.3. Magnetic Switch to HCl Vapor

The selection of metal ions is one of the most important factors that determines the structures and functions of MOFs.[17] Different metal ions used to construct MOFs can affect their applications in many fields such as optics and magnetics. CoMOF-Solv is synthesized by changing Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oto Co(NO3)2·6H2O(See the synthesis part of Supporting Information), which is fine purple crystals. Due to weak diffraction signal, we are unable to determine its single crystal structure using SCXRD. Instead, we simulated the PXRD spectrum using ZnMOF-Solv topology, and luckily the PXRD result of CoMOF-Solv is nearly identical to such simulated data (Figure 4a), indicating that CoMOF-Solv is a pure phase and possesses the same 3D porous topology as ZnMOF-Solv.[18] Pawley refinement to the PXRD data of CoMOF and ZnMOF revealed nearly identical unit cell parameters, which proves that ZnMOF and CoMOF are isomorphic (Figure S21, Supporting Information). CoMOF-Solv showed a similar TG curve with ZnMOF-Solv, further indicating their similar crystal structures (Figure S22a, Supporting Information). In addition, the SEM of CoMOF-Solv showed that its surface was smooth and very clean (Figure S3, Supporting Information). The UV-Vis absorption spectrum shows that CoMOF (CoMOF-Solv is soaked in methanol for 12 hand then dried) has a strong absorption band in the range of 400–760 nm with a absorption peak centered at 557  nm (Figure  4b), which is slightly red-shifted as compared

to Co(NO3)2·6H2O(500 nm) (Figure S23, Supporting Information). It is worth noting that CoMOF does not emit fluorescence as Co2+is reported to be an effective fluorescence quencher.[19] In addition, CoMOF showed a surface area of 823.2633 m2 g-1(Figure S24, Supporting Information), similar to that of ZnMOF.

Inspired by recent work that (EQUATION)configured MOF showed magnetic properties changes between paramagnetism and ferrimagnetism upon CO2adsorption/desorption,[20] we suspect that our CoMOF could also show magnetic switch upon HCl adsorption. To test this hypothesis, we fumigated CoMOF with HCl vapor for 2h. The TG of CoMOF-HCl was also tested, and the results showed that it was consistent with the guest molecules of ZnMOF-HCl (Figure S22b, Supporting Information). The resultant CoMOF-HCl showed dark green appearance, different from the purple colored CoMOF (Figure  4b), with a red-shifted absorption spectrum (the absorption peak shifted from 557  nm for CoMOF to 670 nmfor CoMOF-HCl). The molar magnetic susceptibility (MATH)of CoMOF and CoMOF-HCl was further tested under the temperature range of 2–300 K (Figure  4c).[21] As the temperature decreases, the value of CoMOF gradually decreases. When the temperature is close to 2 K, the value rises sharply and reaches the maximum value. The change trend of under the condition of an external DC field indicates the ferrimagnetic behavior for CoMOF. On the contrary, CoMOF-HCl exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior, as revealed by the partial upward trend of value when the temperature is close to 2 K. The Loop results show that neither CoMOF nor CoMOF-HCl has obvious hysteresis (Figure S25, Supporting Information). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results indicate that the metal center Co ions in CoMOF and CoMOF-HCl are both divalent (Figure 4d), therefore excluding the cause of magnetic switch by Co valence state changes. XPS detected the main peaks as 781.72  eV (sat. 786.72  eV) and 797.63  eV (sat. 803.63  eV), which can be classified as Co (MATH)and Co (MATH)and the XPS of C, N and O elements are consistent with the structure (Figure S26, Supporting Information). CoMOF-HCl could be recovered to its initial ferromagnetic condition upon heating at 350°Cfor 2hto remove adsorbed HCl molecules, proving its magnetic switching behavior (Figure  4c). In addition, the similar PXRD spectra of CoMOF-HCl-350 °C and CoMOF-HCl indicates that the coordinated HCl is not lost under heating at 350°C(Figure S27, Supporting Information), suggesting that coordinated HCl does not contribute to the magnetic change. Such magnetic switch shall be due to the presence of adsorbed HCl molecules in the pores, which provides weak antiferromagnetic interactions to CoMOF-HCl.[23] To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the magnetic switching of MOF synthesized by AIE ligands has been realized.

So far, high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is still widely selected as the qualitative and quantitative analysis of His. However, HPLC is expensive,

3. Conclusion

In summary, we herein reported new AIE MOFs with unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞topology and demonstrated their promising potentials in HCl vapor detection via luminescence or magnetic switch. With the twisted structures of AIE ligands, the coordination between TCPE and Zn2+or Co2+ions leads to SBUs with different coordination nodes and charge states. The synthesized AIE MOF possesses a unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration for the first time. Such frame structure renders ZnMOF the ability to show luminescence switch in response to HCl vapor with high sensitivity and selectivity. When changing the Zn2+to Co2+ions, CoMOF surprisingly demonstrated magnetic switch from ferrimagnetic to antiferromagnetic behavior upon adsorbing HCl vapor. This work represents the first discovery of the magnetic switch of AIEbased MOFs during stimulus response to the best of our knowledge. In addition, the nonemissive CoMOF also exhibited specific fluorescence light-up when meeting His with high sensitivity owing to the exposure of large amount of unsaturated Co2+ions for His coupling. The study reveals the promises and advantages of introducing twisted and rotary AIE ligands to MOFs construction, which shall open new windows to the development of MOFs with new topology and smart stimuli-responsive behaviors.

Smart Metal–Organic Frameworks with Reversible Luminescence/Magnetic Switch Behavior for HCl Vapor Detection

Zhong-Hong Zhu, Zhiqiang Ni, Hua-Hong Zou, Guangxue Feng,* and Ben Zhong Tang*

Smart luminescent metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) demonstrate promising performance in the detection of toxic gases. The incorporation of twisted or rotary organic ligands with aggregation-induced emission (AIE) characteristics can provide further opportunities in designing such smart MOFs with new topologies and stimuli-responsive behaviors. Herein, novel AIE MOFs are reported with reversible luminescence or a magnetic switch for HCl vapor detection. The twisted conformation of tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)ethylene (TCPE) ligand leads to the unique (MATH)(MATH)(MATH)metal clusters, (MATH)ligand) configuration for ZnMOF and CoMOF. Different from conventional MOFs with [M- L]∞topology, ZnMOF and CoMOF exhibit a blue-to-yellow greenish fluorescence transition and a ferrimagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic switch behavior, respectively, upon recognition of HCl vapor. The adsorbed HCl molecules rather than coordinated ones are determined to be the main reason, and such luminescence and magnetic switch can be induced in a reversible manner via HCl vapor adsorption/desorption processes with high reliability. This work of AIE MOFs with twisted and rotary ligands shall pave new avenue in design of smart MOFs with new topologies and stimuli-responsive behavior for real-time sensing and detection applications.

1. Introduction

Detection of toxic chemical vapors (e.g., NH3, H2S, HCl, NOxetc.) is attracting increasing attention owing to the health, environment and humanitarian concerns.[1] One of the particular examples is HCl vapor which is largely generated in fertilizer production, electroplating, textile and rubber industry, and its acute exposure could cause hoarseness, ulceration of respiratory tract and pulmonary edema, etc.[2] In addition, as a highly toxic and corrosive species, the workplace exposure limit for HCl is 5 ppm. Individuals cannot stand being exposed to HCl vapor in the range of 50–100  ppm and exposure to 1300–2000 ppm of HCl is deadly.[3] Hence, smart materials capable of toxic gases especially HCl vapor detection under ambient conditions is vitally important in modern age. Currently, the fluorescence detection of HCl vapor is mainly based on organic fluorescent molecular films or complexes, and their detection limits are about 20–80  ppm. Therefore, it is urgent

to develop smart materials with lower detection limits towards HCl vapor.[4] These smart materials should possess large specific surface area, good gas accessibility, quick responsive time and high sensitivity. In this regard, luminescent metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with inherent porosity and great synthetic versatility represent one of such ideal smart materials.[5]

MOFs are well-defined crystalline solid constructed from metal ions or clusters and organic linkers.[6] The vast choices of metal second building units (SBUs), organic linkers and topologies provide infinite active sites for gas interaction and detection.[7] The skeletons, metal nodes and the porous space could all be utilized to tune luminescence during such detection process.[8] Moreover, the definite crystal structure information and exact connection sequence of MOFs also promote the in-depth mechanism study.[7c] Therefore, significant progress has been made in the use of luminescent MOFs for toxic gas detection in recent years, including NOxH2S, SOxvoltaic organic compounds, etc.[9] However, luminescent MOFs for HCl vapor detection especially in a repeatable manner are still very rare due to their inertness and instability to the corrosive HCl vapors.

The discovery of fluorogens with aggregation-induced emission (AIE) (AIEgens) provides great opportunities for design of luminescent materials.[10] AIEgens usually possess propeller structures, which show negligible fluorescence in solution but exhibit largely intensified emission upon restriction of intramolecular motions (RIMs) in aggregated state.[11] Constructing luminescent MOFs with AIE ligands could block intramolecular motions to certain degree to generate bright emission for optical applications.[12] Moreover, the porous space provides exceptional opportunities to further modulate the intramolecular motions of AIE ligands in solid phase for design of smart luminescent MOFs.[13] In recent years, AIE MOFs with different metal cations (MATH), Mg2+, Sr2+, Zr4+, etc.) have gradually appeared, we and others have shown the promising performance of AIE MOFs in different applications.[14] However, the development of AIE MOFs for corrosive gas especially HCl vapor detection are still rare. Moreover, the twisted geometry of AIE ligands shall afford great opportunities for design MOFs with new topologies and more stimuli-responsive behaviors that might achieve such goals but remains to be explored.

Herein, we report two 3D MOFs (ZnMOF and CoMOF) with new topologies of [metal clusters –ligand (MATH)configuration for HCl vapor detection via luminescence or magnetic switch. The distort tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)ethylene (TCPE) ligands were connected to multiple SBUs with different charge states (MATH)in a single MOF. The resultant ZnMOF and CoMOF exhibited the unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration, which affords these MOFs the specific luminescence or magnetic switch behavior upon adsorbing and disrobing HCl vapor. HCl adsorption leads to a fast blue-to-yellow greenish fluorescence transition for ZnMOF, and a ferrimagnetic-toantiferromagnetic switch behavior for CoMOF (Scheme 1). Further analysis reveals that the adsorbed HCl molecules rather than coordinated ones contribute to such switch due to the introduced dipole effects and interchain antiferromagnetic interactions by guest HCl molecules. Hence, ZnMOF

[Figure: Scheme 1. Schematic illustration of [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configured AIE MOFs for HCl vapor induced reversible luminescence or magnetic switch.]

and CoMOF exhibited reversible luminescence and magnetic switch behavior, respectively. In addition, such unique topology also exposed large number of unsaturated Co2+ions in CoMOF, which leads to a fast and sensitive fluorescence light-up detection of histidine (His) via Co2+/H i scoupling induced MOF collapse. Our work of smart AIE MOFs with [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration that show HCl vapor induced reversible luminescence or magnetic switch shall pave new avenues for the design of new luminescent MOF-based sensors.

2. Results and Discussion

2.1. Synthesis and Characterization of AIE MOFs

Previous work reported that the solvothermal reaction between TCPE and Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oresulted in ZnTCPE, which showed staggered 2D MOF sheets made from paddlewheel shaped Zn2(TCPE)4SBUs bridged by TCPE ligands (Figure 1a).[13a,b] In this work, 3D ZnMOF-Solv was obtained by solvothermal reaction between TCPE and Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oin diethylformamide (DEF)/water (v/v = 1/1)mixture at 85°C(see the synthesis part of the Supporting Information). Single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) analysis reveals that ZnMOF-Solv crystallizes in the C2/cspace group of the monoclinic system (Tables S1 and S2, Supporting Information), with a very large single crystal unit cell volume of 47 192 (5) Å3 . Different from ZnTCPE which possesses neutrally charged SBUs, there exists three different geometries for TCPE ligands in the independent unit of ZnMOF-Solv, which coordinated with Zn2+ions via different coordination modes and formed Zn SBUs with three different charge states (MATH)(Figure  1b). In detail, Zn2(TCPE)2(H2O)2(NO3)cluster with charge is composed of two four-coordinated Zn2+ions with a triangular pyramid coordination configuration. The neutrally charged Zn2(TCPE)3(H2O)(NO3)cluster contains one five-coordinated Zn2+ion (pyramid coordination configuration) and one four-coordinated Zn2+ion (triangular pyramid coordination configuration). Two four-coordinated Zn2+ions (triangular pyramid coordination configuration) and one six-coordinated Zn2+ion (double quadrangular pyramid coordination configuration) linked via five TPCE, three end-coordinated H2Omolecules, one µ3-bridged O2-, form charged Zn3(O)(L1)5(H2O)3cluster. The alternating connection between these Zn clusters and TCPE forms an effective (MATH)(MATH)configuration with a pore size of 8.90 Å (Figure 1b). In the pores of ZnMOF-Solv, unsaturated Zn2+ions and O atoms are exposed. Density functional theory calculation based on such conformation also revealed similar distinct electrostatic surface potential distributions for these Zn SBUs, in consistence with their different charge states (Figure S1, Supporting Information). To the best of our knowledge, the synthesized ZnMOF-Solv represents one of these rare MOFs with multiple SBUs possessing different charge states,[15] which also is the first time to realize AIE MOF with [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration. Polycrystalline powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) shows that a large number of ZnMOF-Solv crystal samples we obtained are pure phases (Figure S2, Supporting Information). In addition, the scanning electron microscope (SEM) also showed that the surface of the columnar ZnMOF-Solv crystal is very clean

(Figure S3, Supporting Information). The thermogravimetric (TG-DTG) results indicated that ZnMOF-Solv had two weight loss processes before 300°C, corresponding to the loss of free 21 H2Omolecules (9.55%)and 6 DEF molecules (15.24%)in its pores (Figure S4, Supporting Information). As the temperature further rises above 400°C, the ZnMOF-Solv framework rapidly decomposes. The weak X-ray diffraction for the activated ZnMOF (soaking in methanol for 12 hand followed by drying) prevents further structure confirmation for ZnMOF, while it showed similar PXRD spectrum as compared to ZnMOF-Solv, indicating that the main crystal structures of ZnMOF remain the same as ZnMOF-Solv. ZnMOF are colorless and transparent block crystals under observation of a 20X stereo microscope, and these crystals show blue luminescence under the irradiation of a 365 nmultraviolet (UV) lamp (Figure S5, Supporting Information). ZnMOF showed a very similar emission spectrum as compared to TCPE powder, indicating the luminescence of ZnMOF is originated from TCPE. While the much higher fluorescence intensity of ZnMOF over TCPE shall be due to the MOF coordination, which immobilizes TCPE ligand to increase the emission via RIM. It should be noted that ZnMOF showed a very high tolerance towards acidic and alkali environment, as indicated by the unchanged PXRD data after immersing in aqueous solutions with different pH values for 24 h. (Figure S6, Supporting Information). Furthermore, the porous nature of ZnMOF was also confirmed by Brunauer− Emmett−Teller (BET) analysis, where the saturated N2uptake

2.2. Luminescence Response to HCl Vapor

Considering the unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration in ZnMOF, we hypothesize that it can effectively show fluorescence response to gases with strong dipole effects, such as HCl vapor. To test this hypothesis, ZnMOF was fumigated with the HCl vapor from a HCl solution (12%)in a closed glass bottle 20°C, CHClvapor = 223.7ppm).[16] Within a very short fumigation time (<15 s), ZnMOF showed a fast white-to-yellow color change under daylight, and a blue-to-yellow greenish emission transition under a 365  nm UV lamp (Figure 2a). Solid-state fluorescence spectra revealed the linearly bathochromic-shifted emission maxima from 445 to 510 nmas well as linearly descended fluorescence intensity along with increased fumigation time (Figure  2b and Figure S8, Supporting Information). We further fumigated ZnMOF with HCl vapor from different HCl solutions at a fixed fumigation time (5 s). As expected, the bathochromic-shifted emission peaks and weakened emission intensities along with increased HCl solution concentration were observed (Figure 2c). By converting the HCl solution to HCl vapor concentration, ZnMOF showed a very excellent HCl vapor detection capability by monitoring the emission wavelength or intensity changes. On the contrary, ZnMOF-HCl showed one weight loss process before 300°C, which corresponds to the loss of 36 free HCl molecules (33.20%). With temperature rising above 400°C, ZnMOF-HCl framework rapidly decomposes with two DTG peaks (MATH)and (MATH)). 2.3. Magnetic Switch to HCl Vapor

The selection of metal ions is one of the most important factors that determines the structures and functions of MOFs.[17] Different metal ions used to construct MOFs can affect their applications in many fields such as optics and magnetics. CoMOF-Solv is synthesized by changing Zn(NO3)2·6H2Oto Co(NO3)2·6H2O(See the synthesis part of Supporting Information), which is fine purple crystals. Due to weak diffraction signal, we are unable to determine its single crystal structure using SCXRD. Instead, we simulated the PXRD spectrum using ZnMOF-Solv topology, and luckily the PXRD result of CoMOF-Solv is nearly identical to such simulated data (Figure 4a), indicating that CoMOF-Solv is a pure phase and possesses the same 3D porous topology as ZnMOF-Solv.[18] Pawley refinement to the PXRD data of CoMOF and ZnMOF revealed nearly identical unit cell parameters, which proves that ZnMOF and CoMOF are isomorphic (Figure S21, Supporting Information). CoMOF-Solv showed a similar TG curve with ZnMOF-Solv, further indicating their similar crystal structures (Figure S22a, Supporting Information). In addition, the SEM of CoMOF-Solv showed that its surface was smooth and very clean (Figure S3, Supporting Information). The UV-Vis absorption spectrum shows that CoMOF (CoMOF-Solv is soaked in methanol for 12 hand then dried) has a strong absorption band in the range of 400–760 nm with a absorption peak centered at 557  nm (Figure  4b), which is slightly red-shifted as compared

to Co(NO3)2·6H2O(500 nm) (Figure S23, Supporting Information). It is worth noting that CoMOF does not emit fluorescence as Co2+is reported to be an effective fluorescence quencher.[19] In addition, CoMOF showed a surface area of 823.2633 m2 g-1(Figure S24, Supporting Information), similar to that of ZnMOF.

Inspired by recent work that (EQUATION)configured MOF showed magnetic properties changes between paramagnetism and ferrimagnetism upon CO2adsorption/desorption,[20] we suspect that our CoMOF could also show magnetic switch upon HCl adsorption. To test this hypothesis, we fumigated CoMOF with HCl vapor for 2h. The TG of CoMOF-HCl was also tested, and the results showed that it was consistent with the guest molecules of ZnMOF-HCl (Figure S22b, Supporting Information). The resultant CoMOF-HCl showed dark green appearance, different from the purple colored CoMOF (Figure  4b), with a red-shifted absorption spectrum (the absorption peak shifted from 557  nm for CoMOF to 670 nmfor CoMOF-HCl). The molar magnetic susceptibility (MATH)of CoMOF and CoMOF-HCl was further tested under the temperature range of 2–300 K (Figure  4c).[21] As the temperature decreases, the value of CoMOF gradually decreases. When the temperature is close to 2 K, the value rises sharply and reaches the maximum value. The change trend of under the condition of an external DC field indicates the ferrimagnetic behavior for CoMOF. On the contrary, CoMOF-HCl exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior, as revealed by the partial upward trend of value when the temperature is close to 2 K. The Loop results show that neither CoMOF nor CoMOF-HCl has obvious hysteresis (Figure S25, Supporting Information). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results indicate that the metal center Co ions in CoMOF and CoMOF-HCl are both divalent (Figure 4d), therefore excluding the cause of magnetic switch by Co valence state changes. XPS detected the main peaks as 781.72  eV (sat. 786.72  eV) and 797.63  eV (sat. 803.63  eV), which can be classified as Co (MATH)and Co (MATH)and the XPS of C, N and O elements are consistent with the structure (Figure S26, Supporting Information). CoMOF-HCl could be recovered to its initial ferromagnetic condition upon heating at 350°Cfor 2hto remove adsorbed HCl molecules, proving its magnetic switching behavior (Figure  4c). In addition, the similar PXRD spectra of CoMOF-HCl-350 °C and CoMOF-HCl indicates that the coordinated HCl is not lost under heating at 350°C(Figure S27, Supporting Information), suggesting that coordinated HCl does not contribute to the magnetic change. Such magnetic switch shall be due to the presence of adsorbed HCl molecules in the pores, which provides weak antiferromagnetic interactions to CoMOF-HCl.[23] To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the magnetic switching of MOF synthesized by AIE ligands has been realized.

So far, high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is still widely selected as the qualitative and quantitative analysis of His. However, HPLC is expensive,

3. Conclusion

In summary, we herein reported new AIE MOFs with unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞topology and demonstrated their promising potentials in HCl vapor detection via luminescence or magnetic switch. With the twisted structures of AIE ligands, the coordination between TCPE and Zn2+or Co2+ions leads to SBUs with different coordination nodes and charge states. The synthesized AIE MOF possesses a unique [M+ - L- M- - L- M]∞configuration for the first time. Such frame structure renders ZnMOF the ability to show luminescence switch in response to HCl vapor with high sensitivity and selectivity. When changing the Zn2+to Co2+ions, CoMOF surprisingly demonstrated magnetic switch from ferrimagnetic to antiferromagnetic behavior upon adsorbing HCl vapor. This work represents the first discovery of the magnetic switch of AIEbased MOFs during stimulus response to the best of our knowledge. In addition, the nonemissive CoMOF also exhibited specific fluorescence light-up when meeting His with high sensitivity owing to the exposure of large amount of unsaturated Co2+ions for His coupling. The study reveals the promises and advantages of introducing twisted and rotary AIE ligands to MOFs construction, which shall open new windows to the development of MOFs with new topology and smart stimuli-responsive behaviors.

This anomalous behavior, which is surprising since all the salts mentioned have closely related crystal structures, continues to be the subject of numerous studies.[3a, 8]

(Nitrogen van der Waals radius  (MATH) [12]).]

ands, as has been shown for lithium and copper(I) salts[9] (by observing  7Li and  63Cu).

arranged in linear strings, each surrounded by four stacks of acceptor molecules. In 1-Tl the acceptor molecules are tilted through  37.1° relative to the  -axis. [Figure: Fig. 2. Perspective view of the eightfold coordination of the Tl ions to the CN groups in [2,5-DMe-DCNQI]2Tl (1-Tl).  ,  ,  .]

(MATH) and  (MATH)). In Figure 1, therefore, one of the two thallium atoms is to be visualized as being above the plane of the diagram while the other is below the plane.

As can be seen in Figure 3 (top), 1-Tl has a high conductivity at room temperature ( σ = 50S cm-1) showing it to be a one-dimensional metal-like semiconductor.

[Figure: Fig. 3. Temperature dependence of the conductivity (top), ESR intensity   (middle) and Knight shift (bottom) for [2,5-DMe-DCNQI]   TI (1-TI).]

A comparison of the ionic radii[11] shows that the crystal structures of the different radical ion salts are not determined solely by the sizes of the metal ions. Whereas in the series 1-Li, 1-Na, 1-K the space group changes as the ionic radius increases  (MATH) and  P4/n respectively),[2c,3c] the same highly symmetrical space group  I41/a is found for both the copper and the silver salts.[2c,8] These structural differences are not caused either by the distances between the acceptor molecules, which remain unchanged as they are fixed by the thickness of the  -systems, nor by the metal ion distances, which vary only slightly. Instead they are due to the different metal-nitrile group distances, which are shortest for 1-Cu, 1-Ag and 1-Li (see Table 1). In 1-Tl the Tl-N distance[11,12] is equal to the sum of the van der Waals radii  (MATH). In 1-Cu and 1-Ag, in contrast, the metal-nitrogen distance is considerably less than the sum of the van der Waals radii

(Table 1), an indication of the back bonding of the nitrile groups which is known to occur in these cases.

This type of interaction can be studied by measuring NMR Knight shifts. A Knight shift appears when there is a non-zero electron spin density (s wavefunction) at the nucleus being observed; this produces an additional magnetic field contribution due to hyperfine interaction, causing a shift of the nuclear resonance line.

A general method for investigating spin density is possible by combining this with measurements of intensities in the ESR spectrum and of the static susceptibility (SQUID method). Where the susceptibility is temperature-dependent the Knight shift also changes in proportion to it.

Up to now a significant Knight shift has only been detected for  63Cu in 1-Cu, and now also for  205Tl in 1-Tl. In the following, the data in each case are compared with those for a diamagnetic reference substance and for the corresponding metal.

For the   nucleus in 1-Cu at  290K a Knight shift of 2000 ppm is found (referenced to CuCl), and as the temperature is reduced, the shift increases to  3300 ppm,[10b] thus exceeding the value for metallic copper (2370 ppm).[9]

In contrast, no Knight shift could be detected for the  7Li nucleus in 1-Li (referenced to LiCl), thus confirming the purely ionic structure of 1-Li.

More interestingly, 1-Tl is the first non-copper radical anion salt in which a significant Knight shift of the  205Tl nucleus (referenced to  TINO3) has been observed (4200 ppm at 290 K). This is seen very clearly on comparing the temperature dependence of the Knight shift and of the ESR susceptibility (Fig. 3, bottom and middle). As the temperature is reduced, both show a sharp decrease at about 100 K, which we have interpreted in terms of a phase transition at  Tc = 100K. The correlation between the two curves is maintained down to 20 K.

The single crystal electrical conductivity of 1-Tl shows a temperature dependence similar to that described above, and already begins to fall steeply at  150K (Fig.3, top). Analogous behavior is found for all salts of the type [2,5-X,Y-DCNQI]  2M(MATH) or alkali metal), whose conduction properties have already been investigated in detail.[8,10a] The expression describing the conductivity is that for a metal-like semiconductor with a narrow energy gap   (Eq.1).

$$\sigma (T) = \sigma_ {0} T ^ {- \alpha} e ^ {- \Delta E / k T} \tag {1}$$

This means that in the high-temperature region there is a slow increase in conductivity with decreasing temperature, whereas the behavior at low temperatures is of a thermally-activated type. The latter behavior is further reinforced by the appearance at the phase transition of a larger energy gap, which is also apparent from the ESR and Knight shift measurements. As a result, below  85K the conductivity decreases by more than four orders of magnitude within a  30K interval. As the Knight shift in 1-Li, 1-Na and 1-Rb is practically zero, the Tl salt described here occupies a position intermediate between the alkali metal salts of 1 on the one hand and 1-Cu on the other hand. Although there is a transfer of spin density from the acceptor onto the Tl ion, there is scarcely any shortening of the Tl-N distance. This results in a semiconductor-like behavior, i.e. an absence of multidimensional metallic character.

3. Conclusions

Highly selective inverse CO2/C2H2separation has been realized in an ultramicroporous metal–organic framework Cu-F-pymo. This exclusively capture of CO2over C2H2is attributed to the partially desolvated Cu-F-pymo, in which the preferential sites for C2H2are blocked by the residual water molecules, thus suppressing the adsorption for C2H2. As evidenced by sorption experiments and modeling studies, highly efficient sieving effect avoids the coadsorption of C2H2and ensures high purity and separation productivity in cycling column breakthrough tests. This report highlights the importance of pore modification by controlling guest occupation within MOFs, that will inspire future development of advanced porous materials in adsorptive separations.

The adsorption binding for CO2/C2H2in the partially dehydrated structure is further investigated by GCMC simulations. The adsorption behaviors of CO2and C2H2are studied in the full activated structure and a model in which each pore B of Cu-F-pymo is occupied by one water molecule per unit cell (Figure S20, Supporting Information). The GCMC-derived density field reveals different distribution of adsorbed CO2and C2H2molecules in full activated Cu-F-pymo: CO2molecules are preferentially adsorbed in the pore B whereas C2H2molecules dominantly occupy pore A. We carefully studied the pore surface within confinement of the pore A by mapping the DFT-calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) on the Connolly surface, where strong positive potential is found on the middle of the cavity surrounded by multiple H atoms on the ligands, while negative potential is distributed on both vertexes. This charge-distribution on the cavity surface is complementary to C2H2molecules, enabling highly selective recognition over CO2(Figure S22, Supporting Information). The preferential binding site for C2H2is searched by simulated annealing, which reveals that the C2H2molecule is bound in the pore A through multiple hydrogen bonding with O and F atoms, accompanied by van der Waals (vdW) interactions (Figure S22c, Supporting Information), which is consistent with the primary C2H2binding sites unraveled in the previous report.[11b] In contrast, negligible C2H2uptake is found in the partially activated model, while CO2can still be captured with a reduced amount of 3 molecules per unit cell despite the presence of residual guest water molecules. Such significant prohibition of C2H2adsorption verifies the feasibility of blocking C2H2-favored pockets for optimal inverse selective and molecular sieving of CO2from C2H2(Figure S21, Supporting Information). Cu-F-pymo at elevated temperature, termed as Cu-F-pymo-b, to verify this mechanism. These results demonstrated the judicious manipulation of residual guest water molecules could modify pore environment and thus achieve optimal gas separation performance.

To evaluate the actual CO2/C2H2separation performance of Cu-F-pymo, column breakthrough experiments were carried out, in which CO2/C2H2(50/50, v/v) gas mixture flowed over a packed column filled with Cu-F-pymo particles at a rate of 1.5 m L m i n-1at 298 K (Figure 4a). Between each cycle, the column can be easily regenerated by purging the column with helium at room temperature. Molecules that form high-conductivity molecular solids, particularly organic acceptors, have been limited thus far to cyanoquinoid derivatives such as TCNQ[3]and DCNQI[4] and the metal complex [M (d m i t)2](dmit = 1,3-dithiole-2-thioxo-4,5-dithiolato).[5] Molecular conductors with various electrondonor frameworks based on heterocyclic structures containing a chalcogen atom such as tetrathiafulvalene (TTF)[6] and tetramethyltetraselenofulvalene (TMTSF)[7] have also been realized, and studies are underway to discover a fundamental molecule with a stable electron-accepting framework to form molecular conductors with a desired transport behavior. Herein, we report a modifiable electron acceptor with 5,6,11,12-tetraazanaphthacene (TANC) as a new fundamental framework and the preparation of a high-conductivity crystal (1) from Cu(I)–TANC coordination polymers.

TANC was prepared by modifying a synthetic procedure first reported by Hill.[8] The yellow precipitate obtained from the thermal condensation between -phenylenediamine and oxamide contains 2,2’-bibenzimidazole and 5,11-dihydro-5,6,11,12-tetraazanaphthacene (FFV) in a 3:1 ratio. This mixture was oxidized with PbO2in MeCN to give brown crystals of TANC in 20%yield. The cyclic voltammogram of TANC in MeCN exhibits two reversible one-step, oneelectron waves in the reverse sweep (MATH)and E1/22 = - 0.88Vvs (MATH), which means that TANC is a weaker electron acceptor than organic acceptors such as TCNQ and DCNQI that form high-conductivity materials.[9] Unfortunately, TANC cannot be employed as an organic semiconductor with n-type characteristics.

The TANC radical anion can be isolated from an electron disproportionate reaction between FFV and TANC under basic conditions. This compound was obtained as a green precipitate under anaerobic conditions, which immediately turns gray upon exposure to air. The ESR spectrum of the precipitate exhibits a typical anisotropic peak (MATH)and g= 2.0091) that stabilizes at room temperature (see the Supporting Information).

The high-conductivity crystal 1, which has the composition (MATH), was obtained from the reaction between TANC and [Cu(MeCN)4]BF4in MeOH/MeCN in the form of thin, plate-like, indigo-blue crystals. The presence of half an equivalent of nonstoichiometric (MATH)ions was determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements and quantitative chemical analysis for (MATH)ions. These (MATH)ions are generated by the dissociation of (MATH)anions in the reaction mixture.

Plots of the resistivity against 1/Tfor 1 yield a roughly curved line, which indicates a behavior different from that of a typical thermally excited semiconductor (see the Supporting Information). Therefore, the temperature-dependent resistivity of 1 at high pressure was measured up to approximately 8 GPa by using a cubic anvil apparatus.[13, 14] The resistivity increases uniformly until approximately 6.5 GPa, and it decreases slightly at 8 GPa (see the Supporting Information). This variation in the insulating behavior with pressure for 1 is similar to that of Cu–DCNQI systems, which also exhibit an increase in resistivity under high pressure.[15] The sharp decrease in the resistivity above 6.5 GPaat 300Kmay be attributed to the enhanced overlap of orbitals in TANC molecules. The temperature dependence of the resistivity can be well fitted by the variable-range-hopping (VRH) formula even under high pressures,[16] which suggests that the spatially disordered (MATH)ions play an important role in the electron-transport behavior of 1. We therefore require a model different from that of the Cu–DCNQI system to understand the pressure-enhanced insulating behavior. The large conductivity anisotropy (MATH)1) suggests that the energy levels of the Cu 4s and 3d orbitals are significantly higher and lower than that of the TANC LUMO, respectively. Hence, the (MATH)ions make no contribution to the conduction band. This implies that the hybridization between the Cu 3d orbital and the TANC LUMO is negligible at ambient pressure. The random potential generated by the spatially disordered (MATH)ions may become stronger upon application of pressure because the distance between the layers with stacked TANC columns and those with disordered (MATH)ions decreases with an increase in pressure. As a result, the

application of pressure may increase the purity of the onedimensionality and the strength of the random potential as a result of disordered (MATH)ions. In other words, the 1D VRH is enhanced with an increase in pressure up to 6.5 GPa.

We have reported the preparation of a new highconductivity crystal 1, which is constructed from coordination polymers containing (MATH)ions and novel TANC acceptors. By employing the simple fundamental framework of TANC, it should be possible to convert the crystal structure into that of other analogues and introduce a variety of substituented groups such as a series of TCNQ and DCNQI acceptors. Furthermore, according to the measurements of the temperature-dependent resistivity under high pressure and the conductivity anisotropy, it seems likely that the conduction mechanism of 1 follows the 1D VRH formula based on the disordered (MATH)ions, which affects the stacking of the TANC columns below 6.5 GPa. It should be possible to establish the mechanism for the decrease in resistivity above 6.5 GPaby preparing other Cu molecular conductors with TANC derivatives.

Molecules that form high-conductivity molecular solids, particularly organic acceptors, have been limited thus far to cyanoquinoid derivatives such as TCNQ[3]and DCNQI[4] and the metal complex [M (d m i t)2](dmit = 1,3-dithiole-2-thioxo-4,5-dithiolato).[5] Molecular conductors with various electrondonor frameworks based on heterocyclic structures containing a chalcogen atom such as tetrathiafulvalene (TTF)[6] and tetramethyltetraselenofulvalene (TMTSF)[7] have also been realized, and studies are underway to discover a fundamental molecule with a stable electron-accepting framework to form molecular conductors with a desired transport behavior. Herein, we report a modifiable electron acceptor with 5,6,11,12-tetraazanaphthacene (TANC) as a new fundamental framework and the preparation of a high-conductivity crystal (1) from Cu(I)–TANC coordination polymers.

TANC was prepared by modifying a synthetic procedure first reported by Hill.[8] The yellow precipitate obtained from the thermal condensation between -phenylenediamine and oxamide contains 2,2’-bibenzimidazole and 5,11-dihydro-5,6,11,12-tetraazanaphthacene (FFV) in a 3:1 ratio. This mixture was oxidized with PbO2in MeCN to give brown crystals of TANC in 20%yield. The cyclic voltammogram of TANC in MeCN exhibits two reversible one-step, oneelectron waves in the reverse sweep (MATH)and E1/22 = - 0.88Vvs (MATH), which means that TANC is a weaker electron acceptor than organic acceptors such as TCNQ and DCNQI that form high-conductivity materials.[9] Unfortunately, TANC cannot be employed as an organic semiconductor with n-type characteristics.

The TANC radical anion can be isolated from an electron disproportionate reaction between FFV and TANC under basic conditions. This compound was obtained as a green precipitate under anaerobic conditions, which immediately turns gray upon exposure to air. The ESR spectrum of the precipitate exhibits a typical anisotropic peak (MATH)and g= 2.0091) that stabilizes at room temperature (see the Supporting Information).

The high-conductivity crystal 1, which has the composition (MATH), was obtained from the reaction between TANC and [Cu(MeCN)4]BF4in MeOH/MeCN in the form of thin, plate-like, indigo-blue crystals. The presence of half an equivalent of nonstoichiometric (MATH)ions was determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements and quantitative chemical analysis for (MATH)ions. These (MATH)ions are generated by the dissociation of (MATH)anions in the reaction mixture.

1: [Cu(MeCN)4]BF40.34 g, 1.0 mmol) and TANC (40 mg, 0.17 mmol) were mixed in MeCN (36 mL) and stirred for 10 min. The solution was filtered and divided into (MATH)portions. MeOH (8 mL) was added to each portion and the mixture was slowly evaporated at room temperature. Deep-blue crystals were deposited from the concentrated solution as thin, platelike rhombuses. Yield: 25.0 mg (50%). Elemental analysis for C14H8CuF0.5N4: calcd C 55.08, H 2.64, Cu 20.81, F 3.11, N 18.35; found C 55.33, H 2.64, Cu 20.73, F 3.40, N 18.41.

Conductivity anisotropy measurements were performed for 1 at room temperature for the crystal directions (100) and (010) using the Montgomery method.[11] The conductivity, , is 6.90×10-3Scm-1for the (001) direction, which corresponds to the smallest edge length among the three planes. This behavior as a 1D molecular conductor can also be explained by extended HMckel calculations based on the crystal structure of 1. This yields a 1D energy band along the stacking a axis with a bandwidth of 0.28 eVand an interchain interaction one-tenth that of the intrachain interaction. The tight-binding approximation of the LUMO band yields a 1D energy band and an open Fermi surface (Figure 3 a).

The whole band calculation, including the Cu orbitals, shows that the Cu 3d bands are located around the HOMO band and are completely occupied (Figure 3 b). This result is consistent with the existence of only Cu+species (absence of Cu2+), as observed by XPS. The density of the S = 1/2local spin was estimated to be 1.15%from the Curie tail (see the Supporting Information). Owing to the coordination of the TANC molecules to the Cu atom, the orbital overlap between the TANC LUMO and the Cu orbitals is considerable: 7.5 × 10-3to the Cu 3d orbitals and 17.3 × 10-3to the Cu4porbitals. However, the hybridization of the Cu 3d orbitals with the TANC LUMO is weak because the 3d levels are located entirely below the LUMO level.

As the Cu3dorbitals are separated from the LUMO level by more than 1 eV, the Cu 3d–LUMO hybridization yields t= 2 × 0.0752/Δ = 0.01 eVfor the indirect interchain interaction between the TANC molecules through the Cu atom. These values are similar in order to those for the direct interchain interaction between the TANC molecules and are consistent with the results of the conductivity anisotropy measurements. The tight-binding energy band including this indirect interaction is depicted in Figure 3b, which shows that the 1D band remains essentially unchanged. Therefore, the Cu 3d orbitals do not contribute significantly to the interchain interaction because the Cu atom exists as Cu+.

Plots of the resistivity against 1/Tfor 1 yield a roughly curved line, which indicates a behavior different from that of a typical thermally excited semiconductor (see the Supporting Information). Therefore, the temperature-dependent resistivity of 1 at high pressure was measured up to approximately 8 GPa by using a cubic anvil apparatus.[13, 14] The resistivity increases uniformly until approximately 6.5 GPa, and it decreases slightly at 8 GPa (see the Supporting Information). This variation in the insulating behavior with pressure for 1 is similar to that of Cu–DCNQI systems, which also exhibit an increase in resistivity under high pressure.[15] The sharp decrease in the resistivity above 6.5 GPaat 300Kmay be attributed to the enhanced overlap of orbitals in TANC molecules. However, it is difficult to understand the pressureenhanced insulating state. The temperature dependence of the resistivity can be well fitted by the variable-range-hopping (VRH) formula even under high pressures,[16] which suggests that the spatially disordered (MATH)ions play an important role in the electron-transport behavior of 1. We therefore require a model different from that of the Cu–DCNQI system to understand the pressure-enhanced insulating behavior. The large conductivity anisotropy (MATH)1) suggests that the energy levels of the Cu 4s and 3d orbitals are significantly higher and lower than that of the TANC LUMO, respectively. Hence, the (MATH)ions make no contribution to the conduction band. This implies that the hybridization between the Cu 3d orbital and the TANC LUMO is negligible at ambient pressure. The random potential generated by the spatially disordered (MATH)ions may become stronger upon application of pressure because the distance between the layers with stacked TANC columns and those with disordered (MATH)ions decreases with an increase in pressure. As a result, the

application of pressure may increase the purity of the onedimensionality and the strength of the random potential as a result of disordered (MATH)ions. In other words, the 1D VRH is enhanced with an increase in pressure up to 6.5 GPa.

We have reported the preparation of a new highconductivity crystal 1, which is constructed from coordination polymers containing (MATH)ions and novel TANC acceptors. By employing the simple fundamental framework of TANC, it should be possible to convert the crystal structure into that of other analogues and introduce a variety of substituented groups such as a series of TCNQ and DCNQI acceptors. Furthermore, according to the measurements of the temperature-dependent resistivity under high pressure and the conductivity anisotropy, it seems likely that the conduction mechanism of 1 follows the 1D VRH formula based on the disordered (MATH)ions, which affects the stacking of the TANC columns below 6.5 GPa. It should be possible to establish the mechanism for the decrease in resistivity above 6.5 GPaby preparing other Cu molecular conductors with TANC derivatives.
