tates rational strategies and building support materials with unique topologies and extraordinary properties.12 The rational stratagem in designing new MOFs supports focuses on (1) the choice of metal centre, which will give robust secondary building units (SBUs) and (2) an organic linker which can be functionalised for the desired application.13,14 Lanthanides metal centres are attractive for MOF synthesis,15,16 they mostly form robust SBUs which give rise to the overall stability of the materials. MOF supports can be used for applications that may arise from the special electronic, magnetic, photochemical, catalytic, and luminescence properties.17 Furthermore, lanthanide ions offer higher coordination modes than 3d transition metals, leading to extraordinary structures which are highly unlikely to be made when using 3d transition metal ions.15 This is due to the restricted radial extension of the 4f valence orbitals which allows ligands to approach the metal centre in a variety of orientations, resulting in MOFs with high chemical and thermal stability.18 The primary building unit is the organic linker, and bipyridyl moieties are among the most studied organic linkers in MOF design,19,20 these linkers are thermally and chemical stable entities which give rise to a variety of applications including catalysis.2 The availability of and sites warranty the possibility to functionalise the linker for both chemical1 and bio-catalysis.21 Functionalised bipyridine-based moieties have been used widely in catalysis,2 especially CO2hydrogenations in homogenous setups, yielding very competitive turnover numbers (TON) in producing

formate and light alcohols.2 Platinum group metals are known for their excellent catalytic capabilities; hence, researchers have thoroughly investigated functionalising the bipyridine MOF backbone with these metal complexes.22,23 In hydrogenation reactions, these metals produce a high yield with outstanding selectivity especially in CO2hydrogenation to formate. These metals facilitate H2heterolytic fusion, which is a prerequisite step in hydrogenation when using molecular hydrogen. Hydrogenation of CO2to formate is vital, as formate is an excellent hydrogen carrier, which facilitates production of blue hydrogen and in turn blue hydrogen is attractive as the world envisions hydrogen economy. An et al. have supported an iridium–bipyridyl complex on UiO-67 MOF for the hydrogenation of CO2. 24 Many scientists have supported iridium on various supports with outstanding catalytic activity for the formation of formate (Table S1†).

Herein, we designed and synthesised two novel 3D isostructural lanthanide-based MOFs (JMS-6 and JMS-7) using the bipyridyl dicarboxylate linker. The new rod MOFs exhibit rare topological features,25 good chemical and thermal stability. The activated phases of the MOFs were functionalised using pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) chloride and applied in catalytic hydrogenation of CO2to formate. Under optimised conditions, with minimum catalyst loading, Ir(III)-6aand Ir(III)–7agave the highest TON of 813 and 621, respectively, in formate production.

Experimental

General

All reagents and chemicals were purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further treatment. Cerium nitrate hexahydrate, neodymium nitrate hexahydrate, 2,2′-bipyridyl-4,4'-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc), dimethylformamide, sodium acetate, potassium hydroxide, potassium carbonate, sodium hydrogen carbonate, triethylamine (Et3N), isopropyl alcohol, tetrahydrofuran, iridium trihydrate, acetonitrile, methanol, 1,2,3,4,5-pentamethylcyclopenta-1,3-diene, dichloromethane and ethanol were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The reagents were used without further purification.

Synthesis of JMS-6 [Nd(bpdc)3/2(dmf)2(H2O)2]n. 2,2'-Bipyridine-4,4′-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc)(12.3 mg, 0.05 mmol) and triethylamine [10.6 mg, 0.1 mmol]) was mixed with 10 mLDMF and preheated to dissolve. To the clear solution was added Nd(NO3)3·6H2O(22.9 mg, 0.05 mmol). The reaction mixture was stirred for 5 minutes and left at room temperature for 3 weeks. Purplish spiky crystals JMS-6 were obtained. JMS-6 was activated at 200°Cin an oven for 24 hto give JMS-6a as a grey polycrystalline powder.

Synthesis of JMS-7 [Ce(bpdc)3/2(dmf)2(H2O)2]n. 2,2'-Bipyridine- ·4,4'-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc)(5.0 mg, 0.025 mmol) was dissolved in 5 mL DMF and preheated to dissolve and 0.25 mLof 0.5M HCl was added. To the clear solution, Ce(NO3)3·6H2O(8.4 mg, 0.025 mmol) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred for 5 minutes and heated in the

oven for 72hat 60°C. White spiky crystals JMS-7 were obtained. JMS-7 was activated at 200°Cin an oven for 24 hto give JMS-7a as a pale-yellow polycrystalline powder.

Synthesis of pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) dichloride dimer [Cp*IrCl2]2. Iridium trichloride trihydrate (1.0 g, 4.2 mmol) and 1,2,3,4,5-pentamethylcyclopenta-1,3- diene (0.6 g, 4.4 mmol)were placed in round-bottom flask fitted with a reflux condenser. Reagent-grade methanol (30 mL)and a magnetic stirring bar are were introduced into the round-bottom flask. A nitrogen bubbler was attached to the top of the condenser; the apparatus was purged with nitrogen for 5 min, followed by refluxing under nitrogen for 48h. After 48h, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and the dark red crystalline precipitate formed. The dark red solid was separated and washed with diethyl ether (MATH)10 cm3) and air-dried to give a product with 95%yield.29

Preparation of Ir(III)@JMS-6a and Ir(III)@JMS-7a

Cyclometalation of JMS-6a and JMS-7a was done by soaking the activated MOFs in a methanolic solution of CH3COONatogether with pentamethylcyclopentadienyl dichloroiridium(III) dimer complex [(C5(CH3)5IrCl2)]2(0.25 mmol) for 48hat room temperature. The product was filtered, washed with methanol and dried at 50°Cfor 3hto yield Ir(III)functionalised MOFs. Scheme S1†shows how the Ir complex is grafted onto the MOF backbone.

Single crystal data collection

Single crystal data collections of JMS-6 and JMS-7 were both recorded at 100Kon a Bruker KAPPA APEX II DUO diffractometer that was equipped with graphite-monochromated Mo Kα radiation (MATH). Unit-cell refinement and data reduction were performed using the program SAINT.26 Lorentz polarisation and absorption correction was applied. The structures of JMS-6 and JMS-7 were solved by direct methods (program SHELXS) and refined anisotropically on F2full-matrix least-squares with SHELXL27 within the X-SEED28 interface. Anisotropic thermal parameters were applied to non-hydrogen atoms while all hydrogen atoms were calculated and added at idealized positions Crystallographic and refinement parameters of JMS-6 and JMS-7 are presented in Table S2.†The structures were deposited in the Cambridge Database and given deposition numbers CCDC 2211390 and 2211391.†

Powder X-ray diffraction

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were collected using a BRUKER D2 diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation). X-rays were generated with a current flow of 10 mAand a voltage of 30 kV. Data was collected from 2θ range of 4°to 35°using a step size of 0.05°.

Thermal analysis

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using a TA Discovery Instrument TA-Q50 with a heating rate of 10°C(MATH)within a temperature range of 25-500°Cunder a dry nitrogen purge gas flow of 50 m L m i n-1. Differential scanning

calorimetry (DSC) was performed using the TA Discovery instrument with a heating rate of 10°Cmin-1within a temperature range of 25-400°Cunder a dry nitrogen purge gas flow of 50 m L m i n-1.

Inductively coupled plasma optical emission and elemental analysis. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission (ICP-OES) analysis was performed on a Spectro Arcos instrument that was calibrated using known magnesium, manganese, and palladium standards. Samples were microwavedigested in aqua regia (4 mL of HNO3, 1 mL of HCl) and analysed directly.

High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) analysis. The catalysts were analysed using electron microscopes. The morphological studies were performed on a JEOL Model JEM 2100F electron transmission electron microscopy (TEM) system operating at a voltage of 200 kV. Before analysis, the catalytic samples were dispersed in methanol and sonicated for 30 min. Thereafter, they were placed on a carboncoated copper grid and dried at room temperature.

Scanning electron microscopy-energy-dispersive (SEM-EDX) analysis. The samples were analysed using the Tescan Vega 3LMH scanning electron microscopy (SEM) system. The samples were placed on sticky carbon tape and carbon-coated using an Agar-Turbo carbon sputter.

Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) analysis. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of the samples were recorded in the range of 400 - 4000 cm-1on a PerkinElmer FT-IR spectrophotometer (Model BX II) that was fitted with an attenuated total reflectance (ATR) probe.

NMR studies. 1Hand (MATH)NMR spectra were acquired on a Bruker Ultra shield 500 MHzspectrometer. Chemical shifts are reported in units of ppm. A comparison of 1HNMR of the

(1,2,3,4,5-pentamethylcyclopenta-1,3-diene) and pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) dichloride dimer shows the disappearance of the all proton signal in the precursor and appearance of a new singlet signal at 1.64 ppm in the product (Fig. S1†).

Results and discussion

Structural description

JMS-6 and JMS-7 are isostructural; hence the structural description of JMS-7 is given here. Single crystal X-ray diffraction revealed that JMS-7 crystallises in the triclinic crystal system and space group Pˉ1. In the asymmetric unit we modelled one metal centre coordinated to one and a half bpdc linkers, one coordinated DMF molecule, two water molecules and one uncoordinated DMF molecule. The Ce(III) metal centre is coordinated to eight oxygen atoms, five from bpdc linker, two from water molecules and one from DMF molecule, resulting in a coordination number of 8 and a bicapped trigonal prismatic geometry (Fig. 1a).

The structure of JMS-7 is made up of Ce2C2O4secondary building unit (SBU) rod which grows along the -axis (Fig. 1b). The SBUs are connected by double and single bpdc linkers which propagates along the and -axis to give a 3D structure depicted in Fig. 1c. The volume occupied by coordinated and

[Figure: Fig. 1 (a) A view of the geometry around Ce(III) metal centre, (b) secondary building unit of JMS-7 viewed along the a-axis, (c) packing diagram of JMS-7 viewed along the -axis.]

uncoordinated DMF in the asymmetric unit, together with two H2Omolecules constitutes 27%of the unit cell volume as estimated in Platon30 using a probe radius of 1.2 Å. These solvent molecules occupy the channels illustrated in Fig. 1c.

The calculated and experimental diffraction peaks of JMS-6 and JMS-7 are in good agreement, confirming the phase purity of the synthesised MOFs (Fig. 2). The calculated PXRD patterns were generated from single crystal data using LAZY PULVERIX31 embedded in XSEED.27 Upon activation to give JMS-6a and JMS-7a, there was a significant change in the PXRD pattern. A calculated pattern of the non-solvated crystal structure (Fig. 2) was used to understand if a phase change was associated with the extrusion of the guest molecules. The PXRD patterns of JMS-6a and JMS-7a were generated after deleting all solvent molecules which were modelled in the

asymmetric unit. This was then followed by refining the structure in the absence of the both coordinated and uncoordinated molecules. The calculated PXRD of the non-solvated MOFs matched well with the activated phase, ruling out the possibility of structural transformation induced by guest removal. Removal of guest solvents causes the shift of peaks to higher angles due to framework contraction. This occurrence was similar for both JMS-6 and JMS-7 (Fig. 2). The same observations were noted in an isostructural La(III) MOF.25

Thermal analysis

Thermal analysis of JMS-6 by TGA and DSC (Fig. 3a) shows a 17%weight loss between (MATH), corresponding to the loss of two water molecules and one uncoordinated DMF molecule (calculated 16%). The 10%weight loss between 220-304°C

Although JMS-6 and JMS-7 are isostructural, the total weight loss is different. As illustrated in Fig. 3b, JMS-7 has an initial weight loss of 6.5%between 36-73°C, corresponding to removal of surface solvent and two coordinated water molecules (calculated 5.2%. The weight loss (11%)between 73-84°Cwas due to the loss of one uncoordinated DMF molecule (calculated 10.62%) and a further 10%weight loss between 220-303°Cwas due to the loss of coordinated DMF molecule (calculated 10.62%). The thermograms of both the as-synthesised and activated MOFs are quite comparable, however the total weight loss varies due to the surface solvent which was present in JMS-7. Decomposition of both JMS-6 and JMS-7 is observed above 418°C. The TGA thermograms of both activated MOFs (JMS-6a and JMS-7a) are featureless until decomposition, suggesting complete removal of both coordinated and uncoordinated guest molecules. DSC thermograms of both JMS-6 and JMS-7 show endotherms at 138°Cand 128°Crespectively, attributed to the extrusion of both the coordinated and uncoordinated solvent molecules.

Chemical stability studies of JMS-6 and JMS-7

Chemical stability studies were carried out by soaking the activated material, JMS-6a and JMS-7a in several solvents for 24 hours. The recovered samples were analysed using FT-IR and PXRD to check for any structural changes. TGA was also used to determine the effects of the solvents on the overall thermal stability of the frameworks.

Both JMS-6a (Fig. 4a) and JMS-7a (Fig. S2a†) are stable is all the solvents (water, tetrahydrofuran, ethanol, acetonitrile, isopropyl alcohol, and methanol). Surprisingly, the lower peak which disappeared upon guest removal in both JMS-6 and JMS-7 is retained upon soaking the activated material in water and methanol for 24 h. This phenomenon may indicate that

both the water and methanol can occupy the coordinated sites left by the DMF and water molecules, resulting in a PXRD pattern which is similar to the as synthesised material. FT-IR studies revealed that the position of the asymmetric and symmetric carboxylate stretches were not affected by soaking the MOFs in solvents (Fig. 4b and S2b†). Fig. 5 shows the thermal stability of both JMS-6a and JMS-7a is reduced after soaking them in solvents. The decomposition is observed at 350°Cin the soaked samples as opposed to 408°Cin the as-synthesised material. Hydrogenation of carbon dioxide is normally done in the presence of an organic or inorganic base. Therefore, it is important to predetermine the stability of the MOFs in these bases. Fig. S3†shows that both JMS-6a and JMS-7a are stable in trimethylamine and in KOH (Fig. S3†).

Conclusions

Two new isostructural MOFs JMS-6 and JMS-7 were successfully synthesised using different synthetic protocols. Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) complex was anchored on the MOF backbone using cyclometalation approach onto the bipyridyl linkers. ICP-OES and EDX confirmed successful functionalisation on the MOFs. XPS revealed that the electronic environments of the N and Ir atoms support successful coordination of the two atoms. The functio-

nalised forms of the MOFs, Ir(m)@JMS-6aand Ir(III)~7awere applied in the catalytic hydrogenation of CO2to formate. Under optimised conditions, Ir(III)-6aand Ir(III)@JMS-7a exhibited a TON of 813 and 613 respectively. Both MOFs could be recycled up to three times with Ir(III)–7amaintaining an activity of 90%which was 10%higher than that of Ir(III) @JMS-6a. This work provides an alternative way of supporting highly active molecular catalysts in MOFs.

The proposed mechanism for CO2hydrogenation to formate is based on literature reports (Scheme 1)19,33 and our

The plausible mechanism shows that the initial step is the introduction of the molecular hydrogen into the catalytic centre, followed by dissociation of the H2molecule form two singly bonded H atoms (step 2). The Ir–H species facilitate the entrance of carbon dioxide which forms a partial bond with the hydride species in step 5.24 The final step involves the formation of formate and reconstruction of the Ir–H species.

Two novel metal–organic frameworks functionalised with pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) chloride for catalytic conversion of carbon dioxide to formate†

Maureen Gumbo,a,b Banothile C. E. Makhubela *b and Gift Mehlana *a

Hydrogenation of CO2to formate is a vital reaction, because formate is an excellent hydrogen carrier, which yields blue hydrogen. Blue hydrogen is comparatively cheaper and attractive as the world envisions the hydrogen economy. In this work, two isostructural lanthanide-based MOFs (JMS-6 and JMS-7 [Ln (MATH)were prepared and used as support materials for molecular catalysts. The bipyridyl MOF backbone were functionalised using pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) chloride to give Ir(III) @JMS-6a and Ir(III)@JMS-7a. XPS of the functionalised MOFs show downfield shifts in the N 1s binding energy indicating successful grafting of the complex to the MOF. Hydrogenation experiments in the presence of an organic base showed that the functionalised MOFs were active towards converting CO2to formate. Ir(III) @JMS-6a and Ir(III)@JMS-7a exhibited the highest turnover numbers of 813 and 621 respectively. ICP-OES indicated insignificant leaching during catalysis. TEM images and XPS data of the recovered catalyst ruled out the presence of (MATH), confirming that the activity observed was attributed to the molecular Iridium(III) centres.

Introduction

Anthropogenic activities have resulted in excessive amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2). As a result, CO2capture and utilisation strategies have gained traction over the years. In carbon dioxide utilisation strategies, homogenous catalysts are by far the most effective catalysts, with turnover frequency (TOF) as high as 118000 h-1. 1 Homogenous catalysis, on the other hand faces drawbacks such as catalyst recovery which limits their use in successive cycles. One way to overcome this drawback is to support highly active catalysts on solid supports.2,3

Solid supports such as mesoporous silica (SB15),4 polymers,5 polystyrene, zeolites, alignate,6 covalent organic frameworks (COFs)7,8and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs)9,10 have been employed, in heterogenizing catalytically active molecular complexes. MOFs are structural materials of lowdensity and large-unit-cell-volume,11 that are outstanding supports due to their tunable and flexible synthesis.11 This facili-

tates rational strategies and building support materials with unique topologies and extraordinary properties.12 The rational stratagem in designing new MOFs supports focuses on (1) the choice of metal centre, which will give robust secondary building units (SBUs) and (2) an organic linker which can be functionalised for the desired application.13,14 Lanthanides metal centres are attractive for MOF synthesis,15,16 they mostly form robust SBUs which give rise to the overall stability of the materials. MOF supports can be used for applications that may arise from the special electronic, magnetic, photochemical, catalytic, and luminescence properties.17 Furthermore, lanthanide ions offer higher coordination modes than 3d transition metals, leading to extraordinary structures which are highly unlikely to be made when using 3d transition metal ions.15 This is due to the restricted radial extension of the 4f valence orbitals which allows ligands to approach the metal centre in a variety of orientations, resulting in MOFs with high chemical and thermal stability.18 The primary building unit is the organic linker, and bipyridyl moieties are among the most studied organic linkers in MOF design,19,20 these linkers are thermally and chemical stable entities which give rise to a variety of applications including catalysis.2 The availability of and sites warranty the possibility to functionalise the linker for both chemical1 and bio-catalysis.21 Functionalised bipyridine-based moieties have been used widely in catalysis,2 especially CO2hydrogenations in homogenous setups, yielding very competitive turnover numbers (TON) in producing

formate and light alcohols.2 Platinum group metals are known for their excellent catalytic capabilities; hence, researchers have thoroughly investigated functionalising the bipyridine MOF backbone with these metal complexes.22,23 In hydrogenation reactions, these metals produce a high yield with outstanding selectivity especially in CO2hydrogenation to formate. These metals facilitate H2heterolytic fusion, which is a prerequisite step in hydrogenation when using molecular hydrogen. Hydrogenation of CO2to formate is vital, as formate is an excellent hydrogen carrier, which facilitates production of blue hydrogen and in turn blue hydrogen is attractive as the world envisions hydrogen economy. An et al. have supported an iridium–bipyridyl complex on UiO-67 MOF for the hydrogenation of CO2. 24 Many scientists have supported iridium on various supports with outstanding catalytic activity for the formation of formate (Table S1†).

Herein, we designed and synthesised two novel 3D isostructural lanthanide-based MOFs (JMS-6 and JMS-7) using the bipyridyl dicarboxylate linker. The new rod MOFs exhibit rare topological features,25 good chemical and thermal stability. The activated phases of the MOFs were functionalised using pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) chloride and applied in catalytic hydrogenation of CO2to formate. Under optimised conditions, with minimum catalyst loading, Ir(III)-6aand Ir(III)–7agave the highest TON of 813 and 621, respectively, in formate production.

Experimental

General

All reagents and chemicals were purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further treatment. Cerium nitrate hexahydrate, neodymium nitrate hexahydrate, 2,2′-bipyridyl-4,4'-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc), dimethylformamide, sodium acetate, potassium hydroxide, potassium carbonate, sodium hydrogen carbonate, triethylamine (Et3N), isopropyl alcohol, tetrahydrofuran, iridium trihydrate, acetonitrile, methanol, 1,2,3,4,5-pentamethylcyclopenta-1,3-diene, dichloromethane and ethanol were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The reagents were used without further purification.

Synthesis of JMS-6 [Nd(bpdc)3/2(dmf)2(H2O)2]n. 2,2'-Bipyridine-4,4′-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc)(12.3 mg, 0.05 mmol) and triethylamine [10.6 mg, 0.1 mmol]) was mixed with 10 mLDMF and preheated to dissolve. To the clear solution was added Nd(NO3)3·6H2O(22.9 mg, 0.05 mmol). The reaction mixture was stirred for 5 minutes and left at room temperature for 3 weeks. Purplish spiky crystals JMS-6 were obtained. JMS-6 was activated at 200°Cin an oven for 24 hto give JMS-6a as a grey polycrystalline powder.

Synthesis of JMS-7 [Ce(bpdc)3/2(dmf)2(H2O)2]n. 2,2'-Bipyridine- ·4,4'-dicarboxylic acid (H2bpdc)(5.0 mg, 0.025 mmol) was dissolved in 5 mL DMF and preheated to dissolve and 0.25 mLof 0.5M HCl was added. To the clear solution, Ce(NO3)3·6H2O(8.4 mg, 0.025 mmol) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred for 5 minutes and heated in the

oven for 72hat 60°C. White spiky crystals JMS-7 were obtained. JMS-7 was activated at 200°Cin an oven for 24 hto give JMS-7a as a pale-yellow polycrystalline powder.

Synthesis of pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) dichloride dimer [Cp*IrCl2]2. Iridium trichloride trihydrate (1.0 g, 4.2 mmol) and 1,2,3,4,5-pentamethylcyclopenta-1,3- diene (0.6 g, 4.4 mmol)were placed in round-bottom flask fitted with a reflux condenser. Reagent-grade methanol (30 mL)and a magnetic stirring bar are were introduced into the round-bottom flask. A nitrogen bubbler was attached to the top of the condenser; the apparatus was purged with nitrogen for 5 min, followed by refluxing under nitrogen for 48h. After 48h, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and the dark red crystalline precipitate formed. The dark red solid was separated and washed with diethyl ether (MATH)10 cm3) and air-dried to give a product with 95%yield.29

Preparation of Ir(III)@JMS-6a and Ir(III)@JMS-7a

Cyclometalation of JMS-6a and JMS-7a was done by soaking the activated MOFs in a methanolic solution of CH3COONatogether with pentamethylcyclopentadienyl dichloroiridium(III) dimer complex [(C5(CH3)5IrCl2)]2(0.25 mmol) for 48hat room temperature. The product was filtered, washed with methanol and dried at 50°Cfor 3hto yield Ir(III)functionalised MOFs. Scheme S1†shows how the Ir complex is grafted onto the MOF backbone.

Single crystal data collection

Single crystal data collections of JMS-6 and JMS-7 were both recorded at 100Kon a Bruker KAPPA APEX II DUO diffractometer that was equipped with graphite-monochromated Mo Kα radiation (MATH). Unit-cell refinement and data reduction were performed using the program SAINT.26 Lorentz polarisation and absorption correction was applied. The structures of JMS-6 and JMS-7 were solved by direct methods (program SHELXS) and refined anisotropically on F2full-matrix least-squares with SHELXL27 within the X-SEED28 interface. Anisotropic thermal parameters were applied to non-hydrogen atoms while all hydrogen atoms were calculated and added at idealized positions Crystallographic and refinement parameters of JMS-6 and JMS-7 are presented in Table S2.†The structures were deposited in the Cambridge Database and given deposition numbers CCDC 2211390 and 2211391.†

Powder X-ray diffraction

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were collected using a BRUKER D2 diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation). X-rays were generated with a current flow of 10 mAand a voltage of 30 kV. Data was collected from 2θ range of 4°to 35°using a step size of 0.05°.

Thermal analysis

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using a TA Discovery Instrument TA-Q50 with a heating rate of 10°C(MATH)within a temperature range of 25-500°Cunder a dry nitrogen purge gas flow of 50 m L m i n-1. Differential scanning

calorimetry (DSC) was performed using the TA Discovery instrument with a heating rate of 10°Cmin-1within a temperature range of 25-400°Cunder a dry nitrogen purge gas flow of 50 m L m i n-1.

Inductively coupled plasma optical emission and elemental analysis. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission (ICP-OES) analysis was performed on a Spectro Arcos instrument that was calibrated using known magnesium, manganese, and palladium standards. Samples were microwavedigested in aqua regia (4 mL of HNO3, 1 mL of HCl) and analysed directly.

The morphological studies were performed on a JEOL Model JEM 2100F electron transmission electron microscopy (TEM) system operating at a voltage of 200 kV. Before analysis, the catalytic samples were dispersed in methanol and sonicated for 30 min. Thereafter, they were placed on a carboncoated copper grid and dried at room temperature.

Scanning electron microscopy-energy-dispersive (SEM-EDX) analysis. The samples were analysed using the Tescan Vega 3LMH scanning electron microscopy (SEM) system. The samples were placed on sticky carbon tape and carbon-coated using an Agar-Turbo carbon sputter.

Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) analysis. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of the samples were recorded in the range of 400 - 4000 cm-1on a PerkinElmer FT-IR spectrophotometer (Model BX II) that was fitted with an attenuated total reflectance (ATR) probe.

Results and discussion

Structural description

JMS-6 and JMS-7 are isostructural; hence the structural description of JMS-7 is given here. Single crystal X-ray diffraction revealed that JMS-7 crystallises in the triclinic crystal system and space group Pˉ1. In the asymmetric unit we modelled one metal centre coordinated to one and a half bpdc linkers, one coordinated DMF molecule, two water molecules and one uncoordinated DMF molecule. The Ce(III) metal centre is coordinated to eight oxygen atoms, five from bpdc linker, two from water molecules and one from DMF molecule, resulting in a coordination number of 8 and a bicapped trigonal prismatic geometry (Fig. 1a).

The structure of JMS-7 is made up of Ce2C2O4secondary building unit (SBU) rod which grows along the -axis (Fig. 1b). The SBUs are connected by double and single bpdc linkers which propagates along the and -axis to give a 3D structure depicted in Fig. 1c. The volume occupied by coordinated and

uncoordinated DMF in the asymmetric unit, together with two H2Omolecules constitutes 27%of the unit cell volume as estimated in Platon30 using a probe radius of 1.2 Å. These solvent molecules occupy the channels illustrated in Fig. 1c.

The calculated and experimental diffraction peaks of JMS-6 and JMS-7 are in good agreement, confirming the phase purity of the synthesised MOFs (Fig. 2). The calculated PXRD patterns were generated from single crystal data using LAZY PULVERIX31 embedded in XSEED.27 Upon activation to give JMS-6a and JMS-7a, there was a significant change in the PXRD pattern. A calculated pattern of the non-solvated crystal structure (Fig. 2) was used to understand if a phase change was associated with the extrusion of the guest molecules. The PXRD patterns of JMS-6a and JMS-7a were generated after deleting all solvent molecules which were modelled in the

asymmetric unit. This was then followed by refining the structure in the absence of the both coordinated and uncoordinated molecules. The calculated PXRD of the non-solvated MOFs matched well with the activated phase, ruling out the possibility of structural transformation induced by guest removal. Removal of guest solvents causes the shift of peaks to higher angles due to framework contraction. This occurrence was similar for both JMS-6 and JMS-7 (Fig. 2). The same observations were noted in an isostructural La(III) MOF.25

Thermal analysis

Thermal analysis of JMS-6 by TGA and DSC (Fig. 3a) shows a 17%weight loss between (MATH), corresponding to the loss of two water molecules and one uncoordinated DMF molecule (calculated 16%). The 10%weight loss between 220-304°C

[Figure: Fig. 3 Thermal analysis of (a) JMS-6 and, (b) JMS-7.]

was due to the coordinated DMF molecule modelled in the crystal structure (calculated 10.66%). The TGA thermogram is featureless between 325–440 , indicating high thermal stability.

Although JMS-6 and JMS-7 are isostructural, the total weight loss is different. As illustrated in Fig. 3b, JMS-7 has an initial weight loss of 6.5%between 36-73°C, corresponding to removal of surface solvent and two coordinated water molecules (calculated 5.2%. The weight loss (11%)between 73-84°Cwas due to the loss of one uncoordinated DMF molecule (calculated 10.62%) and a further 10%weight loss between 220-303°Cwas due to the loss of coordinated DMF molecule (calculated 10.62%). The thermograms of both the as-synthesised and activated MOFs are quite comparable, however the total weight loss varies due to the surface solvent which was present in JMS-7. Decomposition of both JMS-6 and JMS-7 is observed above 418°C. The TGA thermograms of both activated MOFs (JMS-6a and JMS-7a) are featureless until decomposition, suggesting complete removal of both coordinated and uncoordinated guest molecules. Chemical stability studies of JMS-6 and JMS-7

Conclusions

Two new isostructural MOFs JMS-6 and JMS-7 were successfully synthesised using different synthetic protocols. Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium(III) complex was anchored on the MOF backbone using cyclometalation approach onto the bipyridyl linkers. ICP-OES and EDX confirmed successful functionalisation on the MOFs. XPS revealed that the electronic environments of the N and Ir atoms support successful coordination of the two atoms. The functio-

nalised forms of the MOFs, Ir(m)@JMS-6aand Ir(III)~7awere applied in the catalytic hydrogenation of CO2to formate. Under optimised conditions, Ir(III)-6aand Ir(III)@JMS-7a exhibited a TON of 813 and 613 respectively. Both MOFs could be recycled up to three times with Ir(III)–7amaintaining an activity of 90%which was 10%higher than that of Ir(III) @JMS-6a. This work provides an alternative way of supporting highly active molecular catalysts in MOFs.

The proposed mechanism for CO2hydrogenation to formate is based on literature reports (Scheme 1)19,33 and our

XPS results. The plausible mechanism shows that the initial step is the introduction of the molecular hydrogen into the catalytic centre, followed by dissociation of the H2molecule form two singly bonded H atoms (step 2). The third step shows a partial bond forming between H and Cl atom, this will later form HCl, a good leaving group.33 This results in formation of the Ir–H species in step 4, which is the rate determining step for the catalysis reaction. Alkali metal crystalline polymer electrolytes

Chuhong Zhang, Stephen Gamble, David Ainsworth, Alexandra M. Z. Slawin, Yuri G. Andreev and Peter G. Bruce*

Polymer electrolytes have been studied extensively because uniquely they combine ionic conductivity with solid yet flexible mechanical properties, rendering them important for all-solid-state devices including batteries, electrochromic displays and smart windows . For some 30 years, ionic conductivity in polymers was considered to occur only in the amorphous state above  . Crystalline polymers were believed to be insulators. This changed with the discovery of  (MATH) conductivity in crystalline poly(ethylene oxide) :  LiAsF6 (refs 4, 5). However, new crystalline polymer electrolytes have proved elusive, questioning whether the 6:1 complex has particular structural features making it a unique exception to the rule that only amorphous polymers conduct. Here, we demonstrate that ionic conductivity in crystalline polymers is not unique to the 6:1 complex by reporting several new crystalline polymer electrolytes containing different alkali metal salts ( (MATH),  (MATH) and  (MATH)), including the best conductor poly(ethylene oxide) :  NaAsF6 discovered so far, with a conductivity 1.5 orders of magnitude higher than poly(ethylene oxide) :  LiAsF6. These are the first crystalline polymer electrolytes with a different composition and structures to that of the 6:1  (MATH) complex.

Polymer electrolytes are composed of salts dissolved in solid, coordinating, polymers, such as poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO). First discovered by Wright and co-workers in 1973, their significance as a new and unique class of solid ionic conductor was recognized by Armand[6,7]. Elegant NMR studies demonstrated that ionic conductivity occurred in the amorphous state above the glass transition temperature  , where crucially such conductivity was facilitated by the local segmental motion of the polymer chains (liquid-like conduction)[8]. This view of ion transport came to dominate the field for many years, although Armand had earlier suggested transport along ordered PEO coils[7]. Theories of ion transport in such a dynamic environment, especially the dynamic bond percolation model, served to reinforce the view of ion transport occurring by 'liquid-like' conduction[9,10]. In summary, we have shown that ion transport in crystalline polymers is not uniquely a feature of the 6:1 structure or lithium ion conductors, but is more general and hence significant. In particular, the first example of a crystalline polymer supporting sodium ion conductivity is reported. This is also the first example of a crystalline polymer in which both cations and anions are mobile and that shows a phase transition between two conducting polymorphs. The conductivity of the  PEO8:NaAsF6 is 1.5 orders of magnitude higher than that of  PEO6:LiAsF6 at  25°C. However, higher resistances at grain boundaries compared with the bulk would result in either two semicircles or, if the impedance was dominated by the former, one semicircle with a capacitance orders of magnitude higher than is observed. The linearity of the   versus  1/T plots in Fig. 1 is consistent with ion hopping in a crystalline polymer electrolyte, as opposed to the curved Arrhenius plots typical of amorphous polymers. The most striking feature of the Arrhenius plot for  PEO8:NaAsF6 is the change of slope at  ~25°C between high-temperature low-activation energy  (44kJ mol-1) and low-temperature high-activation energy  (291kJ mol-1) regions. The transport number (fraction of current carried by each ion) was determined at 17 and  40°C using the d.c. polarization method (see the Methods section; ref. 16). The values of  (MATH) (fraction of current carried by  (MATH)) are  0.41± 0.05 and  0.17± 0.05 respectively at 17 and  40°C.

Considering the linearity of the Arrhenius plot in more detail, if the  (MATH) and  (MATH) ions each migrated completely independently, then there is no reason to anticipate that their activation energies should be the same. As the cation and anion conductivities occur in parallel, the overall conductivity,  (MATH), is given by  (MATH). Each will follow an exponential dependence on temperature, such as  (MATH), as expected for a hopping conductor<sup>17</sup>. The sum of two exponentials,   and  , would lead to a curved Arrhenius plot unless the activation energies,   and  Ean, for migration of the two ions are the same. The linearity in each of the two regions in Fig. 1 points to a conduction mechanism in which the fundamental processes governing cation and anion transport are linked. Although there is no large-scale liquid-like segmental motion of the polymer chains driving conductivity in these materials, it is unlikely that the polymer chains in such soft crystalline solids are static. Instead, as an ion hops from one coordination site to another, the originally occupied site will relax and the new site will deform to accommodate the incoming ion. Therefore, ionic motion is anticipated to be coupled to local modes of the PEO chains, with these modes acting as the gatekeeper for both cation motion inside the tunnels and anion motion between the tunnels (see the below discussion of crystal structure). Such a suggestion is consistent with the data shown here but would require computer simulation or spectroscopic studies to probe what are likely to be low-frequency collective modes.

Examining the 'knee' in the Arrhenius plots in more detail, Fig. 1, consideration of the DSC data, Fig. 4, indicates a pair of closely spaced endotherms that may be associated with the 'knee' in Fig. 1, strongly implying that the higher temperature endotherm results from a change in the crystal structure. PXRD data collected at several temperatures above and below the knee are reported in Fig. 5. The diffraction patterns at 25 and  40°C, just above the knee, are identical but different from those below the knee at   and  -180°C. The insets highlight the difference in the powder patterns and hence confirm the change in the crystal structure associated with the knee in Fig. 1. The presence of a pair of closely spaced peaks implies that the structure changes in two stages, presumably with an intermediate structure existing over only a few degrees centigrade between the two peaks.

A single-crystal structure determination was carried out well below the conductivity 'knee' (see Supplementary Information PEO8NaAsF6lt.cif). The powder pattern simulated from the single-crystal data agrees well with the experimental pattern at the same temperature,  -180°C, Fig. 5. Although the crystal structures below and above the conductivity knee are clearly different, Fig. 5, examination of the two structures shows that these differences are subtle, Fig. 3. Both structures contain tunnels, with each tunnel being formed by a single PEO chain folding into a helix. The 8:1 structures are however different from the 6:1 structure of  PEO6:LiAsF6. In the latter case, although the cations are also in tunnels, they are formed by two PEO chains folding in a nonhelical fashion. In the case of the  PEO8:NaAsF6, the  (MATH)ions are coordinated by eight ether oxygens, six of which form a ring similar in shape to a crown ether, with the other two oxygens lying above and below the ring, Fig. 3. The coordination geometry may be viewed as a distorted hexagonal-based bi-pyramid. In contrast, in the 6:1 structure, the  (MATH)ion is coordinated by five ether oxygens, three from one chain and two from the other. The  Na+-O bond lengths lie in the range  2.44-2.67Å at room temperature, in good accord with the values found in related sodium coordination compounds and with the average value of  2.54Å (refs 18-20). The anions are located between the PEO tunnels. Anion transport exists in the 8:1 phase in contrast to the 6:1 material, although in both cases the anions reside between the cation tunnels. The crystal structures are however different and present a differently shaped environment for the anions. It is difficult to rationalize the differences in the anion transport with confidence from the crystal structures alone. As discussed above, we anticipate that ion transport in a soft solid will involve significant relaxation of the polymer chains as the ions move; therefore, establishing a detailed relationship between ion transport and the structure

would require simulations that can include the polymer chain dynamics; the static picture alone is unlikely to give a sufficient representation of the transport process to permit establishment of a precise relationship between structure and conductivity. Molecular dynamics simulations are now giving valuable insight into transport in the 6:1 complexes  and similar studies are required on the 8:1 complex to understand the different transport properties. The fact that the cations and anions are separated by a single polymer chain is consistent with the idea that the local dynamics of such a chain may act as the gatekeeper for both anion and cation transport, in keeping with the single activation energy and linearity of the Arrhenius plot, as discussed above.

The small, but clearly important, differences between the crystal structures are highlighted in Fig. 3. The main differences are that the  Na+-O distances perpendicular to the ring (that is, the distance to the two apical ether oxygens) are  0.11Å longer in the room-temperature phase compared with the low-temperature structure, and that four of the  F--H distances are  0.5Å longer. These differences, although relatively small, clearly lie at the heart of the change in the slope of the Arrhenius plots in Fig. 1. Again, simulations of these two structures may reveal that these small structural differences are amplified in the dynamics within the two structures in a way that obviously correlates with the significant differences in the activation energies.

On the basis of this result, rocking-chair batteries were constructed using  Na0.44MnO2 electrodes as described in the Methods section. The  Na0.44MnO2 phase is a framework intercalation compound with tunnels suitable for  (MATH) transport and has been used before as an electrode for sodium cells[23,24]. It has a rest potential of  ~2.7V versus  Na+/Na, which lies well within the stability window of the electrolyte. The cells were operated at  45°C. Charge and discharge involves moving  (MATH) between the two electrodes. As can be seen in Fig. 6, cycling may be sustained, thus demonstrating that the electrolyte can be used in cells.

In summary, we have shown that ion transport in crystalline polymers is not uniquely a feature of the 6:1 structure or lithium ion conductors, but is more general and hence significant. In particular, the first example of a crystalline polymer supporting sodium ion conductivity is reported. This is also the first example of a crystalline polymer in which both cations and anions are mobile and that shows a phase transition between two conducting polymorphs. The conductivity of the  PEO8:NaAsF6 is 1.5 orders of magnitude higher than that of  PEO6:LiAsF6 at  25°C. As has been demonstrated for the  (MATH) conducting 6:1 complexes, we can anticipate that doping, modifying chain ends and so on will raise the conductivity of the 8:1 complexes beyond the values for the pure crystalline phase[5,25,26].

Stepwise Construction of Multivariate Metal–Organic Frameworks from a Predesigned Zr16 Cluster

Baoshan Hou, Chao Qin, Chunyi Sun, Xinlong Wang* & Zhongmin Su*

Key Lab of Polyoxometalate Science of Ministry of Education, National and Local United Engineering Laboratory for Power Battery, Northeast Normal University, Changchun, Jilin 130024

*Corresponding authors: wangxl824@nenu.edu.cn; zmsu@nenu.edu.cn

Cite this: CCS Chem. 2021, 3, 287–293

A series of multivariate metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with predictable topologies are stepwise constructed from a predesigned versatile hexadecnuclear zirconium cluster. The [Zr16]cluster is constructed from a center classic (MATH)(MATH)cluster and two capped (MATH)(MATH)(SQA squaric acid, DMF dimethylformamide) clusters which have 24 potential coordination sites to link metal ions and four formate groups to be substituted by other organic ligands. Based on this predesigned cluster, one two-dimensional (2D) MOF [Zr16-BPDC]′ (MATH)-biphenyl dicarboxylic acid) and two three-dimensional (3D) extended multinary MOFs (MATH)-BPDC-Ln] (MATH)and Tb) have been obtained through a kinetic-controlled step-by-step synthesis, based on single-crystal-to-single-crystal structural transformation. Moreover, by means of the lanthanides codoping strategy, the Eu/Tb mixed multinary MOF (MATH)-BPDC-Eu0.8Tb0.2] with temperature-

dependent luminescent behavior can serve as a luminescent thermometer from 80 to 280 K. This work provides new insight into the discovery of new zirconium cluster-based molecular building blocks and the design of functional multivariate MOFs.

Keywords: multivariate metal–organic frameworks, molecular building block, zirconium cluster, crystal engineering, single-crystal-to-single-crystal transformation

Introduction

Crystal engineering is the design of functional crystalline materials with specific physical and chemical properties based on the understanding of the intermolecular interactions during the crystal growth and packing.1 The greatest challenge of crystal engineering is that the final crystal structures cannot be predicted easily from the structures and geometries of reactants.2 To solve this

problem, the concept of supramolecular synthon was introduced to implement the process of supramolecular assembly and crystallization.3 In the field of coordination compounds and metal–organic materials, crystal engineering is utilized as a strategy to target assembly of three-dimensional (3D) structures based on the extension of building blocks.4–8 As an evolving subject, the molecular building blocks (MBBs) approach was developed by Wuest9 and Hosseini,10,11 which are special

molecules with multiple peripheral sites that have strong directional interaction. Followed by the concept of secondary building units (SBUs) devised by Yaghi and co-workers,4,12,13 metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with predictive topologies were designed based on the extension of specific SBUs. Recently, a new stepwise synthetic approach has been developed, which involves a presynthesized inorganic precursor and a subsequent substitution process that occurs between the precursor and the organic ligand.14,15 These strategies undeniably shed light on the prediction, design, and synthesis of the resulting structures with desired functionality.

In a recent review, Helal et al.16 proposed that the future of MOFs will take inspiration from biological systems and have multiple building units and functionality within one crystal structure with specific arrangement sequences. Multicomponent MOFs, including multimetallic MOFs and multilinker MOFs, with desired multifunctionalities are particularly interesting because of their potential applications in gas storage and separation, drug delivery, and molecular sensors. How to introduce heterogeneity by designing and arranging their order is still a challenge for crystal engineering because of the lack of rational control over the self-assembly in a one-pot reaction.17,18 In 2010, Yaghi and co-workers19 incorporated as many as eight functional groups into multivariate MOFs (MTV-MOFs), showing outstanding features distinct from their parent frameworks. Later, Liu and Telfer20 demonstrated a new strategy to design mix-linker MOFs by incorporating multifunctional linkers with various geometries and connectivities. Zhou et al.21,22 developed linker installation strategies to precisely anchor suitable linkers into zirconium-based MOFs (Zr-MOFs) via single-crystal-tosingle-crystal (SCSC) structural transformation. All these strategies make the crystal engineering and design of MTV-MOFs more reasonable and predictable. However, these reported MTV-MOFs are synthesized either by a one-pot reaction using multifunctional linkers or by postsynthetic modification (PSM) from MOF to MOF. Inspired by the synthon theory from crystal engineering, we try to design and construct a multicomponent MOF similar to that in organic synthesis. The whole assembly process is controlled by kinetics, which means the MOF should be synthesized to bottom-up and stepwise obtain a predictable topology structure from a predesigned molecule. To pursue a specific molecule that could be used as a precursor for the subsequent incorporation of organic and inorganic components, three key requirements need to be addressed: (1) the precursory synthon molecule needs to be stable and remains structurally intact through the modification process; (2) the precursor should have an intrinsic geometry as well as a specific coordination direction to guarantee the predictability of stepwise modification; and (3) the precursor must contain potential coordination sites for the incorporation of hetero organic and inorganic components.

Results and Discussion

The [Zr16]cluster was synthesized from Cp2ZrCl2and H2SQAin DMF at 60°Single-crystal -ray diffraction analysis reveals that [Zr16]cluster crystallizes in the tetragonal, space group P4/mnc (Supporting Information Table S2). Specifically, the structure of [Zr16]cluster is composed of one [Zr6(µ3-OH)4(µ3-O)4(SOA)8(COO)4]i n the center and two capped (MATH)(MATH)clusters, which are bridged by SQA ligands, as shown in Figure 2a. The central [Zr6]cluster is coordinated with 12 organic ligands, including 8 SQA ligands and 4 formate groups, from the hydrolysis of DMF and exhibits a cuboctahedral geometry.30,31 While the capped [Zr5]cluster with a quadrangular pyramid geometry is linked with four SQA, four HSQA ligands, and four DMF molecules, the [Zr16]cluster has the tetragonal prismatic configuration with a size of (MATH)(Supporting Information Figure S1). The most interesting feature of the [Zr16]cluster is that it contains multiple potential coordination sites. Specifically, there are eight SQA ligands with one potential binding site in the middle and eight HSQA ligands with two coordination sites hanging on both sides of the [Zr16]cluster (Supporting Information Figure S2). Moreover, there are also four formate groups at the equatorial position, which can be substituted by other carboxylate ligands on account of the instability of this monocoordination mode. These

distinctive features qualify the [Zr16] cluster as a potential MBB to construct multicomponent MOFs.

After carefully examining the space packing of the [Zr16]cluster, we found that the distance between two opposite formate groups of adjacent clusters is 11.81 Å with a short parallel misalignment distance 2.25 Å (Supporting Information Figure S3), which is close to the′ length of the 4,4'-biphenyl dicarboxylic acid (H2BPDC)ligand (11.24 Å). So, we select the H2BPDCligand to substitute the formate groups and connect the adjacent [Zr16]clusters (Supporting Information Figure S4). As we speculated, when the presynthesized [Zr16]single crystals were immersed in the DMF solution of H2BPDCat 80°Covernight, the BPDC ligands substituted formate groups successfully and interlinked [Zr16]clusters into a 2D grid layer, (MATH)(MATH)( (MATH)-BPDC]; Figures 2b and 2d). Compared with the crystal data of [Zr16]cluster, (MATH)-BPDC] still crystallized in the tetragonal system but with a different space group . A slight decrease of cell parameter on the -axis (from 34.23 to 32.31 Å) and the a/b-axis (from 19.52 to 18.97 Å) was observed because the distance between [Zr16]clusters is shortened by the formation of coordination bonds in BPDC and Zr atoms (from 11.81 to 11.25 Å). Another effect of this ligand substitution is that the cluster undergoes a slight rotation (MATH)in the space packing, resulting in the change of space group.

Conclusion

A stable and versatile zirconium cluster [Zr16]with tetra gonal prismatic geometry has been synthesized under a mild condition. Crystallographic analysis reveals that there are 24 unsaturated coordination sites capable of coordinating with metal ions and four formate groups that can be substituted by other organic ligands in this cluster. Such an unprecedented feature makes the cluster an ideal MBB to construct multivariate Zr-MOFs. Under kinetic controls and SCSC transformations, one 2D and two 3D Zr-MOF with different organic ligands and metal ions have been constructed through a step-by-step synthesis. These multinary MOFs have the potential as collaborative luminescence systems, to be luminescence ratiometric thermometers. With this versatile cluster, we believe that more multinary MOFs with expected functionalities will be synthesized in the future.

A series of multivariate metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with predictable topologies are stepwise constructed from a predesigned versatile hexadecnuclear zirconium cluster. The [Zr16]cluster is constructed from a center classic (MATH)(MATH)cluster and two capped (MATH)(MATH)(SQA squaric acid, DMF dimethylformamide) clusters which have 24 potential coordination sites to link metal ions and four formate groups to be substituted by other organic ligands. Based on this predesigned cluster, one two-dimensional (2D) MOF [Zr16-BPDC]′ (MATH)-biphenyl dicarboxylic acid) and two three-dimensional (3D) extended multinary MOFs (MATH)-BPDC-Ln] (MATH)and Tb) have been obtained through a kinetic-controlled step-by-step synthesis, based on single-crystal-to-single-crystal structural transformation. Moreover, by means of the lanthanides codoping strategy, the Eu/Tb mixed multinary MOF (MATH)-BPDC-Eu0.8Tb0.2] with temperature-

dependent luminescent behavior can serve as a luminescent thermometer from 80 to 280 K. This work provides new insight into the discovery of new zirconium cluster-based molecular building blocks and the design of functional multivariate MOFs.

Keywords: multivariate metal–organic frameworks, molecular building block, zirconium cluster, crystal engineering, single-crystal-to-single-crystal transformation

Introduction

Crystal engineering is the design of functional crystalline materials with specific physical and chemical properties based on the understanding of the intermolecular interactions during the crystal growth and packing.1 The greatest challenge of crystal engineering is that the final crystal structures cannot be predicted easily from the structures and geometries of reactants.2 To solve this

problem, the concept of supramolecular synthon was introduced to implement the process of supramolecular assembly and crystallization.3 In the field of coordination compounds and metal–organic materials, crystal engineering is utilized as a strategy to target assembly of three-dimensional (3D) structures based on the extension of building blocks.4–8 As an evolving subject, the molecular building blocks (MBBs) approach was developed by Wuest9 and Hosseini,10,11 which are special

molecules with multiple peripheral sites that have strong directional interaction. Followed by the concept of secondary building units (SBUs) devised by Yaghi and co-workers,4,12,13 metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with predictive topologies were designed based on the extension of specific SBUs. Recently, a new stepwise synthetic approach has been developed, which involves a presynthesized inorganic precursor and a subsequent substitution process that occurs between the precursor and the organic ligand.14,15 These strategies undeniably shed light on the prediction, design, and synthesis of the resulting structures with desired functionality.

In a recent review, Helal et al.16 proposed that the future of MOFs will take inspiration from biological systems and have multiple building units and functionality within one crystal structure with specific arrangement sequences. Multicomponent MOFs, including multimetallic MOFs and multilinker MOFs, with desired multifunctionalities are particularly interesting because of their potential applications in gas storage and separation, drug delivery, and molecular sensors. How to introduce heterogeneity by designing and arranging their order is still a challenge for crystal engineering because of the lack of rational control over the self-assembly in a one-pot reaction.17,18 In 2010, Yaghi and co-workers19 incorporated as many as eight functional groups into multivariate MOFs (MTV-MOFs), showing outstanding features distinct from their parent frameworks. Later, Liu and Telfer20 demonstrated a new strategy to design mix-linker MOFs by incorporating multifunctional linkers with various geometries and connectivities. Zhou et al.21,22 developed linker installation strategies to precisely anchor suitable linkers into zirconium-based MOFs (Zr-MOFs) via single-crystal-tosingle-crystal (SCSC) structural transformation. All these strategies make the crystal engineering and design of MTV-MOFs more reasonable and predictable. However, these reported MTV-MOFs are synthesized either by a one-pot reaction using multifunctional linkers or by postsynthetic modification (PSM) from MOF to MOF. Inspired by the synthon theory from crystal engineering, we try to design and construct a multicomponent MOF similar to that in organic synthesis. The whole assembly process is controlled by kinetics, which means the MOF should be synthesized to bottom-up and stepwise obtain a predictable topology structure from a predesigned molecule. To pursue a specific molecule that could be used as a precursor for the subsequent incorporation of organic and inorganic components, three key requirements need to be addressed: (1) the precursory synthon molecule needs to be stable and remains structurally intact through the modification process; (2) the precursor should have an intrinsic geometry as well as a specific coordination direction to guarantee the predictability of stepwise modification; and (3) the precursor must contain potential coordination sites for the incorporation of hetero organic and inorganic components.

The central [Zr6]cluster is coordinated with 12 organic ligands, including 8 SQA ligands and 4 formate groups, from the hydrolysis of DMF and exhibits a cuboctahedral geometry.30,31 While the capped [Zr5]cluster with a quadrangular pyramid geometry is linked with four SQA, four HSQA ligands, and four DMF molecules, the [Zr16]cluster has the tetragonal prismatic configuration with a size of (MATH)(Supporting Information Figure S1). Conclusion

A stable and versatile zirconium cluster [Zr16]with tetra gonal prismatic geometry has been synthesized under a mild condition. Crystallographic analysis reveals that there are 24 unsaturated coordination sites capable of coordinating with metal ions and four formate groups that can be substituted by other organic ligands in this cluster. Such an unprecedented feature makes the cluster an ideal MBB to construct multivariate Zr-MOFs. Under kinetic controls and SCSC transformations, one 2D and two 3D Zr-MOF with different organic ligands and metal ions have been constructed through a step-by-step synthesis. These multinary MOFs have the potential as collaborative luminescence systems, to be luminescence ratiometric thermometers. With this versatile cluster, we believe that more multinary MOFs with expected functionalities will be synthesized in the future.

## Introduction

In mechanochemistry, tensile forces have traditionally been utilized to promote various bond cleavage events, which can enable productive chemistry through ring opening, rearrangement, and catalyst activation. , More recently, this strategy has been applied toward preserving chemical bonds by suppressing an undesired unimolecular decomposition pathway—a retro-Michael pathway of a maleimide-thiol adduct ( A). Despite these advances in mechanochemistry, the static force provided by rigid materials has, to the best of our knowledge, previously not been utilized toward the preservation of ligand geometry that are sensitive to bending effects. In cases where reductive elimination is problematic in transition-metal catalysis, rigidification of ligands could potentially suppress such unimolecular decomposition pathways. Traditionally, solid-state supports have addressed bimolecular decomposition pathways of catalysts; however, unimolecular decomposition pathways of homogeneous catalysts have previously not been suppressed with solid-state supports. As a model system, we were interested in leveraging architectural stabilization to prevent a unimolecular decomposition pathway of IPrAu(III)(biphenyl)X (where IPr is [1,3-bis(2,6-diisopropylphenyl)imidazole-2-ylidene] and X– is a non-coordinating counteranion), which is known to undergo reductive elimination to yield biphenylene and IPrAu(I)X (B). We reasoned that a bifunctionalized IPrAu(III)(biphenyl)X catalyst could be incorporated into a robust porous material to architecturally lock the geometry of the catalyst. Contrary to common solid-state supports, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) allow for the precise placement of molecules in a well-ordered fashion, which can constrain the geometry of incorporated guests within the framework. Here, we demonstrate that a unimolecular decomposition pathway of IPrAu(III)(biphenyl)X catalyst is prohibited due to architectural stabilization in MOFs by preserving the geometry of the gold(III) complex such that the linear geometry of the biphenyl ligand is maintained (B). Deviation of its linear geometry is architecturally forbidden because reductive elimination in a rigid MOF would either necessitate the formation of a defect site or result in strain throughout the material. In particular, we demonstrate two strategies for introducing a gold(III) catalyst into MOFs with two distinct biphenyldicarboxylate (BPDC) binding modes, which resulted in no observation of the reductive elimination products in contrast to its homogeneous analogs.

## Results and Discussion

In order to probe the architectural stabilization of a gold(III) catalyst in MOFs, we first incorporated a gold(III) precatalyst, IPrAu(III)(BPDC)Cl, into two MOFs through a mixed-linker synthesis and a solvent-assisted linker exchange (see for details). IPrAu(III)(BPDC)Cl was encompassed into a microporous IRMOF-10 system through a mixed-linker synthesis strategy with 5%–16% occupancy of gold(III) precatalyst to yield IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 ( A). A partial structure of IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 (5% gold occupancy) with primitive cubic (pcu) topology was confirmed via single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SXRD) and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD). However, the electron density of the gold, chloride, and IPr moieties could not be assigned with the IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 SXRD data. The chemical composition of IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 was determined by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis and inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) of the digested samples with an observed IPrAu(III)(BPDC)Cl to BPDC ratio of 16:84 and zinc to gold ratio of 89:11. Mixed-linker syntheses with a targeted H2IPrAu(III)(BPDC)Cl/H2BPDC ratio > 5:95 in IRMOF-10 yielded crystals that were not suitable for SXRD characterization due to an increase in defects, which affected the overall crystallinity; an increase in defects was attributed to steric clash in the framework between gold(III) complexes bearing bulky IPr ligands. Low gold(III) loading and high symmetry in IRMOF-10 with 5% occupancy of gold(III) complex precluded the possibility of obtaining a full crystal structure of the precatalyst in IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 via SXRD to ensure that the catalytic moiety is indeed geometrically constrained between secondary building units (SBUs).

In order to mitigate steric clash and increase the occupancy of the gold(III) species in MOFs, bio-MOF-100, a mesoporous MOF featuring larger pores (∼4.5 nm), was chosen as a support for SXRD characterization of the gold(III) precatalyst and catalyst. Interestingly, bio-MOF-100 features two symmetrically distinct BPDC moieties in its asymmetric unit. This feature offers the opportunity to selectively displace one type of BPDC in the framework and thus make it amenable to low guest loading with high occupancy and, as a consequence, enable SXRD characterization (see ). Additionally, bio-MOF-100 possesses a unique binding mode of BPDC to the SBU compared to that of IRMOF-10, which offers an alternative strategy of rigidifying the biphenyl ligand. IPrAu(III)(BPDC)Cl was incorporated into mesoporous bio-MOF-100 through a solvent-assisted linker exchange with up to 40% occupancy of gold(III) precatalyst per substitutable site to yield IPrAu(III)Cl-bio-MOF-100 (B), where the occupancy of gold(III) precatalyst was assigned via SXRD. With 40% occupancy of gold(III) precatalyst, gold, chloride, and 7 atoms of the IPr ligand could be assigned in the IPrAu(III)Cl-bio-MOF-100 SXRD crystal structure . The chemical composition of IPrAu(III)Cl-bio-MOF-100 was further confirmed by 1H NMR and ICP-AES analysis of digested samples.

The catalytically active, cationic gold(III) species in the IRMOF-10 system were accessed by the treatment of IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 with 1 equiv of AgSbF6 (relative to gold) to access IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10, which is analogous to the conditions for activation of the homogeneous complex. Chloride abstraction was evidenced by the reactivity observed in the IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10-catalyzed cycloisomerization reaction of 1,5-enyne substrate 1 to yield the corresponding bicyclohexene product 2 ( , entry 1). In contrast, the addition of substrate 1 to IPrAu(III)Cl-IRMOF-10 without AgSbF6 treatment, under otherwise equivalent conditions, resulted in no background reactivity (entry 2). Additionally, subjecting pristine IRMOF, with or without AgSbF6 treatment, to substrate 1 did not yield any product (entries 3 and 4). These observations support the conclusion that the zinc-based SBUs and silver salt are not responsible for the reactivity observed with IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10. Additionally, another IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10-catalyzed cycloisomerization reaction yielded a product distribution that was consistent with that of the homogeneous gold(III) analog, which further supports the conclusion that cationic gold(III) species are responsible for the observed reactivity .

Efforts toward accessing cationic gold(III) species in bio-MOF-100 through AgSbF6 treatment resulted in a decrease in crystallinity. We posited that this MOF degradation might be attributed to protonation of the BPDC linkers by HSbF6 generated from the hydrolysis of AgSbF6 in the presence of adventitious water. Addition of NaBArF 4, a common halide-abstracting agent that is less prone to hydrolysis, also yielded poorly crystalline frameworks, presumably due to hard acid-hard base interactions between sodium cations and the carboxylate-based linkers. Thus, TlPF6 was chosen as the halide-abstracting agent, as it is less sensitive toward hydrolysis and features a soft thallium cation. After TlPF6 treatment of IPrAu(III)Cl-bio-MOF-100, the sample retained crystallinity, yielding the desired IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100. SXRD measurement revealed the preservation of 40% gold(III) occupancy in the framework, which is consistent with that of the precatalyst structure. In the crystal structure of IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100, the chloride ligand was no longer observed, which indicates successful halide abstraction from the precatalyst to form the desired cationic catalyst .

IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100 had very low reactivity toward the cycloisomerization reaction of substrate 1 to product 2; this low reactivity was attributed to a potential decrease in the rate of diffusion of nonpolar substrates through the intrinsically anionic bio-MOF-100 framework. Raising the temperature to increase the rate of diffusion of 1 was, however, not compatible with this cycloisomerization reaction due to the thermal instability of 1,5-enynes. Thus, alkynyl cylcoheptatriene substrate 3 was chosen as a model substrate, as it has higher thermal stability than 1 and is known to undergo a gold-catalyzed cycloisomerization reaction to yield the corresponding indene products 4 and 5. Addition of 3 to IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100 resulted in formation of desired products 4 and 5 at elevated temperatures with consistent product selectivity with that of the homogeneous gold(III) analog ( , entry 1; ). Similar to the IRMOF-based gold(III) reactivity, no product was observed in the corresponding control experiments with bio-MOF-100 (entries 2–4). These data further demonstrate that chloride abstraction from the gold(III) precatalyst was successful by TlPF6 treatment of IPrAu(III)Cl-bio-MOF-100.

The chemical stability of this cationic gold(III) catalyst in IRMOF-10 and bio-MOF-100 was compared with the stability of their homogeneous counterparts. Reductive elimination of IPrAu(III)(biphenyl)SbF6 is known to be exacerbated in the presence of a trap for cationic gold(I) species, 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (TMB), to yield a Au(I)-TMB adduct ( , entry 3). In contrast, no 2,7-biphenylene dicarboxylic acid or Au(I)-TMB adduct was observed with the MOF analogs under equivalent conditions in the supernatant by digestion 1H NMR analysis or ICP-AES (entries 1 and 2). Additionally, we observed 78% decomposition of a homogeneous gold(III) analog to the corresponding reductive elimination products when heated to 55°C (entry 5). In bio-MOF-100, the gold(III) occupancy remained unperturbed under these conditions, and no reductive elimination products were observed in the supernatant by 1H NMR analysis or ICP-AES (entry 4). These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the architectural stabilization afforded by IRMOF-10 and bio-MOF-100 is robust enough to prevent this unimolecular decomposition.

As a further evaluation that catalysis was occurring in the pores of the framework rather than at the surface or in bulk solution, the impact of substrate size was evaluated in IRMOF-10, as it features smaller pore dimensions than bio-MOF-100 . A Au(III)-IRMOF-10-catalyzed reaction of 1,5-enyne substrate 6, which is slightly larger along one dimension, did not show a substantial decrease in reactivity compared to substrate 1. On the other hand, when the steric bulk was extended along two dimensions with substrate 7, a decrease in reactivity to 2% conversion after 22 h was observed. Further extension of steric bulk along these two dimensions with substrate 8 resulted in no observed product formation by 1H NMR. In contrast, full conversion was observed with substrates 1, 6, 7, and 8 with 4 mol % homogeneous IPrAu(biphenyl)SbF6 after 22 h (see ). These data are consistent with the hypothesis that the catalysis observed with IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10 occurs within the pores, and the leaching of catalytically active species into solution is unlikely. The lack of catalytically active species in solution further highlights the effectiveness of architectural stabilization to prohibit the formation of undesired gold(I) species in bulk solution.

After evaluating the stability of both Au(III)-MOF systems toward reductive elimination, the reuse of both systems was evaluated to further assess the impact of the architectural stability of these frameworks on the catalyst recyclability and longevity. To this end, employing IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10 with 3 mol % gold loading as a catalyst, 44% and 46% conversion of enyne 1 to bicyclohexene 2 was observed in cycles 1 and 2, respectively ( A). Reactivity toward the cycloisomerization of 1 persisted in cycles 3–5, albeit at lower conversions. We hypothesized that this decrease in reactivity might be attributed to the slow trapping of Au(III)Cl species in the presence of AgCl within the pores, which is a phenomenon that has previously been observed with solid-supported cationic gold species. Indeed, we observed a rebound in reactivity upon treatment of IPrAu(III)SbF6-IRMOF-10 with 1 equiv of AgSbF6 (relative to gold) in cycle 6 with continued reactivity over the subsequent cycle. Recyclable reactivity over 7 cycles was also observed with IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100-catalyzed cycloisomerization reaction of 3 to yield 4 and 5 (B), and recyclable reactivity was also observed at shorter reaction durations . Additionally, no loss in the reactivity of IPrAu(III)PF6-bio-MOF-100 was observed after storing the catalyst for 29 days, demonstrating that catalyst deactivation does not occur even after long-term storage. Recyclability reactivity in both IRMOF-10 and bio-MOF-100 further demonstrates the robustness of these systems engendered by architectural stabilization. This architectural stabilization strategy should prove general to access other immobilized transition-metal catalysts that are otherwise prone to unimolecular decomposition pathways and are consequently unstable or inaccessible in solution.

General Information

Unless stated otherwise, all reactions were performed in oven-dried or flame-dried glassware. Reactions were sealed with rubber septa under a nitrogen atmosphere and were stirred with Teflon-coated magnetic stir bars. Dry tetrahydrofuran (THF), dimethylformamide (DMF), diethyl ether (Et2O), and dichloromethane (DCM) were obtained by passing these previously degassed solvents through activated alumina columns. All other reagents were used as received. For all reactions conducted in a glove box, reagents were thoroughly dried and degassed by standard methods prior to use. Reactions were monitored by thin layer chromatography (TLC) on Silicycle SiliaplateTM glass backed TLC plates (250 μm, 60 Å porosity, F-254 indicator) and visualized by UV irradiation. Volatile solvents were removed under reduced pressure with a rotary evaporator and subsequent high vacuum on a Schlenk line. 1 Hand 13C-NMR spectra were taken with Bruker spectrometers operating at 300, 400, 500, 600, or 900 MHz. Chemical shifts are reported relative to the residual solvent signal. NMR data are reported as follows: chemical shift (multiplicity, coupling constants where applicable, number of hydrogens). Splitting is reported with the following symbols: (MATH)singlet, (MATH)doublet, (MATH)triplet, (MATH)quartet, quint quintet, hept heptet, dd doublet of doublets, td triplet of doublets, tt triplet of triplets, and m multiplet. High-resolution mass spectra (HRMS) were obtained with a Thermo LTQ-FT-ICR (7T, ESI) by the QB3 mass spectral facility at the University of California, Berkeley. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SXRD) data was collected using a Bruker D-8-Venture diffractometer. The Bruker D8-Venture diffractometer is equipped with a PHOTON100 CMOS detector and a micro-focus X-ray tube with a Cutarget (λ = 1.54178 Å)and Mo-target (λ = 0.71073 Å). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns were acquired with a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer CuKaradiation, (MATH). Inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectra (ICP-AES) were obtained with an ICP Optima 7000 DV instrument at the Microanalytical Facility at the University of California, Berkeley. ICP-AES samples were treated at (MATH)for 1hprior to digestion in aqua regia. FTIR measurements were taken on a Bruker Vertex 80 in the Center for Catalysis at University of California, Berkeley.
