Intermolecular sensitization of the rotary motion of motor 1 in solution was studied with UV–vis absorption, 1H NMR, and Raman spectroscopies (c, d, and ). In the UV–vis absorption spectra the region characteristic of the main absorption band of the molecular motor 1 (maximum ≈ 400 nm, c, blue solid line) is dominated by the strong Soret band of PdTCPP (c, black solid line). Nevertheless, irradiation of the argon-purged solution of 1 and PdTCPP (1:1 ratio of 1:PdTCPP) at 530 nm (Q-band of the porphyrin) led to a bathochromic shift of the absorption in the region of the Soret band (c, red solid line), consistent with formation of the metastable isomer of the molecular motor (c, blue dashed lines). Subsequent warming of the sample led to the recovery of the original spectrum, consistent with the recovery of the stable isomer by thermal helix inversion (b, red dashed line). An isosbestic point was maintained at 323 nm throughout both photochemical and thermal processes, as expected for unimolecular reactions . Furthermore, the irradiation/thermal isomerization cycles could be performed for at least five consecutive cycles without noticeable fatigue or degradation (c, inset). The rate of the thermal helix inversion of bispyridyl motor 1 in the presence of PdTCPP in DMF was determined by following the exponential decrease of the absorbance at 440 nm over a range of temperatures (6–14 °C, ). Eyring plot analysis showed that the Gibbs free energy of activation of the thermal helix inversion of the metastable isomer of 1 in this mixture (Δ‡ G(20 °C) = 88.0 ± 0.4 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 = 9.1 min, ) is essentially the same as the previously determined value in DMF (Δ‡ G(20 °C) = 87.7 ± 0.6 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 = 8.0 min), thereby demonstrating that bispyridyl motor 1 can operate similarly via direct excitation and triplet sensitization. In the Raman spectra of the equimolar mixture of PdTCPP and 1 in DMF, bands characteristic of PdTCPP partially overlap and obscure bands characteristic of 1 (d, black spectrum). Nonetheless, the features consistent with sequential photochemical and thermal isomerization of 1 could be readily observed with Raman spectroscopy. Irradiation of this mixture at 530 nm at low temperature (−20 °C, sufficient to prevent thermal helix inversion over the time scale of the experiment) led to a decrease in the Raman scattering at 1580 cm–1 with a concomitant increase at 1550 cm–1. Warming to room temperature led to gradual recovery of the initial spectrum (d). The intermolecular energy transfer-induced photoisomerization of motor 1 was monitored with low-temperature 1H NMR spectroscopy . After irradiation of an equimolar mixture of 1 and PdTCPP at 530 nm and −30 °C, a new set of upfield-shifted 1H NMR resonances was observed in the aliphatic part of the spectrum, characteristic of the metastable isomer. Warming the sample resulted in full recovery of the original spectrum and hence of the stable isomer. The photostationary state ratio of metastable and stable isomers of 1, established upon irradiation at 530 nm, was approximately 1:1 , consistent with changes observed by Raman spectroscopy (d), which showed a ∼50% decrease in the intensity of the bands characteristic of the stable isomer (1580 cm–1).

## Energy Transfer, Photochemical, and Thermal Isomerization in the Solid State

Since pillared Zn paddlewheel MOFs are known to lose crystallinity or undergo structural collapse upon solvent removal, all of the experiments involving PdTCPP MOFs were conducted in solvent (DMF)-saturated conditions. The extent of the energy transfer between 1 and PdTCPP linkers in motorized MOF was determined with steady-state and time-resolved emission spectroscopy.

Upon excitation at 530 nm the parent PdTCPP MOF showed a similar emission spectrum to that of PdTCPP in DMF with a small hypsochromic shift of both fluorescence and phosphorescence (a). Conversely, in the emission spectrum of the motorized PdTCPP MOF a strong decrease in the phosphorescence intensity was observed, consistent with the energy transfer between the linkers (a). Furthermore, a significant drop in the porphyrin phosphorescence lifetime was observed from ca. 100 μs for the parent MOF to ca. 10 μs for the motorized MOF . The difference between the phosphorescence lifetimes of PdTCPP in solution and in the parent MOF originates from the effect of excessive scattering from the latter; nevertheless, the large decrease in emission lifetime between parent and motorized MOF clearly indicates energy transfer between 1 and PdTCPP linkers in MOF.

The rotary motion of motor 1 inserted in the MOF scaffold was followed with NIR–Raman spectroscopy (see for other spectra). Previously, we demonstrated that this technique is particularly convenient to study the photochemical and thermal isomerization of rotary molecular motors in condensed phase as it allows for unambiguous correlation of spectral data with the structural changes that these molecules exhibit in response to light and heat stimuli. Upon exposure of the polycrystalline motorized PdTCPP MOF sample to green light (530 nm) a gradual decrease in the Raman intensity at 1580 cm–1 with concomitant increase in scattering intensity at 1550 cm–1 was observed (b). Similar spectral features were detected upon photochemical isomerization of molecular motor 1 in solution and therefore could be ascribed to the same photochemical process. Furthermore, Raman spectroscopy showed that for thin samples the photostationary state of 1 reached via triplet sensitization in motorized PdTCPP MOF was similar to that in solution . Taking into consideration the molar absorptivity of PdTCPP at 532 nm and the concentration of molecular motor 1 in the crystal of the motorized MOF, the penetration depth for the excitation light in these crystals is likely no more than a few micrometers, and therefore, we envision the future application of these materials to be based on the surface-mounted MOFs (SURMOFs) or single-crystal devices. When the irradiation was discontinued, the initial Raman spectrum was recovered gradually, indicating thermal relaxation of the metastable to stable isomer. The barrier of the thermal relaxation at room temperature was determined by monitoring the changes in the bands area characteristic of the metastable isomer ( and ). The Gibbs free energy of activation for this process (Δ‡ G(20 °C)) was 88.7 ± 0.8 kJ mol–1 (t 1/2 ≈ 13 min) and corresponded well to the barrier determined in DMF solution (88.0 ± 0.4 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 ≈ 9 min). The good agreement between the barriers in solution and the solid material shows that molecular motor 1 can perform its large amplitude rotary motion uncompromised while incorporated in PdTCPP MOF. Furthermore, irradiation/thermal relaxation steps could be repeated over five cycles (b, inset) without any noticeable sign of fatigue or photodegradation, indicating high stability of the framework.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, we established that the photoisomerization of the molecular motor pillars in a porphyrin Zn paddlewheel MOF can be driven with visible light by triplet sensitization. The desired motorized MOF was constructed by postsynthetic linker exchange (SALE) from the newly developed parent PdTCPP MOF bearing DPG pillars. Exchange of these pillars with the longer bispyridyl motor 1 resulted in the expected expansion of the elementary cell in the c direction as shown by the SC X-ray and PXRD data. Due to the spatial coarrangement of the chromophores in the motorized MOF, the energy transfer between photosensitizer (2D layers) and molecular motor (pillars) was found to be efficient, and the photochemical isomerization of the molecular motor could be achieved with green 530 nm light. Additionally, it was shown that the rate of the thermal helix inversion step of the molecular motors incorporated in the material scaffold is essentially the same as that observed in solution, owing to the large free volume present in the framework. The demonstration of visible-light-driven rotary motion of a molecular motor in a metal–organic framework opens many perspectives for future applications, such as membranes and pumps able to accelerate flow of gases or in combination with catalytic function and miniaturized chemical reactors able to accelerate inflow of reactants and outflow of products, powered by noninvasive visible light. Furthermore, we envision that this strategy may be used to expand the scope of photosensitizers and molecular motors to achieve an even further shift of the excitation wavelength toward red light.

1. General Information

All reagents were obtained from commercial sources: Pd-meso-tetra(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin (PdTCPP, Frontier Scientific®), meso-α, -Di(4-pyridyl) glycol (DPG, TCI), DMF (Acros Organics), absolute ethanol (Biosolve), HBF4( 48 wt%in H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) Zn(NO3)2·6H2O(Sigma-Aldrich) and used as received without further purification. Molecular motor 1 was synthesized according to a literature procedure.1 Elemental (C,H,N) Analysis was performed on an Elementar Vario MICRO cube: Elemental Analyzer, ICP-OES was performed on a PerkinElmer optical emission spectrometer Optima 7000 DV. NMR spectra were obtained using a Varian Mercury Plus 1H, 13C: 100 MHz), Bruker Avance NEO 1H, 13C: 150 MHz) or Varian Innova 1Hinstruments. Chemical shifts are reported in δ units (ppm) relative to the residual solvent signal of DMSO- 1HNMR, (MATH); 13CNMR, δ 39.5 ppm) or THF- ( 1HNMR, δ 1.72 ppm, 3.58 ppm). The splitting pattern is designated as follows: s (singlet), d (doublet), t (triplet), m (multiplet), br (broad), p (quintet), dd (doublet of doublets) ddd (doublet of doublets of doublets). UV/Vis absorption spectra were measured on a Hewlett-Packard 8453 diode array spectrometer in a 1 cm quartz cuvette. The Raman spectra were recorded on home-built system comprising a 1064 nm(Cobolt RumbaTM) (MATH)laser, equipped with Raman probe (MATH)transmitted power density) and connected to spectrograph (AndorTM Technology, SR-303I-B). Raman spectra at 785 nmwere recorded using a PerkinElmer RamanStation400F with at sample. The steady-state emission spectra of solid samples and in solution were recorded on Spectrofluorometer FS5 (Edinburgh Instruments) equipped with SC-20 sample holder. Phosphorescence quantum yields were determined using Spectrofluorometer FS5 (Edinburgh Instruments) equipped with SC-30 integrating sphere. The phosphorescence lifetimes in solution were determined using Spectrofluorometer FS5 (Edinburgh Instruments) equipped with SC-20 sample holder. The phosphorescence lifetimes of solid MOFs were recorded on home-built system comprising 532 nmexcitation laser (SpitLight 400, InnoLas) and Omni-λ 300 (Zolix) monochromator/spectrograph and digital phosphor oscilloscope (DPO 4032, Tektronix). All the irradiation experiments were performed using Thorlab LEDs (M530F2 530 nm Thorlab LED). Solvents used for spectroscopic studies were of spectroscopic grade (UVASOL, Merck). PXRD data were obtained a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα source (λ = 0.15406 nm)in a Debye-Scherrer geometry. SC Xray data was collected using Bruker-AXS D8 Venture diffractometer with rotating anode and Cu radiation Ω = 1.54184 Å) at a temperature of 100(2).

2. Synthetic Procedures

Synthesis of the PdTCPP-DPG MOF. A 4 mL screw-cap glass vial was loaded with 4.45 mg(4.97 , 1.0 equiv.) of PdTCPP, 2.15 mg 9.94 µmol, 2.0 equiv.) of DPG, 40 µLof stock solution (110 mg in 1 mL of EtOH) of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O(4.43 mg, 14.8 µmol, 3.0 equiv.) and 32 µLof HBF4stock solution in EtOH (prepared by dilution of 100 µLof 48%aqueous HBF4acid in 1mL of EtOH) and diluted with 0.75 mLof DMF and 0.25 mLof EtOH. The mixture was sonicated in an ultrasonic bath for complete dissolution and placed in 80°Cin an oven for 24hupon which plate shaped deep purple crystals were formed. The crystals were collected and washed thoroughly with DMF yielding ca. 5 mg of dried crystals (after removal of DMF). For large scale synthesis (up to 89 mgof PdTCPP) the starting materials were mixed in appropriate ratios in a larger vial and split evenly into 1 mL batches. For 1HNMR studies the sample was washed thoroughly with DCM and dried in vacuum to remove most of the solvent from the pores of the material, next 0.5 mLof DMSO- with 3 drops of D2SO4were added and the sample was sonicated until full dissolution of the material. 1HNMR (MATH), DMSO- ) δ (ppm) 8.82 – 8.77 (m, 4H), 8.67 (s, 8H), 8.26 (d, J = 7.8Hz, 8H), 8.16 (d, J = 7.8Hz, 8H), 7.96 – 7.92 (m, 4H), 4.91 (s, 2H). Synthesis of motorized MOF via SALE. Crystals of parent PdTCPP-DPG MOF (approximately 5 mg) were placed in a 4 mL screw cap vial, and larger patches of crystals were gently pulverized with a Pasteur pipette, and 1 mL solution of molecular motor 1 (approximately 20 mg) in DMF was added. 3. Experimental Procedures

UV/Vis studies. For the UV/Vis studies solutions were degassed by sparging with argon for ca. 1 min in a 1 cm quartz cuvette equipped with a septum-sealed screw cap. For the kinetic studies solutions were irradiated at 530 nmat a range of temperatures 6-14°C, every 2°C) until no further changes were observed in the UV/Vis spectrum. The irradiation was discontinued and the changes in absorbance at 440 nmwere followed in time. For the alternating irradiation and thermal helix inversion cycles the solutions were irradiated at RT until no further changes were observed in the UV/Vis spectrum and kept at RT in the dark for the thermal process.

1HNMR analysis. For the in situ 1HNMR studies the solution of PdTCPP and 1 (3.0 mmol for both components) in THF- was purged in the NMR tube with argon for ca. 30 sec, submerged with an Evans NMR tube equipped with optical fibre and sealed with Parafilm.

Raman Studies. In solution Raman spectra were recorded in 1 cm quartz cuvette equipped with a tightly sealed screw cap in a sample holder equipped with a TC1 temperature controller (Quantum Northwest). The equimolar solution of PdTCPP and 1 (15.0 mM, DMF, ca. 1 mL) was degassed in the cuvette by purging with Argon and irradiated at 530 nmwith stirring for approximately 30 min at -20°Cto reach PSS. Subsequently, the solution was warmed up to room temperature to facilitate the thermal helix inversion. In solid, DMF wet samples of DPG and motorized PdTCPP MOFs were placed between two quartz slides and sealed with Teflon tape to prevent drying. For variable power experiments power of the laser was tuned by changing the aperture of the slit and the transmitted power was measured using using a FieldMate laser power meter (RoHS compliant).

Emission Studies. For emission studies in solution DMF was degassed by five freeze-pump-thaw cycles and placed inside a glovebox. All the solutions were prepared innside a glove box in a 1 cm quartz cuvettes equipped with a septum-sealed screw cap by dilution of the same DMF stock solutions of PdTCPP and molecular motor 1 to a final concentration of PdTCPP of (MATH). For emission studies in the solid, a suspension of PdTCPP-DPG or motorized PdTCPP MOFs crystals in DMF

were placed in a mm NMR tube equipped with J. Young valve and degassed by 5 freeze-pumpthaw cycles.

Elemental Analysis. For elemental analysis MOFs samples were washed thoroughly with DMF then with DCM, dried and kept under a vacuum for 24 h prior to the analysis.

PXRD Studies. PXRD data of MOFs was collected for samples enclosed in spinning glass 1.0 mmcapillaries (Hampton Research, HR6-122) with supernatant liquid. MOFs crystals were gently ground with a glass Pasteur pipette and transferred to the capillaries which were subsequently sealed with wax and placed on the goniometer head for mounting on the diffractometer.

## Introduction

Development of artificial molecular machines and motors allows for the design and construction of tailor-made molecular architectures capable of executing precisely controlled nanoscale structural motion. Among these artificial systems, overcrowded alkene-based molecular motors attract considerable attention due to their chirality controlled photochemically driven repetitive unidirectional rotary motion. Although it has been demonstrated that these molecules can perform various tasks in solution, such as control over the stereochemical outcome of catalytic reactions, Brownian motion precludes the cooperative action required to achieve functions beyond molecular dimensions. Achieving ensemble action with artificial molecular machines therefore requires that the randomizing effects of the thermal motion are eliminated by assembly on surfaces or integration into the larger systems. Incorporation and immobilization of these molecules in various supramolecular architectures, including organo- and hydrogels, polymers, liquid crystals, or self-assembled monolayers, provided a way to amplify and harness their light-induced rotational motion to form responsive materials with tunable properties, including adaptive polymers, artificial muscles, and responsive surfaces. For overcrowded alkene-based materials the use of UV light to drive the molecular motion limits such efforts due to limited penetration depth (due to the scattering) and potential damage by destructive photochemical processes. Therefore, development of reliable and practical visible-light excitation strategies that are compatible with a chosen material represents a major challenge crucial for further advancement of these dynamic systems.

The most common approaches to red shifting of the excitation wavelength of the overcrowded alkene-based molecular motors are based on HOMO–LUMO gap engineering featuring extension of the aromatic system, functionalization with donor–acceptor substituents, or formation of metal complexes. Although successful, these approaches may reduce the quantum yield of photoisomerization and are so far limited in the absorption shift (only to the blue part of the visible spectrum; maximum of absorption ca. 450 nm). Furthermore, the resulting molecular architectures are synthetically more challenging to incorporate in a given material scaffold. An alternative approach to achieve visible-light-driven rotation of these molecules is to take advantage of intra- or intermolecular sensitization through triplet energy transfer from a second chromophore. This strategy not only reduces the synthetic efforts but also allows one to tune the excitation wavelength over a broad spectral range limited only by the choice of a photosensitizer and triplet–triplet energy transfer requirements. Furthermore, it has been successfully applied to operate several types of photoswitches by visible light including azobenzenes, stilbenes, and dithienylethenes.

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) constitute a class of hybrid materials composed of inorganic nodes and organic linkers connected in a three-dimensional crystalline, highly porous network. Due to the high inherent porosity in these structures, sufficient internal free volume is present to allow for stimuli-responsive structural transformations or rotational and translational motion of parts of the organic linkers organized in the crystalline solid. In addition, the structural diversity and chemical tunability of these materials makes them ideal platforms to achieve spatial co-organization of functional molecules and chromophores. Recent studies on light-harvesting multicomponent MOFs revealed that facile and long-distance energy migration can be achieved between light-absorbing nodes and/or linkers in MOFs of various architectures. Furthermore, the incorporation of photochromic dithienylethene struts in a layered porphyrin MOFs provided a method for photocontrol over energy transfer between adjacent chromophores and efficiency of singlet oxygen generation.

Recently, we demonstrated that a molecular motor incorporated as a strut in a pillared-paddlewheel MOF is capable of performing unhindered, large-amplitude unidirectional rotary motion fueled by UV light and heat. In the present study, we show that such rotary motion can be driven by visible light through linker-to-linker energy transfer. The framework was constructed from two functional linkers: a porphyrin used as both linker dictating the connectivity of the framework and light-harvesting unit and a bispyridyl-derived molecular motor serving as a pillar and able to undergo rotary motion . In the resulting supramolecular architecture the backbone of the framework is not only a passive “scaffolding” but also plays an active role by absorbing visible light and transferring the collected energy to the molecular motor struts, thus driving its rotary motion. This dual-function MOF was obtained using a postsynthetic functionalization method from a parent Zn pillared-paddlewheel MOF bearing a palladium–porphyrin tetracarboxylic acid linker (PdTCPP) (, top left) and bispyridyl pillars (, bottom left). The chosen MOF scaffold provides the proximity of both linkers, allowing for efficient energy transfer between the chromophores and the large free volume that is essential for unhindered rotation of the light-driven molecular motor in the solid state . A key challenge, presented by this approach, is in demonstrating the functioning of the material by spectroscopic methods due to the overwhelming spectroscopic properties of the porphyrin chromophore. This unit, which is central to the visible-light-driven functionality, also precludes standard spectroscopic analysis of the motor function; however, near-infrared Raman spectroscopy (1064 nm) enables full characterization of the motor function.

## Design, Synthesis, and Characterization of a Motorized Metal–Organic Framework

For the desired MOF a zinc pillared-paddlewheel scaffold was used, related to the framework we reported recently. In the chosen structure, the nodes of the framework, which is the zinc paddlewheel clusters, are connected by porphyrin tetracarboxylic acid linkers (PdTCPP) forming two-dimensional layers, which are pillared by the bispyridine-derived linker 1 . We designed the system in such a way that the size of the PdTCPP linker will ensure sufficient lateral separation of the pillars bearing a molecular motor function, generating free volume critical for uncompromised rotation of the molecular motor (in the designed structure, the distance between the nodes in the [100] and [010] planes is approximately 17 Å, ). Furthermore, the length of bispyridyl-derived molecular motor pillar 1 (N–N distance 15.6 Å) should separate the porphyrin layers sufficiently to prevent competing interlayer porphyrin–porphyrin exciton transport. Finally, the nodes of the framework were based on closed-shell d10 configuration Zn2+ cations in order to exclude any undesired energy transfer between PdTCPP and nodes. Since MOFs of this topology are typically synthesized under relatively harsh conditions with the presence of strong mineral acids, it was decided to prepare the final material using a postsynthetic method, i.e., solvent-assisted linker exchange (SALE) developed by Farha and Hupp. In this process, bispyridine-derived pillars of the pillared MOFs can be exchanged for different bispyridyl linkers of similar length under neutral conditions, which prevents side reactions and decomposition of the acid-sensitive linkers. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that with this method shorter pillars can also be exchanged for longer pillars, thereby making this approach suitable for fabrication of MOFs with larger unit cell parameters. Initial attempts to grow the desired parent structure with N,N′-di(4-pyridyl)-1,4,5,8-naphthalenetetracarboxydiimide were largely unsuccessful and gave mixtures of products consisting predominately of interpenetrated frameworks analogous to the previously described interpenetrated porphyrinic frameworks. To overcome this tendency of formation of the interpenetrated structure a shorter linker, meso-α,β-di(4-pyridyl) glycol (DPG, see a for structure), was employed. A novel pillared-paddlewheel framework was synthesized in a solvothermal reaction between PdTCPP, DPG, Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, and tetrafluoroboric acid in a binary solvent mixture (DMF/EtOH) providing square-shaped crystals (b, top). It is of note that when the reaction was carried out under less acidic conditions predominantly needle-like crystals of a 3-fold interpenetrated framework with zigzag structure were obtained . Characterization by 1H NMR (d 6-DMSO) spectroscopy of the digested (using D2SO4) square-shaped crystals of the pillared-paddlewheel MOF showed the expected 1:1 ratio of DPG and PdTCPP linkers . The initial refinement of the single-crystal (SC) X-ray diffraction data collected from the target MOF revealed the expected layered structure composed of PdTCPP and Zn cations, while the DPG pillars could not be resolved, presumably due to rotational disorder . Nevertheless, the interlayer distance of 9.2 Å (N–N distance between pyridyl nitrogens coordinated to paddlewheel clusters) determined from the structure corresponded well with the N–N distance (9.4 Å, see ) in the DPG linker, indicating that DPG pillars are intercalating the layers of the framework . The powder X-ray diffraction data (PXRD), acquired under solvent-saturated conditions, corroborated bulk crystallinity and phase purity of the sample (d and ). Furthermore, Pawley refinement showed negligible differences between the experimental and the simulated diffraction patterns, further indicating formation of the target pillared structure (, ). Elemental analysis corroborated the anticipated elemental composition of the parent MOF (see SI, ). Subsequently, the parent DPG pillars were exchanged for bispyridyl molecular motor 1 by means of SALE (a), which was carried out by soaking the crystals of parent MOF in a DMF solution of bispyridyl molecular motor 1 at 80 °C for 48 h (the solution of 1 was replaced with a fresh solution after 24 h) to achieve full exchange as indicated by 1H NMR spectroscopy of digested crystals (b, bottom, ). Comparison of the Raman spectra of parent and motorized PdTCPP MOFs revealed the presence of additional bands characteristic of molecular motor 1 in the spectrum of motorized MOF, further supporting the successful exchange of the pillars (c). As with the parent MOF, the SC X-ray structure of motorized MOF could only be partially resolved. From the refinement of the data the PdTCPP units and Zn paddlewheel clusters forming a layered structure could be confirmed, while the disorder between the layers precluded the interpretation of the electron density of the intercalating units . Nevertheless, the clear increase in the interlayer distance to 15.7 Å (N–N distance between pyridyl nitrogens coordinated to paddlewheel clusters) corroborated the incorporation of longer pillars, consistent with the length of the molecular motor 1 (N–N distance in DFT-optimized structure B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) 15.4 Å). In addition, the expansion of the elementary unit cell in the [001] direction was confirmed by the changes observed in positions of the peaks in the PXRD diffractograms. In comparison to the PXRD of the parent MOF, significant shifts to a smaller diffraction angle were observed for the peaks ascribed to reflections from planes perpendicular and oblique to the [001] direction, while peaks corresponding to reflections from planes parallel to the [001] direction remained unchanged (d and ). Furthermore, Pawley refinement showed good agreement between the dimensions of the targeted motorized PdTCPP MOF unit cell and the experimental PXRD pattern (, ). Finally, elemental analysis was consistent with the anticipated elemental composition of the parent MOF (see SI, ).

## Energy Transfer, Photochemical, and Thermal Isomerization in Solution

Intermolecular energy transfer between the porphyrin (PdTCPP) and molecular motor 1 in solution was characterized by emission spectroscopy (b). Deoxygenated solutions of PdTCPP excited at 530 nm show weak fluorescence at 610 nm and a strong emission band characteristic of phosphorescence at 700 nm (b, black line) with a lifetime of ca. 221 μs (, ). For mixtures of PdTCPP and molecular motor 1 the intensity of the phosphorescence was substantially reduced with a decrease in phosphorescence lifetime to ca. 15 μs (1:1 ratio of PdTCPP:1) and ca. 5 μs (1:5 ratio of PdTCPP:1, , ), in line with energy transfer between triplet states of the porphyrin and motor 1 (b, red line). Stern–Volmer plots (emission intensity and lifetime, , respectively) with concentrations of 1 between 0.0 and 223.0 μM were linear, confirming dynamic quenching of the phosphorescence of PdTCPP, thus excluding formation of aggregates in the concentration range studied. Linear fitting of the data gave an intermolecular quenching rate constant k q = 9.0 ± 0.3 × 108 M–1 s–1 approaching the Smoluchowski limit of the diffusion-limited rate constant in DMF (7.6 × 109 M–1 s–1 at 20 °C), suggesting that the energy transfer between PdTCPP and 1 is likely under diffusion control .

Intermolecular sensitization of the rotary motion of motor 1 in solution was studied with UV–vis absorption, 1H NMR, and Raman spectroscopies (c, d, and ). In the UV–vis absorption spectra the region characteristic of the main absorption band of the molecular motor 1 (maximum ≈ 400 nm, c, blue solid line) is dominated by the strong Soret band of PdTCPP (c, black solid line). Nevertheless, irradiation of the argon-purged solution of 1 and PdTCPP (1:1 ratio of 1:PdTCPP) at 530 nm (Q-band of the porphyrin) led to a bathochromic shift of the absorption in the region of the Soret band (c, red solid line), consistent with formation of the metastable isomer of the molecular motor (c, blue dashed lines). Subsequent warming of the sample led to the recovery of the original spectrum, consistent with the recovery of the stable isomer by thermal helix inversion (b, red dashed line). An isosbestic point was maintained at 323 nm throughout both photochemical and thermal processes, as expected for unimolecular reactions . Furthermore, the irradiation/thermal isomerization cycles could be performed for at least five consecutive cycles without noticeable fatigue or degradation (c, inset). The rate of the thermal helix inversion of bispyridyl motor 1 in the presence of PdTCPP in DMF was determined by following the exponential decrease of the absorbance at 440 nm over a range of temperatures (6–14 °C, ). Eyring plot analysis showed that the Gibbs free energy of activation of the thermal helix inversion of the metastable isomer of 1 in this mixture (Δ‡ G(20 °C) = 88.0 ± 0.4 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 = 9.1 min, ) is essentially the same as the previously determined value in DMF (Δ‡ G(20 °C) = 87.7 ± 0.6 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 = 8.0 min), thereby demonstrating that bispyridyl motor 1 can operate similarly via direct excitation and triplet sensitization. In the Raman spectra of the equimolar mixture of PdTCPP and 1 in DMF, bands characteristic of PdTCPP partially overlap and obscure bands characteristic of 1 (d, black spectrum). Nonetheless, the features consistent with sequential photochemical and thermal isomerization of 1 could be readily observed with Raman spectroscopy. Irradiation of this mixture at 530 nm at low temperature (−20 °C, sufficient to prevent thermal helix inversion over the time scale of the experiment) led to a decrease in the Raman scattering at 1580 cm–1 with a concomitant increase at 1550 cm–1. Warming to room temperature led to gradual recovery of the initial spectrum (d). The intermolecular energy transfer-induced photoisomerization of motor 1 was monitored with low-temperature 1H NMR spectroscopy . After irradiation of an equimolar mixture of 1 and PdTCPP at 530 nm and −30 °C, a new set of upfield-shifted 1H NMR resonances was observed in the aliphatic part of the spectrum, characteristic of the metastable isomer. Warming the sample resulted in full recovery of the original spectrum and hence of the stable isomer. The photostationary state ratio of metastable and stable isomers of 1, established upon irradiation at 530 nm, was approximately 1:1 , consistent with changes observed by Raman spectroscopy (d), which showed a ∼50% decrease in the intensity of the bands characteristic of the stable isomer (1580 cm–1).

## Energy Transfer, Photochemical, and Thermal Isomerization in the Solid State

Since pillared Zn paddlewheel MOFs are known to lose crystallinity or undergo structural collapse upon solvent removal, all of the experiments involving PdTCPP MOFs were conducted in solvent (DMF)-saturated conditions. The extent of the energy transfer between 1 and PdTCPP linkers in motorized MOF was determined with steady-state and time-resolved emission spectroscopy.

Upon excitation at 530 nm the parent PdTCPP MOF showed a similar emission spectrum to that of PdTCPP in DMF with a small hypsochromic shift of both fluorescence and phosphorescence (a). Conversely, in the emission spectrum of the motorized PdTCPP MOF a strong decrease in the phosphorescence intensity was observed, consistent with the energy transfer between the linkers (a). Furthermore, a significant drop in the porphyrin phosphorescence lifetime was observed from ca. 100 μs for the parent MOF to ca. 10 μs for the motorized MOF . The difference between the phosphorescence lifetimes of PdTCPP in solution and in the parent MOF originates from the effect of excessive scattering from the latter; nevertheless, the large decrease in emission lifetime between parent and motorized MOF clearly indicates energy transfer between 1 and PdTCPP linkers in MOF.

The rotary motion of motor 1 inserted in the MOF scaffold was followed with NIR–Raman spectroscopy (see for other spectra). Previously, we demonstrated that this technique is particularly convenient to study the photochemical and thermal isomerization of rotary molecular motors in condensed phase as it allows for unambiguous correlation of spectral data with the structural changes that these molecules exhibit in response to light and heat stimuli. Upon exposure of the polycrystalline motorized PdTCPP MOF sample to green light (530 nm) a gradual decrease in the Raman intensity at 1580 cm–1 with concomitant increase in scattering intensity at 1550 cm–1 was observed (b). Similar spectral features were detected upon photochemical isomerization of molecular motor 1 in solution and therefore could be ascribed to the same photochemical process. Furthermore, Raman spectroscopy showed that for thin samples the photostationary state of 1 reached via triplet sensitization in motorized PdTCPP MOF was similar to that in solution . Taking into consideration the molar absorptivity of PdTCPP at 532 nm and the concentration of molecular motor 1 in the crystal of the motorized MOF, the penetration depth for the excitation light in these crystals is likely no more than a few micrometers, and therefore, we envision the future application of these materials to be based on the surface-mounted MOFs (SURMOFs) or single-crystal devices. When the irradiation was discontinued, the initial Raman spectrum was recovered gradually, indicating thermal relaxation of the metastable to stable isomer. The barrier of the thermal relaxation at room temperature was determined by monitoring the changes in the bands area characteristic of the metastable isomer ( and ). The Gibbs free energy of activation for this process (Δ‡ G(20 °C)) was 88.7 ± 0.8 kJ mol–1 (t 1/2 ≈ 13 min) and corresponded well to the barrier determined in DMF solution (88.0 ± 0.4 kJ mol–1, t 1/2 ≈ 9 min). The good agreement between the barriers in solution and the solid material shows that molecular motor 1 can perform its large amplitude rotary motion uncompromised while incorporated in PdTCPP MOF. Furthermore, irradiation/thermal relaxation steps could be repeated over five cycles (b, inset) without any noticeable sign of fatigue or photodegradation, indicating high stability of the framework.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, we established that the photoisomerization of the molecular motor pillars in a porphyrin Zn paddlewheel MOF can be driven with visible light by triplet sensitization. The desired motorized MOF was constructed by postsynthetic linker exchange (SALE) from the newly developed parent PdTCPP MOF bearing DPG pillars. Exchange of these pillars with the longer bispyridyl motor 1 resulted in the expected expansion of the elementary cell in the c direction as shown by the SC X-ray and PXRD data. Due to the spatial coarrangement of the chromophores in the motorized MOF, the energy transfer between photosensitizer (2D layers) and molecular motor (pillars) was found to be efficient, and the photochemical isomerization of the molecular motor could be achieved with green 530 nm light. Additionally, it was shown that the rate of the thermal helix inversion step of the molecular motors incorporated in the material scaffold is essentially the same as that observed in solution, owing to the large free volume present in the framework. The demonstration of visible-light-driven rotary motion of a molecular motor in a metal–organic framework opens many perspectives for future applications, such as membranes and pumps able to accelerate flow of gases or in combination with catalytic function and miniaturized chemical reactors able to accelerate inflow of reactants and outflow of products, powered by noninvasive visible light. Furthermore, we envision that this strategy may be used to expand the scope of photosensitizers and molecular motors to achieve an even further shift of the excitation wavelength toward red light.

3. Experimental Procedures

UV/Vis studies. For the UV/Vis studies solutions were degassed by sparging with argon for ca. 1 min in a 1 cm quartz cuvette equipped with a septum-sealed screw cap. For the kinetic studies solutions were irradiated at 530 nmat a range of temperatures 6-14°C, every 2°C) until no further changes were observed in the UV/Vis spectrum. The irradiation was discontinued and the changes in absorbance at 440 nmwere followed in time. For the alternating irradiation and thermal helix inversion cycles the solutions were irradiated at RT until no further changes were observed in the UV/Vis spectrum and kept at RT in the dark for the thermal process.

1HNMR analysis. For the in situ 1HNMR studies the solution of PdTCPP and 1 (3.0 mmol for both components) in THF- was purged in the NMR tube with argon for ca. 30 sec, submerged with an Evans NMR tube equipped with optical fibre and sealed with Parafilm.

Raman Studies. In solution Raman spectra were recorded in 1 cm quartz cuvette equipped with a tightly sealed screw cap in a sample holder equipped with a TC1 temperature controller (Quantum Northwest). The equimolar solution of PdTCPP and 1 (15.0 mM, DMF, ca. 1 mL) was degassed in the cuvette by purging with Argon and irradiated at 530 nmwith stirring for approximately 30 min at -20°Cto reach PSS. Subsequently, the solution was warmed up to room temperature to facilitate the thermal helix inversion. In solid, DMF wet samples of DPG and motorized PdTCPP MOFs were placed between two quartz slides and sealed with Teflon tape to prevent drying. For variable power experiments power of the laser was tuned by changing the aperture of the slit and the transmitted power was measured using using a FieldMate laser power meter (RoHS compliant).

Emission Studies. For emission studies in solution DMF was degassed by five freeze-pump-thaw cycles and placed inside a glovebox. All the solutions were prepared innside a glove box in a 1 cm quartz cuvettes equipped with a septum-sealed screw cap by dilution of the same DMF stock solutions of PdTCPP and molecular motor 1 to a final concentration of PdTCPP of (MATH). For emission studies in the solid, a suspension of PdTCPP-DPG or motorized PdTCPP MOFs crystals in DMF

were placed in a mm NMR tube equipped with J. Young valve and degassed by 5 freeze-pumpthaw cycles.

Elemental Analysis. For elemental analysis MOFs samples were washed thoroughly with DMF then with DCM, dried and kept under a vacuum for 24 h prior to the analysis.

PXRD Studies. PXRD data of MOFs was collected for samples enclosed in spinning glass 1.0 mmcapillaries (Hampton Research, HR6-122) with supernatant liquid. MOFs crystals were gently ground with a glass Pasteur pipette and transferred to the capillaries which were subsequently sealed with wax and placed on the goniometer head for mounting on the diffractometer.

5. SC-Xray Studies

Single-crystals were mounted on a cryoloop and placed in the nitrogen stream (100 K) of a Bruker-AXS D8 Venture diffractometer. Data collection and processing was carried out using the Bruker APEX3 software suite.2 A multi-scan absorption correction was applied, based on the intensities of symmetry-related reflections measured at different angular settings (SADABS).2 The structures were solved either using SHELXT3 or SHELXS4 and refinement was performed using SHELXL.4 The hydrogen atoms were generated by geometrical considerations, constrained by idealized geometries and allowed to ride on their carrier atoms with an isotropic displacement parameter related to the equivalent displacement parameter of their carrier atoms. Contributions from disordered solvent present in structures of parent, motorized and interpenetrated PdTCPP MOFs as well as disordered pillars between the resolved porphyrin planes in parent and motorized PdTCPP MOFs were removed using the PLATON/SQUEEZE routine.5

## Introduction

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) represent an important class of crystalline porous molecular solids with potential applications in diverse areas. By reducing one dimension of bulky MOFs to single or few layers, two-dimensional (2D) MOF nanosheets (MONs) have emerged as a new member in the family of 2D nanomaterials considering their merits of combining more accessible active sites, super flexibility, and faster diffusion. Much attention has recently been paid to 2D MONs that contain periodically arranged in-plane unformal nanopores for their promising application in highly selective catalysis, separation, and sensing. Among various reported methods, exfoliation of 3D layered MOFs has been shown to be an efficient approach to fabricate 2D nanosheets. Nevertheless, ordered pores remain difficult to generate, due to the limited availability of 3D layered robust MOFs. To address this issue, we illustrate here a strategy for preparing layered porous MOFs by using a bulky hydrophobic and angular organic linker to restrict the growth direction of coordination networks. The weak interlayer hydrophobic interactions allow the easy fabrication of single-crystalline ultrathin 2D porous MONs from the parent 3D MOFs through ultrasonic exfoliation.

Another challenge facing layered MOFs is to identify structural order or observe local structure features with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) because of their extreme sensitivity to the electron beam irradiations. The recent advance in the low-dose high-resolution transmission electron microscopy makes it possible for the direct imaging and structure determination of electron beam-sensitive materials at the atomic level. Utilizing this technique, not only the detailed framework information including the pore architectures and building blocks in MOFs but also the local structure features such as crystal surfaces and interfaces and point- or extended-defects may be identified. Even though, there are still few HRTEM studies on crystalline layered MOFs, because their 2D nature causes greater structural fragility. This is particularly true for chiral MOFs, which remain a virgin land waiting for exploration, although they hold great promise in enantioselective processes. Inspired by the discovery of MOFs made from high-valent metals such as Cr(III) and Zr(IV) that can dramatically increase framework robustness, we envisioned that lanthanide(III)-based 2D MOFs may have sufficient structural stability that enables HRTEM imaging. On the basis of this hypothesis, we designed and synthesized three porous layered Ln-MOFs using the chiral dicarboxylate linker derived from 1,1′-biphenyl phosphoric acid with pendant aromatic groups at the 3,3′-position. The obtained chiral MOFs were easily exfoliated into one- and two-layer single-crystalline nanosheets by ultrasonication. The detailed structural information, i.e., the pore channels and individual building units in the MOFs, was clearly visualized by the low-dose HRTEM technique. To make full use of the single-crystalline and periodic porous structure of 2D MONs, we used them to fabricate free-standing mixed-matrix membranes (MMMs) by a phase-inversion method. In both the solution and membranes, the fluorescence of 2D MONs can be effectively quenched by chiral odor vapors including terpenes and terpenoids via interactions with the free chiral phosphoric acids, exhibiting much enhanced enantioselectivity relative to the homogeneous control system. We speculate that the enhancement is due to the channel confinement effect and conformational rigidity of the sensing phosphoric acid sites in the 2D structure. It is worth noting that the chirality and enantiomeric composition play an important role in the biological activities of terpenoids and their metabolites. Chirality sensing of terpenes and terpenoids, which have a single double bond as the only functional group, such as α-pinene, β-pinene, and camphene, or two alkene moieties, such as limonene, valencene, and β-caryophyllene, is one of the most difficult molecular recognition issues.

## Synthesis and Characterization

The bulky ligand H3 L was prepared from (R)- or (S)-6,6′-dimethyl-5,5′-di(4-methoxycarbonyl)phenyl-3,3′-diiodo-1,1′-biphenyl-2,2′-diol in three steps in 66.5% overall yield. Heating H3 L and LnCl3 ·6H2O in a mixed solvent containing N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) or N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA) at 100 °C afforded colorless crystals of the targeted MOFs with the general framework formula [H2NMe2]2[Ln2(HL)4] (Ln = Eu, 1; Ln = Dy, 2; Ln = Tb, 3) (a). All of them were stable in air and insoluble in water and common organic solvents. They were formulated based on elemental analysis and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The phase purity of the bulk samples was established by comparison of their observed and simulated powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns.

(a) Synthesis of the Ln-MOFs and a microscopic image of the colorless polyhedral crystals. (b, c) Single-crystal structures of the 3D layered Eu-MOF and (c) its one layer. (d) Coordination environments of lanthanide ions. (e) A dilanthanide carboxylate unit (Ln, blue; P, green; O, red; C, gray).

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealed that MOF 1 crystallizes in the orthorhombic chiral space group C222, with one-fourth of the formula unit in the asymmetric unit. The Eu ion is coordinated by eight oxygen atoms of four bidentate-bridging and four chelated carboxylate groups from six different HL ligands. Two adjacent Eu ions are linked by four carboxylate groups to form a dieuropium unit (e). The HL ligand exhibits an exotetradentate coordination fashion, binding three Eu atoms via one chelated and one bidentate-bridging carboxylate groups. The two phenyl subunits are twisted along the pivotal 1,1′-bond with a dihedral angle of 56.5°. Each Eu2 unit in 1 is thus linked by eight HL ligands, and each HL ligand is linked to two Eu2 cores forming a 2D anionic framework in the a-b plane, in which free phosphoric acid groups point outward and are accessible for guest molecules (c,d). The 2D layer has the maximum thickness of 28.3 Å and contains 1D square-shaped channels of ∼1.0 × 1.5 nm2 along the a-axis (measured from van der Waals surfaces). Charges are balanced by [H2NMe2]+ counterions, which were produced during the crystallization of the material. Such 2D layers stack one on top of each other along the c-axis to generate a 3D porous architecture. A space-filling representation of 1 clearly shows the formation of porous channels. The neighboring layers have weak van der Waals interactions between mesityl groups of HL (b). The layered morphology of the bulk MOF crystals was provided by the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image (Figure S2 of the , SI). MOFs 2 and 3 are isostructural to 1 and adopt a similar layered structure. Calculations using PLATON indicated that MOFs 1–3 have about 56.6%, 56.0%, and 55.8% void volume available for guest inclusion, respectively. TGA revealed that the MOFs started to decompose at about 350 °C . Circular dichroism (CD) spectra of 1–3 prepared from (R)- and (S)-enantiomers of H3 L are mirror images of each other, indicating their enantiomeric nature .

Due to the weak van der Waals interactions between adjacent layers along the c axis, these MOFs can be easily exfoliated into 2D porous nanosheets (a-b plane), denoted as MONs, through solvent-assisted liquid sonication (a). The exfoliation can be verified by the Tyndall effect upon irradiation of the colloid suspensions of MONs with a laser beam (b and ). It is found that the colloid suspensions can be stable at r.t. for at least 6 months, indicating the monodispersity of nanosheets . As illustrated in b, TEM images clearly showed the ultrathin and wrinkled 2D nanosheets of 1.0 × 1.5 μm2. In c, the AFM image demonstrates a sheet structure and smooth surface for 1-MONs. The thickness of the 1-MONs was found to be 6.0 ± 0.1 nm (c and ), which is about twice the theoretical thickness of the monolayer (2.83 nm), indicating that 1-MONs consists of two MOF layers. SEM images of 2D 1-MONs also show an inherent sheet structure, consistent with the AFM observation .

By far, HRTEM imaging of MOFs has rarely been reported, and there was only limited resolution achieved, mainly due to the easy structural damage of MOFs under the electron beam. Using the recently developed low-dose HRTEM technique [Section 1 in the ], we have successfully acquired HRTEM images of MOF 1 with much improved resolution (<4 Å). A representative image that was acquired along the [100] direction with a total electron dose as low as ∼20 e– Å–2 is shown in d. The inset in d is the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the corresponding crystal, which matches well with the simulated electron diffraction (ED) pattern along the [100] direction . Furthermore, we corrected the HRTEM image based on the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the objective lens to make it more interpretable. In the CTF-corrected image (e), the “black dots” correspond to the metal clusters, the “gray stripes” correspond to the ligands, and the “white areas” correspond to the channels. The “white areas” between the “black dots” (clusters) with an average size of 1.6 nm in e correspond to the channels, as indicated by the yellow arrows. The simulated image in f shows the same pore size of 1.6 nm. The processed image showed a reasonably good match with the simulated projected potential map (g) and the structure model (f). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the framework of a chiral MOF is directly observed by HRTEM.

## Enantioselective Fluorescent Sensing

As expected, MOF 1 is highly fluorescent, with the emission maximum at 429 nm in the solid state, different from Me2 L, which gives the emission maxima at 384 nm, whereas the colloidal suspension of 1-MONs in CH3CN gave the emission maxima at 386 nm , which was blue-shifted by about 43 nm compared to that of bulk powder, consistent with the reduced interlayer π–π interaction in nanosheets. The presence of chiral channels and readily available phosphoric acid active sites makes it possible for the fluorescent 1-MONs to selectively recognize chiral molecules (a,c). It has been a big challenge to realize special artificial odor sensors for chiral discrimination in drug analysis and environmental monitoring. So, we first studied the recognition and sensing ability of 1-MONs to a variety of terpenoids in solutions. The MONs were dispersed in CH3CN to obtain a uniformly stable suspension with the phosphoric acid unit at a concentration of 10 μM. When (S)-1-MONs was treated with two enantiomers of α-pinene, the emissions at 386 nm were both decreased, but the quenching rate caused by the (−)-α-pinene was slower than that with the (+)-enantiomer. The fluorescence intensity of 1-MONs was maximally decreased by 13.49% and 32.12% compared with the original value, respectively. From the linear Stern–Völmer equation, the measured absorbance [I 0/I] varied as a function of [M] in a linear relationship, indicating a 1:1 stoichiometry of the interaction between the substrate and phosphoric acid of 1-MONs. The K sv constants were calculated to be 905 ± 8 and 2405 ± 38 M–1 with the (−)- and (+)-enantiomers, respectively, producing the quenching ratio [QR = K sv(+)/K sv(−)] of 2.66 (f and ). 1-MONs was also enantioselective toward substrates containing only a double bond functionality including limonene, β-pinene, valencene, and isolongifolene, with the QR values ranging from 1.85 to 2.06. Besides, terpenoids containing only one ketone group can be recognized by 1-MONs as well, affording the QR values of 3.47–4.19. However, 1-MONs failed to well recognize the enantiomers of menthyl acetate (QR = 1.10) (f and ), presumably due to the weak interactions between the ester and phosphoric acid groups in 1-MONs.

1-MONs can also enantioselectively recognize terpenoids having two different functional groups (the double bond and alcohol, ketone, or aldehyde), which may bind the phosphoric acid sites via a bidentate coordination mode (b). The QR values for terpinen-4-ol, (−)-perillyl alcohol, (−)-isopulegol, (−)-linalool, and β-citronellol were calculated to be 1.66, 2.60, 1.29, 4.30, and 3.51, respectively. The linear substrates (−)-linalool and β-citronellol gave higher enantioselectivity than the cyclic substrates, probably because they may easily access the binding sites in the channels more easily than the cyclic substrates. Besides, the binding constant of 1-MONs with (−)-linalool was larger than (−)-β-citronellol (6245 M–1 vs 536 M–1) (d and ). This may be ascribed to that the alcohol and double bond groups in linalool were much closer to the chiral center than β-citronellol, which was beneficial for stereoselective recognition. For β-citronellal, perillaldehyde, and myrtenal with both a double bond and an aldehyde group, although they have high binding constants with 1-MONs, the quenching ratios are only in the range of 1.70–2.35. Interestingly, the binding constants for (+)-carvone and (−)-carvone with 1-MONs are only 2197 and 558 M–1, but the enantioselectivity is high, as evidenced by the QR of 3.93 (g and ). This may be due to the dominant role of ketone groups in the stereoselective recognition, consistent with the observed for monofunctional terpenoids with ketones (menthone and fenchone).

In practical applications, it is beneficial to process MONs into films, which may circumvent the issues of clogging and recycling. So, we examined the sensing behaviors of composite materials integrating 1-MONs with a polymeric binder. After exfoliating the 3D layered MOF bulk crystals to 2D nanosheets, not only the crystalline of MOF can be maintained but also the highly dispersed nanosheet suspensions are easy for membrane fabrication. The as-prepared 1-MONs was used to fabricate MMMs by a phase-inversion method. A poly(ether sulfone) (PES) solution in DMF was mixed with the stock suspension of the 1-MONs (5.0 wt %) and stirred for 3 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife. The glass plate was put into deionized water, and the free-standing 1-MONs-MMM was peeled off from the glass surface. The membrane can be rolled up and returned to its original shape without cracks after being released (a,b), indicating good flexibility of the membrane. Analysis of this membrane by SEM with energy dispersive spectra (EDS) revealed that 1-MONs was well dispersed in the PES membrane (d). The cross-sectional image showed that the membrane thickness was about 30 μm (e), which can facilitate the fast diffusion and transport of analytes. Fluorescence images of the membrane under UV light, which were obtained by fluorescence interference microscopy, further confirmed a homogeneous dispersion of 1-MONs within the PES matrix (c).

## Conclusion

We have reported the design and synthesis of three chiral porous 3D layered Ln-MOFs based on a 1,1′-biphenyl skeleton with pendant mesityl groups at the 3,3′-position. Owing to the weak interlayer stacking, the bulk Eu-MOF crystals can be easily exfoliated into 2D ultrathin single-crystalline nanosheets (two layers), stabilized by a sterically bulky hydrophobic group. The ordered pore channels and metal nodes are clearly observed in the Eu-based framework by our recently developed low-dose TEM technique. As a proof-of-concept application, the obtained 1-MONs-MMM was used as a fluorescence-sensing platform for the detection of both terpenes and terpenoids with excellent selectivity and high sensitivity. This work will promote the rational design, synthesis, and characterization of more ultrathin single-crystalline 2D MONs with intrinsic porosity, which might have various promising applications in membrane separation, sensing, and catalysis.

Phase purity of the MOFs was established by comparison of their observed and simulated powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns. PXRD further revealed that 1-MONs remained almost the same as the pristine samples, revealing its good crystallinity and stability (a). The difference in relative peak intensities of XRD between MOF 1 and 1-MONs may primarily be attributed to the absence of long-range order in the stacking direction and the retention of periodicity within the plane after the exfoliating process. Their N2 adsorption isotherms were measured at 77 K. All exhibit reversible type-I isotherms, which are characteristic of microporous materials. The estimated apparent Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface areas of MOFs 1–3 are 356, 359, and 340 m2 g–1, respectively. On the basis of the maximum N2 uptake, MOFs 1–3 have calculated total pore volumes of 0.186, 0.222, and 0.185 cm3 g–1, respectively. After exfoliation, the 1-MONs displayed a BET surface area of 453 m2 g–1, about 1.3 times higher than that of the bulk MOF (b and ). It may be attributed to the lack of adsorption sites of bulk MOF, which was mainly caused by the close-packed layer structure. This result is associated with the previously described for other delaminated materials. This suggests the nanosheets can retain the porous nature as the pristine framework. Besides, the FT-IR spectra also demonstrated the same structures of the 3D bulk MOF-1 material and 2D 1-MONs .

While the pure PES membrane showed no fluorescence, 1-MONs-MMM displayed a maximum emission at 355 nm . The fluorescence spectra of the 1-MONs-MMM were monitored upon exposure to the saturated vapor of chiral terpenoids for varied and specified periods of time. When 1-MONs-MMM was exposed to the (−)-linalool vapor, the emission at 355 nm was decreased by both the (S)- and (R)- 1-MONs-MMM, but the quenching rate caused by (S)-1-MONs-MMM was much faster than that by the (R)-1-MONs-MMM (e and ). The decreased percentage was estimated using the formula (I 0 – I)/I 0 × 100%, where I 0 is the maximum fluorescence intensity before exposure to the analyte, and I is the maximum intensity after exposure to the analyte. The quenched percentages of (S)- and (R)-1-MONs-MMM were 38.5 and 6.5% after 420 s, with the I 0/I ratios of 1.63 and 1.07, respectively. The enantioselectivity factor [EF = (I 0 /I S – 1)/(I 0 /I R – 1] was determined as 9.03. Importantly, the 1-MONs-MMM was also enantioselective toward a range of monofunctional chiral vapors, including α-pinene, limonene, fenchone, menthyl acetate, (−)-β-pinene, (+)-valencene, (−)-isolongifolene, and (−)-menthone with the EF values ranging from 1.03 to 4.71 (f and ). The trends of fluorescence quenching are consistent with the solution titration with 1-MON suspensions. For terpenoids containing a ketone group, the values are greater than those with a double bond and ester. Comparison of the fluorescent sensing of menthone and menthyl acetate proved that the ester group may prevent the phosphoric acid sites from binding to the substrates. Moreover, the MONs-MMM was enantioselective toward a variety of chiral bifunctional terpenoids in addition to the double bond (g and ). All substrates exhibit comparable and even better enantioselectivity than the solution titration. The EF values of β-citronellol and (−)-linalool can reach 8.26 and 9.03.

Control experiments indicated that the Me2 L-based MMM showed almost no fluorescence changes with (+)- or (−)-limonene and no enantioselectivity. To study the influence of membrane microstructures on the sensing behavior, we fabricated the dense MMM with 5.0 wt % MONs loading by modifying the phase-inversion method . From the sensing experiments, the I/I 0 ratios were found to be 6.10 and 14.90 for the (−)- and (+)-enantiomers of limonene, affording the EF value of 2.69, which was obviously smaller than 4.43 of the porous 1-MONs-MMM . This is presumably due to that the dense membrane inhibited the fast diffusion and transport of analytes, leading to a decrease of interactions between analytes and MONs. We further compared the sensing performance of the porous MMMs with different MONs loadings. With increasing the loadings of 1-MONs from 1.0 wt % to 5.0 wt %, 10.0 wt %, and 20.0 wt %, the enantioselectivity factors gradually increased from 3.55 to 4.43, 4.95, and 5.31, respectively . It is likely that the high loading of MONs is beneficial to the improvement of the selective sensing performance of MMMs. However, increasing the MONs loading to 40.0 wt % led to unsuccessful membrane preparation. Nonetheless, based on the above experimental result and literature reports, it can be speculated that the 2D MONs in the form of a pure crystalline membrane would exhibit outstanding performance in molecular sensing and separation since their unique pore structures and the ultrathin thickness would be fully utilized. Further research in this direction is in progress. Moreover, after each measurement, 1-MONs-MMM could be regenerated by washing with CH3CN three times and heating at 80 °C in a vacuum for about 2 h and directly reused for the next cycle of sensing without significant loss of enantioselectivity (EF = 9.07, 8.83, and 8.69 for runs 1–3 in sensing (−)-linalool, respectively) . After three cycles of sensing, the structure of the 1-MONs-MMM membrane remained almost unchanged, as evidenced by EDS mappings images .

The observed fluorescence quenching in both 1-MONs suspensions and 1-MONs-MMM may be ascribed to static enhancement upon the formation of a MOF-vapor adduct, which can induce changes in the structure of emitting species such as a change and/or rigidification of the conformation and excimer formation. Time-resolved fluorescence measurements of the membrane after exposure to the vapor of chiral (+)- and (−)-limonene showed only a slight change in decay rate, the fluorescence lifetimes (τ0, 2.31 vs 2.30 and 2.42 ns) remained almost unchanged . In the 1-MONs solution system, due to the short excited-state lifetime (<3 ns), low fluorophore concentration (10 μM), and quencher concentration (0–175 μM), the collision probability during the excited state lifetime of the fluorophore was very low, so the collisional quenching was negligible. Additionally, there is no overlap between the absorption (emission) spectra of 1-MONs and the emission (absorption) spectra of limonene , indicating no obvious electron or energy transfer between them. Further study is greatly needed to understand the mechanism of the stereoselective fluorescence quenching.

The alkene or alkene- and oxygen-containing functional groups are not easily targeted with synthetic receptors, and hence, there are limited reports on molecular recognitions of terpene and terpenoid with high enantioselectivity. Among several reported procedures for sensing chiral terpenes and terpenoids, electrochemical methods including organic field effect transistors are of great interest, but they are costly and time-consuming or have unsatisfactory selectivity. Chiral optical sensors are among the most logical choices for fast and simple detections of chiral vapors; but synthetically, they still face a challenge because enantiomers of volatile molecules generally cannot induce an obvious structure difference in chromophore cores, making it hard to be detected. Recent reports highlight the promise of porous frameworks including both MOFs and COFs (covalent organic frameworks) as optical sensors for various important substrates such as volatile organic molecules, explosives, and biomolecules, but their application in chiral recognition and sensing has not yet to be well studied. To the best of our knowledge, there is only one report on chiral COFs for enantioselective fluorescence sensing of terpenes and terpenoids, but where only five chiral odors can be recognized, namely α-pinene, fenchone, limonene, carvone, and terpinen-4-ol. Benefiting from the ultrathin single-crystalline nature, the Eu-MONs has been used for enantioselective fluorescence sensing of a large variety of terpenes and terpenoids having one or more functional groups, with the sensitivity and enantioselectivity comparable with the above-mentioned chiral COFs. The chiral sensing with the MONs should be broadly useful and applicable but not limited to 17 important terpenes and terpenoids, holding the potential to perform online enantiomer detection and discrimination.

1. Materials and general procedures

All reagents and solvents are commercially available and used without further purification. Elemental analyses were performed with an EA1110 CHNS-0 CE elemental analyzer. The FT-IR (KBr pellet) spectra were recorded 400 · 4000 cm-1region) on a Nicolet Magna 750 FT-IR spectrometer. The CD spectra were recorded on a J-800 spectropolarimeter (Jasco, Japan). Thermogravimetric analyses (TGA) were carried out in a N2atmosphere with a heating rate of (MATH)on a thermogravimetric analyzer (Q5000IR). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were collected on a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer using CuKradiation. The calculated PXRD patterns were produced using the Mercury program and single crystal reflection data. 1H, 13Cand 31PNMR experiments were carried out on a MERCURY plus 400 spectrometer operating at resonance frequencies of 400 MHz. The N2gas adsorption isotherms were measured using a Micrometritics ASAP 2020 system at 77Kwith liquid N2bath. (Before the measurement, the fresh crystals were washed with DMF for three times, and then were further soaked in acetone for solvent exchange with replacement of fresh acetone three times. Subsequently, the samples were evacuated at 100°Cfor 10 h.) Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) images were performed on a NOVA NanoSEM 230 instrument equipped with an energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were performed on a Talos F200X/TALOS F200X instrument. Atomic force microscope (AFM) images were obtained on an Environment Control Scanning Probe Microscope (Nanonavi E-Sweep). The samples for AFM measurements were prepared by placing a drop of the diluted nanosheet dispersion onto a fresh cleaved mica. Low-dose high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images were taken on a Cs-corrected FEI cubed Titan 60-300 electron microscope under 300 kV. Specimen searching, zone axis alignment, and prefocusing were conducted at (MATH)magnification. HRTEM images were acquired at (MATH)magnification by using a Gatan K2 direct-detection camera operated in the electron counting mode with the dose fractionation function. The detailed HRTEM image acquisition and processing (zone axis alignment, focus determination, and CTF-correction) methods have been presented in reference.1 The projected electrostatic potential was simulated by the QSTEM software (http://www.qstem.org), with point spread function width of 3 Å.

Single-Crystal X-ray Diffraction. Single-crystal XRD data were collected on a Bruker SMART Apex II CCD-based X-ray diffractometer with Mo-Kα radiation (MATH)0.71073 Å) at 273.15 K. We have collected several datasets for all MOFs, and the best dataset was used for structure solution and refinement. The empirical absorption correction was applied by using the SADABS program (G. M. Sheldrick, SADABS,

program for empirical absorption correction of area detector data; University of Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany, 1996). The structures were solved using direct method, and refined by full-matrix least-squares on F2by the SHELXTL-2015 software package. DFIX, SADI, FLAT, DANG, EADP and SIMU restrains were used to obtain reasonable parameters. In the compounds, all the non-H atoms were refined anisotropically. Contributions to scattering due to these highly disordered solvent molecules were removed using the SQUEEZE routine of PLATON. The structures w ere then refined again using the data generated. Crystal data and details of the data collection are given in Table S1, while the selected bond distances and angles are presented in Table S2. The CIF files have been deposited in the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (CCDC) under deposition number 2048848 (MOF 1), 2048849 (MOF 2) 2048850 (MOF 3).

2.4 Preparation of 1-MONs-MMM

The hybrid MMMs were prepared by the phase-inversion method. 1-MONs (MATH)5.0 wt , 10.0 wt and 20.0 wt ) was dispersed in anhydrous DMF (1.9 mL). The resulting solution was mixed with PES 600 mg) and the mixture was stirred for 2 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife at a given time. The glass plate was then put into deionized water and the free-standing MMM was peeled off from the glass surface. Pure PES and Me2L@PES membranes were prepared in a similar procedure.

The dense 1-MONs-MMM were prepared by the modifying phase-inversion method. 1-MONs (5.0 wt %) was dispersed in anhydrous DMF (1.9 mL). The resulting solution was mixed with PES 600 mg) and the mixture was stirred for 2 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife, and then the solvent was evaporated at 100°Cfor 5 hours. The glass plate was put into water and the membrane was peeled off from the glass surface, producing the translucent and dense (S)-1-MONs@PES MMM (5.0 wt ).

2.5. General procedure for fluorescence sensing

The titration experiments were carried out by adding 50.0 µLsolution of substrates (MATH)in CH3CN) to a solution of 1-MONs or M e2 L(MATH)) in CH3CNevery two minutes. The excitation wavelengths are 302 nmand 307 nmfor MONs and Me2L, respectively.

Membrane sensing: The 1-MONs-MMM was carefully cut into 0.8 cm × 0.8 cm1 rectangles and kept in a desiccator. The membrane was then fixed into the inner surface of a quartz cuvette, 50.0 µLof each analyte was added into the bottom of the quartz cuvette. The quartz cuvette was immediately capped and sealed with parafilm, followed by time-dependent fluorescence test (λex = 290 nm)). The quenching efficiency was estimated using the formula (I0–I)/I0×100%, where IOand are the maximum fluorescence intensity of membrane before and after exposure to the analyte vapor, respectively.

## Introduction

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) represent an important class of crystalline porous molecular solids with potential applications in diverse areas. By reducing one dimension of bulky MOFs to single or few layers, two-dimensional (2D) MOF nanosheets (MONs) have emerged as a new member in the family of 2D nanomaterials considering their merits of combining more accessible active sites, super flexibility, and faster diffusion. Much attention has recently been paid to 2D MONs that contain periodically arranged in-plane unformal nanopores for their promising application in highly selective catalysis, separation, and sensing. Among various reported methods, exfoliation of 3D layered MOFs has been shown to be an efficient approach to fabricate 2D nanosheets. Nevertheless, ordered pores remain difficult to generate, due to the limited availability of 3D layered robust MOFs. To address this issue, we illustrate here a strategy for preparing layered porous MOFs by using a bulky hydrophobic and angular organic linker to restrict the growth direction of coordination networks. The weak interlayer hydrophobic interactions allow the easy fabrication of single-crystalline ultrathin 2D porous MONs from the parent 3D MOFs through ultrasonic exfoliation.

Another challenge facing layered MOFs is to identify structural order or observe local structure features with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) because of their extreme sensitivity to the electron beam irradiations. The recent advance in the low-dose high-resolution transmission electron microscopy makes it possible for the direct imaging and structure determination of electron beam-sensitive materials at the atomic level. Utilizing this technique, not only the detailed framework information including the pore architectures and building blocks in MOFs but also the local structure features such as crystal surfaces and interfaces and point- or extended-defects may be identified. Even though, there are still few HRTEM studies on crystalline layered MOFs, because their 2D nature causes greater structural fragility. This is particularly true for chiral MOFs, which remain a virgin land waiting for exploration, although they hold great promise in enantioselective processes. Inspired by the discovery of MOFs made from high-valent metals such as Cr(III) and Zr(IV) that can dramatically increase framework robustness, we envisioned that lanthanide(III)-based 2D MOFs may have sufficient structural stability that enables HRTEM imaging. On the basis of this hypothesis, we designed and synthesized three porous layered Ln-MOFs using the chiral dicarboxylate linker derived from 1,1′-biphenyl phosphoric acid with pendant aromatic groups at the 3,3′-position. The obtained chiral MOFs were easily exfoliated into one- and two-layer single-crystalline nanosheets by ultrasonication. The detailed structural information, i.e., the pore channels and individual building units in the MOFs, was clearly visualized by the low-dose HRTEM technique. To make full use of the single-crystalline and periodic porous structure of 2D MONs, we used them to fabricate free-standing mixed-matrix membranes (MMMs) by a phase-inversion method. In both the solution and membranes, the fluorescence of 2D MONs can be effectively quenched by chiral odor vapors including terpenes and terpenoids via interactions with the free chiral phosphoric acids, exhibiting much enhanced enantioselectivity relative to the homogeneous control system. We speculate that the enhancement is due to the channel confinement effect and conformational rigidity of the sensing phosphoric acid sites in the 2D structure. It is worth noting that the chirality and enantiomeric composition play an important role in the biological activities of terpenoids and their metabolites. Chirality sensing of terpenes and terpenoids, which have a single double bond as the only functional group, such as α-pinene, β-pinene, and camphene, or two alkene moieties, such as limonene, valencene, and β-caryophyllene, is one of the most difficult molecular recognition issues.

## Synthesis and Characterization

The bulky ligand H3 L was prepared from (R)- or (S)-6,6′-dimethyl-5,5′-di(4-methoxycarbonyl)phenyl-3,3′-diiodo-1,1′-biphenyl-2,2′-diol in three steps in 66.5% overall yield. Heating H3 L and LnCl3 ·6H2O in a mixed solvent containing N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) or N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA) at 100 °C afforded colorless crystals of the targeted MOFs with the general framework formula [H2NMe2]2[Ln2(HL)4] (Ln = Eu, 1; Ln = Dy, 2; Ln = Tb, 3) (a). All of them were stable in air and insoluble in water and common organic solvents. They were formulated based on elemental analysis and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The phase purity of the bulk samples was established by comparison of their observed and simulated powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns.

(a) Synthesis of the Ln-MOFs and a microscopic image of the colorless polyhedral crystals. (b, c) Single-crystal structures of the 3D layered Eu-MOF and (c) its one layer. (d) Coordination environments of lanthanide ions. (e) A dilanthanide carboxylate unit (Ln, blue; P, green; O, red; C, gray).

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealed that MOF 1 crystallizes in the orthorhombic chiral space group C222, with one-fourth of the formula unit in the asymmetric unit. The Eu ion is coordinated by eight oxygen atoms of four bidentate-bridging and four chelated carboxylate groups from six different HL ligands. Two adjacent Eu ions are linked by four carboxylate groups to form a dieuropium unit (e). The HL ligand exhibits an exotetradentate coordination fashion, binding three Eu atoms via one chelated and one bidentate-bridging carboxylate groups. The two phenyl subunits are twisted along the pivotal 1,1′-bond with a dihedral angle of 56.5°. Each Eu2 unit in 1 is thus linked by eight HL ligands, and each HL ligand is linked to two Eu2 cores forming a 2D anionic framework in the a-b plane, in which free phosphoric acid groups point outward and are accessible for guest molecules (c,d). The 2D layer has the maximum thickness of 28.3 Å and contains 1D square-shaped channels of ∼1.0 × 1.5 nm2 along the a-axis (measured from van der Waals surfaces). Charges are balanced by [H2NMe2]+ counterions, which were produced during the crystallization of the material. Such 2D layers stack one on top of each other along the c-axis to generate a 3D porous architecture. A space-filling representation of 1 clearly shows the formation of porous channels. The neighboring layers have weak van der Waals interactions between mesityl groups of HL (b). The layered morphology of the bulk MOF crystals was provided by the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image (Figure S2 of the , SI). MOFs 2 and 3 are isostructural to 1 and adopt a similar layered structure. Calculations using PLATON indicated that MOFs 1–3 have about 56.6%, 56.0%, and 55.8% void volume available for guest inclusion, respectively. TGA revealed that the MOFs started to decompose at about 350 °C . Circular dichroism (CD) spectra of 1–3 prepared from (R)- and (S)-enantiomers of H3 L are mirror images of each other, indicating their enantiomeric nature .

Due to the weak van der Waals interactions between adjacent layers along the c axis, these MOFs can be easily exfoliated into 2D porous nanosheets (a-b plane), denoted as MONs, through solvent-assisted liquid sonication (a). The exfoliation can be verified by the Tyndall effect upon irradiation of the colloid suspensions of MONs with a laser beam (b and ). It is found that the colloid suspensions can be stable at r.t. for at least 6 months, indicating the monodispersity of nanosheets . As illustrated in b, TEM images clearly showed the ultrathin and wrinkled 2D nanosheets of 1.0 × 1.5 μm2. In c, the AFM image demonstrates a sheet structure and smooth surface for 1-MONs. The thickness of the 1-MONs was found to be 6.0 ± 0.1 nm (c and ), which is about twice the theoretical thickness of the monolayer (2.83 nm), indicating that 1-MONs consists of two MOF layers. SEM images of 2D 1-MONs also show an inherent sheet structure, consistent with the AFM observation .
