By far, HRTEM imaging of MOFs has rarely been reported, and there was only limited resolution achieved, mainly due to the easy structural damage of MOFs under the electron beam. Using the recently developed low-dose HRTEM technique [Section 1 in the ], we have successfully acquired HRTEM images of MOF 1 with much improved resolution (<4 Å). A representative image that was acquired along the [100] direction with a total electron dose as low as ∼20 e– Å–2 is shown in d. The inset in d is the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the corresponding crystal, which matches well with the simulated electron diffraction (ED) pattern along the [100] direction . Furthermore, we corrected the HRTEM image based on the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the objective lens to make it more interpretable. In the CTF-corrected image (e), the “black dots” correspond to the metal clusters, the “gray stripes” correspond to the ligands, and the “white areas” correspond to the channels. The “white areas” between the “black dots” (clusters) with an average size of 1.6 nm in e correspond to the channels, as indicated by the yellow arrows. The simulated image in f shows the same pore size of 1.6 nm. The processed image showed a reasonably good match with the simulated projected potential map (g) and the structure model (f). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the framework of a chiral MOF is directly observed by HRTEM.

## Enantioselective Fluorescent Sensing

As expected, MOF 1 is highly fluorescent, with the emission maximum at 429 nm in the solid state, different from Me2 L, which gives the emission maxima at 384 nm, whereas the colloidal suspension of 1-MONs in CH3CN gave the emission maxima at 386 nm , which was blue-shifted by about 43 nm compared to that of bulk powder, consistent with the reduced interlayer π–π interaction in nanosheets. The presence of chiral channels and readily available phosphoric acid active sites makes it possible for the fluorescent 1-MONs to selectively recognize chiral molecules (a,c). It has been a big challenge to realize special artificial odor sensors for chiral discrimination in drug analysis and environmental monitoring. So, we first studied the recognition and sensing ability of 1-MONs to a variety of terpenoids in solutions. The MONs were dispersed in CH3CN to obtain a uniformly stable suspension with the phosphoric acid unit at a concentration of 10 μM. Aliquots with different amounts of the (−)- and (+)-enantiomers of the substrates were added to the 1-MONs suspensions (2 mL), and the fluorescence signals of the suspensions were measured at a specific time interval.

(a,b) Structures of terpenes and terpenoids used in this study. (c) The operation principle of the MON sensor. (d) Stern–Völmer plots of 1-MONs upon titration of (−)-linalool in MeCN. When (S)-1-MONs was treated with two enantiomers of α-pinene, the emissions at 386 nm were both decreased, but the quenching rate caused by the (−)-α-pinene was slower than that with the (+)-enantiomer. The fluorescence intensity of 1-MONs was maximally decreased by 13.49% and 32.12% compared with the original value, respectively. From the linear Stern–Völmer equation, the measured absorbance [I 0/I] varied as a function of [M] in a linear relationship, indicating a 1:1 stoichiometry of the interaction between the substrate and phosphoric acid of 1-MONs. The K sv constants were calculated to be 905 ± 8 and 2405 ± 38 M–1 with the (−)- and (+)-enantiomers, respectively, producing the quenching ratio [QR = K sv(+)/K sv(−)] of 2.66 (f and ). 1-MONs was also enantioselective toward substrates containing only a double bond functionality including limonene, β-pinene, valencene, and isolongifolene, with the QR values ranging from 1.85 to 2.06. Besides, terpenoids containing only one ketone group can be recognized by 1-MONs as well, affording the QR values of 3.47–4.19. However, 1-MONs failed to well recognize the enantiomers of menthyl acetate (QR = 1.10) (f and ), presumably due to the weak interactions between the ester and phosphoric acid groups in 1-MONs.

1-MONs can also enantioselectively recognize terpenoids having two different functional groups (the double bond and alcohol, ketone, or aldehyde), which may bind the phosphoric acid sites via a bidentate coordination mode (b). The QR values for terpinen-4-ol, (−)-perillyl alcohol, (−)-isopulegol, (−)-linalool, and β-citronellol were calculated to be 1.66, 2.60, 1.29, 4.30, and 3.51, respectively. The linear substrates (−)-linalool and β-citronellol gave higher enantioselectivity than the cyclic substrates, probably because they may easily access the binding sites in the channels more easily than the cyclic substrates. Besides, the binding constant of 1-MONs with (−)-linalool was larger than (−)-β-citronellol (6245 M–1 vs 536 M–1) (d and ). This may be ascribed to that the alcohol and double bond groups in linalool were much closer to the chiral center than β-citronellol, which was beneficial for stereoselective recognition. For β-citronellal, perillaldehyde, and myrtenal with both a double bond and an aldehyde group, although they have high binding constants with 1-MONs, the quenching ratios are only in the range of 1.70–2.35. Interestingly, the binding constants for (+)-carvone and (−)-carvone with 1-MONs are only 2197 and 558 M–1, but the enantioselectivity is high, as evidenced by the QR of 3.93 (g and ). This may be due to the dominant role of ketone groups in the stereoselective recognition, consistent with the observed for monofunctional terpenoids with ketones (menthone and fenchone).

In practical applications, it is beneficial to process MONs into films, which may circumvent the issues of clogging and recycling. So, we examined the sensing behaviors of composite materials integrating 1-MONs with a polymeric binder. After exfoliating the 3D layered MOF bulk crystals to 2D nanosheets, not only the crystalline of MOF can be maintained but also the highly dispersed nanosheet suspensions are easy for membrane fabrication. The as-prepared 1-MONs was used to fabricate MMMs by a phase-inversion method. A poly(ether sulfone) (PES) solution in DMF was mixed with the stock suspension of the 1-MONs (5.0 wt %) and stirred for 3 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife. The glass plate was put into deionized water, and the free-standing 1-MONs-MMM was peeled off from the glass surface. The membrane can be rolled up and returned to its original shape without cracks after being released (a,b), indicating good flexibility of the membrane. Analysis of this membrane by SEM with energy dispersive spectra (EDS) revealed that 1-MONs was well dispersed in the PES membrane (d). The cross-sectional image showed that the membrane thickness was about 30 μm (e), which can facilitate the fast diffusion and transport of analytes. Fluorescence images of the membrane under UV light, which were obtained by fluorescence interference microscopy, further confirmed a homogeneous dispersion of 1-MONs within the PES matrix (c).

## Conclusion

We have reported the design and synthesis of three chiral porous 3D layered Ln-MOFs based on a 1,1′-biphenyl skeleton with pendant mesityl groups at the 3,3′-position. Owing to the weak interlayer stacking, the bulk Eu-MOF crystals can be easily exfoliated into 2D ultrathin single-crystalline nanosheets (two layers), stabilized by a sterically bulky hydrophobic group. The ordered pore channels and metal nodes are clearly observed in the Eu-based framework by our recently developed low-dose TEM technique. As a proof-of-concept application, the obtained 1-MONs-MMM was used as a fluorescence-sensing platform for the detection of both terpenes and terpenoids with excellent selectivity and high sensitivity. This work will promote the rational design, synthesis, and characterization of more ultrathin single-crystalline 2D MONs with intrinsic porosity, which might have various promising applications in membrane separation, sensing, and catalysis.

Phase purity of the MOFs was established by comparison of their observed and simulated powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns. PXRD further revealed that 1-MONs remained almost the same as the pristine samples, revealing its good crystallinity and stability (a). The difference in relative peak intensities of XRD between MOF 1 and 1-MONs may primarily be attributed to the absence of long-range order in the stacking direction and the retention of periodicity within the plane after the exfoliating process. Their N2 adsorption isotherms were measured at 77 K. All exhibit reversible type-I isotherms, which are characteristic of microporous materials. The estimated apparent Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface areas of MOFs 1–3 are 356, 359, and 340 m2 g–1, respectively. On the basis of the maximum N2 uptake, MOFs 1–3 have calculated total pore volumes of 0.186, 0.222, and 0.185 cm3 g–1, respectively. After exfoliation, the 1-MONs displayed a BET surface area of 453 m2 g–1, about 1.3 times higher than that of the bulk MOF (b and ). It may be attributed to the lack of adsorption sites of bulk MOF, which was mainly caused by the close-packed layer structure. This result is associated with the previously described for other delaminated materials. This suggests the nanosheets can retain the porous nature as the pristine framework. Besides, the FT-IR spectra also demonstrated the same structures of the 3D bulk MOF-1 material and 2D 1-MONs .

While the pure PES membrane showed no fluorescence, 1-MONs-MMM displayed a maximum emission at 355 nm . The fluorescence spectra of the 1-MONs-MMM were monitored upon exposure to the saturated vapor of chiral terpenoids for varied and specified periods of time. When 1-MONs-MMM was exposed to the (−)-linalool vapor, the emission at 355 nm was decreased by both the (S)- and (R)- 1-MONs-MMM, but the quenching rate caused by (S)-1-MONs-MMM was much faster than that by the (R)-1-MONs-MMM (e and ). The decreased percentage was estimated using the formula (I 0 – I)/I 0 × 100%, where I 0 is the maximum fluorescence intensity before exposure to the analyte, and I is the maximum intensity after exposure to the analyte. The quenched percentages of (S)- and (R)-1-MONs-MMM were 38.5 and 6.5% after 420 s, with the I 0/I ratios of 1.63 and 1.07, respectively. The enantioselectivity factor [EF = (I 0 /I S – 1)/(I 0 /I R – 1] was determined as 9.03. Importantly, the 1-MONs-MMM was also enantioselective toward a range of monofunctional chiral vapors, including α-pinene, limonene, fenchone, menthyl acetate, (−)-β-pinene, (+)-valencene, (−)-isolongifolene, and (−)-menthone with the EF values ranging from 1.03 to 4.71 (f and ). The trends of fluorescence quenching are consistent with the solution titration with 1-MON suspensions. For terpenoids containing a ketone group, the values are greater than those with a double bond and ester. Comparison of the fluorescent sensing of menthone and menthyl acetate proved that the ester group may prevent the phosphoric acid sites from binding to the substrates. Moreover, the MONs-MMM was enantioselective toward a variety of chiral bifunctional terpenoids in addition to the double bond (g and ). All substrates exhibit comparable and even better enantioselectivity than the solution titration. The EF values of β-citronellol and (−)-linalool can reach 8.26 and 9.03.

Control experiments indicated that the Me2 L-based MMM showed almost no fluorescence changes with (+)- or (−)-limonene and no enantioselectivity. To study the influence of membrane microstructures on the sensing behavior, we fabricated the dense MMM with 5.0 wt % MONs loading by modifying the phase-inversion method . From the sensing experiments, the I/I 0 ratios were found to be 6.10 and 14.90 for the (−)- and (+)-enantiomers of limonene, affording the EF value of 2.69, which was obviously smaller than 4.43 of the porous 1-MONs-MMM . This is presumably due to that the dense membrane inhibited the fast diffusion and transport of analytes, leading to a decrease of interactions between analytes and MONs. We further compared the sensing performance of the porous MMMs with different MONs loadings. With increasing the loadings of 1-MONs from 1.0 wt % to 5.0 wt %, 10.0 wt %, and 20.0 wt %, the enantioselectivity factors gradually increased from 3.55 to 4.43, 4.95, and 5.31, respectively . It is likely that the high loading of MONs is beneficial to the improvement of the selective sensing performance of MMMs. However, increasing the MONs loading to 40.0 wt % led to unsuccessful membrane preparation. Nonetheless, based on the above experimental result and literature reports, it can be speculated that the 2D MONs in the form of a pure crystalline membrane would exhibit outstanding performance in molecular sensing and separation since their unique pore structures and the ultrathin thickness would be fully utilized. Further research in this direction is in progress. Moreover, after each measurement, 1-MONs-MMM could be regenerated by washing with CH3CN three times and heating at 80 °C in a vacuum for about 2 h and directly reused for the next cycle of sensing without significant loss of enantioselectivity (EF = 9.07, 8.83, and 8.69 for runs 1–3 in sensing (−)-linalool, respectively) . After three cycles of sensing, the structure of the 1-MONs-MMM membrane remained almost unchanged, as evidenced by EDS mappings images .

The observed fluorescence quenching in both 1-MONs suspensions and 1-MONs-MMM may be ascribed to static enhancement upon the formation of a MOF-vapor adduct, which can induce changes in the structure of emitting species such as a change and/or rigidification of the conformation and excimer formation. Time-resolved fluorescence measurements of the membrane after exposure to the vapor of chiral (+)- and (−)-limonene showed only a slight change in decay rate, the fluorescence lifetimes (τ0, 2.31 vs 2.30 and 2.42 ns) remained almost unchanged . In the 1-MONs solution system, due to the short excited-state lifetime (<3 ns), low fluorophore concentration (10 μM), and quencher concentration (0–175 μM), the collision probability during the excited state lifetime of the fluorophore was very low, so the collisional quenching was negligible. Additionally, there is no overlap between the absorption (emission) spectra of 1-MONs and the emission (absorption) spectra of limonene , indicating no obvious electron or energy transfer between them. Further study is greatly needed to understand the mechanism of the stereoselective fluorescence quenching.

The alkene or alkene- and oxygen-containing functional groups are not easily targeted with synthetic receptors, and hence, there are limited reports on molecular recognitions of terpene and terpenoid with high enantioselectivity. Among several reported procedures for sensing chiral terpenes and terpenoids, electrochemical methods including organic field effect transistors are of great interest, but they are costly and time-consuming or have unsatisfactory selectivity. Chiral optical sensors are among the most logical choices for fast and simple detections of chiral vapors; but synthetically, they still face a challenge because enantiomers of volatile molecules generally cannot induce an obvious structure difference in chromophore cores, making it hard to be detected. Recent reports highlight the promise of porous frameworks including both MOFs and COFs (covalent organic frameworks) as optical sensors for various important substrates such as volatile organic molecules, explosives, and biomolecules, but their application in chiral recognition and sensing has not yet to be well studied. To the best of our knowledge, there is only one report on chiral COFs for enantioselective fluorescence sensing of terpenes and terpenoids, but where only five chiral odors can be recognized, namely α-pinene, fenchone, limonene, carvone, and terpinen-4-ol. Benefiting from the ultrathin single-crystalline nature, the Eu-MONs has been used for enantioselective fluorescence sensing of a large variety of terpenes and terpenoids having one or more functional groups, with the sensitivity and enantioselectivity comparable with the above-mentioned chiral COFs. The chiral sensing with the MONs should be broadly useful and applicable but not limited to 17 important terpenes and terpenoids, holding the potential to perform online enantiomer detection and discrimination.

1. Materials and general procedures

All reagents and solvents are commercially available and used without further purification. Elemental analyses were performed with an EA1110 CHNS-0 CE elemental analyzer. The FT-IR (KBr pellet) spectra were recorded 400 · 4000 cm-1region) on a Nicolet Magna 750 FT-IR spectrometer. The CD spectra were recorded on a J-800 spectropolarimeter (Jasco, Japan). Thermogravimetric analyses (TGA) were carried out in a N2atmosphere with a heating rate of (MATH)on a thermogravimetric analyzer (Q5000IR). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were collected on a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer using CuKradiation. The calculated PXRD patterns were produced using the Mercury program and single crystal reflection data. 1H, 13Cand 31PNMR experiments were carried out on a MERCURY plus 400 spectrometer operating at resonance frequencies of 400 MHz. The N2gas adsorption isotherms were measured using a Micrometritics ASAP 2020 system at 77Kwith liquid N2bath. (Before the measurement, the fresh crystals were washed with DMF for three times, and then were further soaked in acetone for solvent exchange with replacement of fresh acetone three times. Subsequently, the samples were evacuated at 100°Cfor 10 h.) Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) images were performed on a NOVA NanoSEM 230 instrument equipped with an energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were performed on a Talos F200X/TALOS F200X instrument. Atomic force microscope (AFM) images were obtained on an Environment Control Scanning Probe Microscope (Nanonavi E-Sweep). The samples for AFM measurements were prepared by placing a drop of the diluted nanosheet dispersion onto a fresh cleaved mica. Low-dose high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images were taken on a Cs-corrected FEI cubed Titan 60-300 electron microscope under 300 kV. Specimen searching, zone axis alignment, and prefocusing were conducted at (MATH)magnification. HRTEM images were acquired at (MATH)magnification by using a Gatan K2 direct-detection camera operated in the electron counting mode with the dose fractionation function. The detailed HRTEM image acquisition and processing (zone axis alignment, focus determination, and CTF-correction) methods have been presented in reference.1 The projected electrostatic potential was simulated by the QSTEM software (http://www.qstem.org), with point spread function width of 3 Å.

Single-Crystal X-ray Diffraction. Single-crystal XRD data were collected on a Bruker SMART Apex II CCD-based X-ray diffractometer with Mo-Kα radiation (MATH)0.71073 Å) at 273.15 K. We have collected several datasets for all MOFs, and the best dataset was used for structure solution and refinement. The empirical absorption correction was applied by using the SADABS program (G. M. Sheldrick, SADABS,

program for empirical absorption correction of area detector data; University of Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany, 1996). The structures were solved using direct method, and refined by full-matrix least-squares on F2by the SHELXTL-2015 software package. DFIX, SADI, FLAT, DANG, EADP and SIMU restrains were used to obtain reasonable parameters. In the compounds, all the non-H atoms were refined anisotropically. Contributions to scattering due to these highly disordered solvent molecules were removed using the SQUEEZE routine of PLATON. The structures w ere then refined again using the data generated. Crystal data and details of the data collection are given in Table S1, while the selected bond distances and angles are presented in Table S2. The CIF files have been deposited in the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (CCDC) under deposition number 2048848 (MOF 1), 2048849 (MOF 2) 2048850 (MOF 3).

2.4 Preparation of 1-MONs-MMM

The hybrid MMMs were prepared by the phase-inversion method. 1-MONs (MATH)5.0 wt , 10.0 wt and 20.0 wt ) was dispersed in anhydrous DMF (1.9 mL). The resulting solution was mixed with PES 600 mg) and the mixture was stirred for 2 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife at a given time. The glass plate was then put into deionized water and the free-standing MMM was peeled off from the glass surface. Pure PES and Me2L@PES membranes were prepared in a similar procedure.

The dense 1-MONs-MMM were prepared by the modifying phase-inversion method. 1-MONs (5.0 wt %) was dispersed in anhydrous DMF (1.9 mL). The resulting solution was mixed with PES 600 mg) and the mixture was stirred for 2 days to obtain a homogeneous suspension. The suspension was then poured on a flat glass surface with the help of a doctor blade knife, and then the solvent was evaporated at 100°Cfor 5 hours. The glass plate was put into water and the membrane was peeled off from the glass surface, producing the translucent and dense (S)-1-MONs@PES MMM (5.0 wt ).

2.5. General procedure for fluorescence sensing

The titration experiments were carried out by adding 50.0 µLsolution of substrates (MATH)in CH3CN) to a solution of 1-MONs or M e2 L(MATH)) in CH3CNevery two minutes. The excitation wavelengths are 302 nmand 307 nmfor MONs and Me2L, respectively.

Membrane sensing: The 1-MONs-MMM was carefully cut into 0.8 cm × 0.8 cm1 rectangles and kept in a desiccator. The membrane was then fixed into the inner surface of a quartz cuvette, 50.0 µLof each analyte was added into the bottom of the quartz cuvette. The quartz cuvette was immediately capped and sealed with parafilm, followed by time-dependent fluorescence test (λex = 290 nm)). The quenching efficiency was estimated using the formula (I0–I)/I0×100%, where IOand are the maximum fluorescence intensity of membrane before and after exposure to the analyte vapor, respectively.
